title: SVOLT launches series production of its semi-solid-state battery - electrive.com
content:
Chinese battery manufacturer SVOLT has begun series production of semi-solid-state batteries. The first batch of battery packs with 100 kWh capacity has rolled off the production line in Changzhou, Jiangsu Province. These are said to support fast charging with a charging rate of 6C.
Image: SVOLT
SVOLT Chairman Yang Hongxin announced the start of series production this week in a video published on Weibo. According to the announcement, SVOLT has produced the first batch of its so-called ‘Dragon Armor’ battery using series production methods. Hongxin also stated that the 100-kWh battery pack is being considered by ‘multiple’ customers and that details about the vehicles in which it will be used will follow soon.
For context: the ‘Dragon Armor’ battery is an energy storage system based on cells with a semi-solid electrolyte. Such semi-solid-state batteries represent a battery type positioned between traditional lithium-ion batteries with liquid electrolytes and solid-state batteries with fully solid electrolytes. They use a combination of liquid and solid materials in the electrolyte, often referred to as a solid-liquid hybrid. Battery manufacturers hope this technology can deliver improved safety, higher energy density, and a longer lifespan compared to conventional lithium-ion batteries.
Regarding the new SVOLT battery, the company reports that it features liquid cooling on both the top and bottom and supports up to 900 volts. The manufacturer specifies a charging rate of 6C, which, according to the datasheet, allows a range of around 500 kilometres to be recharged in twelve minutes. The lifespan is stated to exceed 3,000 cycles. However, the test conditions and the scope of the first production batch remain unmentioned. Hongxin continues to refrain from naming specific customers.
There are currently few semi-solid-state batteries on the market and even fewer solid-state batteries, which is why battery manufacturers are racing to take the lead in these technologies. SVOLT, currently the tenth-largest battery manufacturer in China, is now making a move. According to SVOLT CEO Yang Hongxin, 2026 will be the first year in which hybrid solid-liquid batteries gain broad acceptance and the technology experiences large-scale market introduction.
In mid-2025, the chairman
already spoke out
and announced test production for Q4 2025 and series production for 2027. According to the latest information, the start of series production has now taken place this autumn. Previous statements indicated that SVOLT’s first-generation semi-solid-state batteries would have an energy density of 300 Wh/kg. For a second generation, which is reportedly already in preparation, the company aims for a value of 360 Wh/kg.
According to an earlier report by
CN EV Post
, SVOLT will supply the semi-solid-state batteries, among other things, for the next-generation models of BMW’s Mini brand. A possible connection here is that SVOLT was spun off from the Chinese automotive group Great Wall Motor (GWM) in 2018, which, in a joint venture with BMW, produces the Mini Cooper Electric and the Mini Aceman. As early as 2023, there were also
rumours of an alleged billion-dollar deal
between BMW and SVOLT. That said, Mini has not yet been officially confirmed as one of the first customers for SVOLT’s semi-solid-state batteries.
SVOLT is also reportedly developing pure solid-state batteries. However, in May, Yang Hongxin stated that commercialisation will take a very long time. He believes that semi-solid-state batteries will represent a common technological path until this technology achieves large-scale mass production, especially since the production costs of semi-solid-state batteries are expected to be on par with those of conventional lithium-ion batteries with liquid electrolytes.

title: 10ISLC Special: Recycled lead has become US national security asset, says BCI – Batteries International
content: Recycled lead has become a strategic national security resource in the United States, with Washington increasingly focused on protecting domestic supplies as demand rises and growing volumes of spent batteries are exported, according to BCI. Speaking at the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference in Colombo, Susan Bernard, vice president of government relations and sustainability at BCI, said recent US trade policy developments could have significant implications for the movement of recovered lead and other battery materials across international borders. “Demand in the US is rising, while spent batteries are leaving the country at a higher rate,” she told delegates. With no domestic primary lead refining capacity, the US relies heavily on recycled lead and its integrated North American supply chain to meet the needs of battery manufacturers. Bernard said North America supplies approximately 85% of the lead required for battery manufacturing each year, with the remaining 15% sourced from trusted trading partners. The importance of that supply chain has become increasingly apparent as Washington expands its use of tariffs, trade measures and national security provisions to protect strategically important materials. On July 30, the US administration issued a presidential determination concerning export controls on recoverable minerals, including lead, tin and antimony. Bernard said the measure invoked the Defense Production Act and directed the Department of Commerce to review and implement measures relating to exports of these materials. The development signals a potentially significant shift in the treatment of spent batteries and recovered metals, which have traditionally moved across borders as part of established recycling and manufacturing supply chains. “Recycled lead is now a national security asset because it is a critical mineral. Export policy will reflect that, whether it is United States or at the plurilateral level,” Bernard said. BCI has advocated for lead to be recognised as a critical mineral since 2018, arguing that its importance to domestic battery manufacturing and energy infrastructure warrants greater attention from federal policymakers. Bernard explained that critical mineral designation can open access to federal funding through agencies including the Department of Energy and Department of Defense, while also bringing materials within the scope of national security trade provisions. However, she stressed that BCI’s position on exports is not intended to restrict legitimate international trade. The association has long supported the responsible recycling of spent batteries, regardless of where that processing takes place, while opposing exports to facilities known or suspected to use environmentally unsound practices. In 1999, BCI adopted a policy supporting higher recycling standards internationally, which was reaffirmed in 2019. Bernard said the association’s current priorities include stronger enforcement of existing export regulations, improved reporting of battery scrap movements and more reliable trade data to support discussions with policymakers. Better information on the quantities of spent batteries leaving the United States would help the industry demonstrate the potential consequences for domestic lead supplies and recycling operations. The wider policy environment is also becoming increasingly complex. Bernard said US trade policy had changed more rapidly over the past year than in previous decades, with overlapping tariff provisions creating considerable uncertainty for battery manufacturers, recyclers and suppliers. BCI now distributes a weekly tariff briefing to members which has grown to 41 pages, illustrating the scale of the regulatory changes affecting the industry. The association is also engaged in discussions surrounding the review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), which underpins the closely integrated North American battery supply chain. Bernard warned that changes to tariffs, trade agreements and export rules can have consequences throughout the industry, from smelting and recycling to battery production. For US battery manufacturers, the emerging issue is not simply the availability of lead globally, but the ability to retain reliable access to recovered material within a rapidly changing international trading system. And with Washington increasingly viewing recycled lead through the lens of national security, the movement of spent batteries across borders could become an important focus of future US trade policy. title: GXO to Deploy Digit 5 Robots in E-Commerce Fulfilment Sites
content:
GXO to Deploy Digit 5 Robots in E-Commerce Fulfilment Sites
Prioritise Us
on Google
GXO Logistics will deploy Agility Robotics' Digit 4 series robots (pictured) to two e-commerce fulfilment sites in the US from Q1 2027. Credit: Agility Robotics
GXO Logistics and Agility Robotics are rolling out Digit 4 humanoid robots to two US e-commerce fulfilment sites from early 2027 followed by Digit 5 units
GXO Logistics is expanding its partnership with Agility Robotics to deploy Digit humanoid robots at two additional US e-commerce fulfilment sites. The deployments are expected to begin in early 2027 at facilities in Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee. GXO will initially use Digit 4 units before transitioning to Digit 5 robots when the newer series becomes commercially available.
GXO Logistics has been an early adopter of robotics technology in its logistics operations. The agreement expands on the companies’ multi-year agreement in 2024 to deploy Agility Robotics’ Digit humanoid robots in a live GXO warehouse environment in Flowery Branch, Georgia. Digit units have moved more than 100,000 totes at the Flowery Branch facility, demonstrating the technology’s ability to perform repetitive material-handling tasks reliably in an active logistics environment.
“Innovation delivers its greatest value when it drives real-world results,” says GXO CEO
Patrick Kelleher
“With Digit surpassing 100,000 totes moved in a live environment, we're proving that humanoids can successfully create measurable value for our customers and a better working environment for our teams,” Patrick adds.
GXO Logistics is deploying Agility Robotics' Digit 4 series robots to its Statesville NC, and Lebanon TN e-commerce fulfilment sites. Credit: GXO Robotics
Early adopter of Digit 5
GXO and Agility Robotics expect deployments at the Statesville and Lebanon facilities to begin in early 2027 using Digit 4 series robots.
Since its first commercial deployments, Digit 4 has largely focused on automating tote-based material handling. The next-generation Digit 5 series will leverage Agility’s proprietary approach to physical AI-based capability training to add more manipulation skills and expand to cover a facility's full workflow: from depalletising goods as they arrive, to machine tending, kitting and sequencing, and quality inspection as items move through the facility, and finally palletising them for shipment as they leave.
Agility Robotics expects this to expand the scope of industries where the next-generation series can be deployed to include: electronics, distribution, reverse logistics, machinery and cold chain operations, including groceries. Agility's Digit 4 series robots are already deployed in
automotive
and fulfilment environments.
GXO Logistics has gained extensive experience of operating Digit 4 series robots at one of its facilities in Georgia.
Key facts about Digit 5 specifications
Payload: Up to 22.7kg
Runtime: Approximately 90 minutes
Charging: Approximately nine minutes
Run-to-charge ratio: 10:1
Weight: 129kg
Height: 1.81m
Reach: Up to 2.2m
Tooling: Swappable end-effectors with ISO-standard mounting flanges
Early access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with increasing availability over the following six to nine months for manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators.
“I’ve said before that repeat business is the truest measure of value in this industry. A customer expanding to new sites is the strongest proof a robot can offer that it’s earning its place on the floor,” comments Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility Robotics.
“The questions customers are asking us have changed. They’re no longer wondering whether humanoids can do real work. They’re deciding where to put them next,” Peggy concludes.
Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility. Credit: Peggy Johnson/LinkedIn
Humanoid robotics in logistics operations
Digit is described as the world's first commercially deployed humanoid robot. The unit combines traditional controls with AI-based learning methods and can be deployed in hours rather than weeks or months.
Each robot contains approximately 5,000 parts and is manufactured at Agility's RoboFab facility in Oregon, US, which has the capacity to produce 10,000 robots annually at peak production.
The current Digit 4 robot is designed to perform tasks including tote loading and unloading and tote recycling.
Because Digit is humanoid in form, it can navigate spaces designed for human workers, including standard shelving systems and narrow aisles, without requiring extensive facility modifications. This design approach allows manufacturers to integrate robotics into existing infrastructure.
Across its commercial operations and customer programs, Digit has accumulated more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation. That experience has informed the development of Digit 5, Agility’s next-generation robot unveiled on 15 September 2026, which is designed for cooperatively safe work in close proximity to people and will address a broader range of industrial workflows.
Safety requirements of robot deployment
Before the mobile humanoids are deployed to work alongside human operators in mixed environments, such as GXO’s logistics environments, Agility is collaborating with NVIDIA to support perception, safety development and certification.
Agility is the first launch partner for NVIDIA's Halos for Robotics platform, pairing Agility's systems with NVIDIA IGX Thor and Halos Core infrastructure, and is integrating
NVIDIA IGX Thor
and additional NVIDIA Halos models into its proprietary safe human detection system for Digit.
These integrations are intended to expand Digit’s current perception capabilities, support connections to a broader ecosystem, and facilitate Agility’s ongoing certification and deployment efforts.
Key companies and technology partners
1. GXO Logistics
: US$13.64bn
Employees
: 105,000
: Patrick Kelleher
GXO is a global contract logistics provider operating fulfilment, distribution and supply-chain facilities for major customers, as well as warehousing, e-commerce and reverse logistics services. It has adopted robotics across its operations and is expanding Agility Robotics’ Digit deployment from Flowery Branch to additional e-commerce sites in North Carolina and Tennessee.
2. NVIDIA
: US$215.94bn
Employees
: 42,000
: Jensen Huang
NVIDIA develops accelerated computing, AI, robotics and simulation technologies. NVIDIA supplies computing and physical-AI technologies supporting Agility’s next-generation robot, Digit 5, which is being developed with NVIDIA IGX Thor onboard compute and NVIDIA Halos safety models to support perception, human detection and safe operation around people. NVIDIA also provides robotics platforms, simulation pipelines and edge-AI technologies designed to support perception, training and deployment of intelligent machines.
3. Agility Robotics
Employees
: Peggy Johnson
Agility Robotics develops Digit, a mobile humanoid robot designed for material handling and industrial workflows. Its Digit platform combines physical AI, autonomous mobility and human-scale design. The company says Digit has accumulated more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation across commercial and customer programmes.

title: WCS & Hershey: Establishing Sustainable Cocoa Supply Chains
content:
WCS & Hershey: Establishing Sustainable Cocoa Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
The Hershey Company is strengthening supply chain resilience with US$2.5m commitment to the Wildlife Conservation Society. Credit: Getty
Hershey is committing to US$2.5m to Wildlife Conservation Society for sustainable cocoa project in Nigeria's Cross River State rainforest region
The Hershey Company has committed US$2.5m to the Wildlife Conservation Society as part of a four-year project in Cross River State, Nigeria. The partnership aims to
strengthen supply chain resilience
in a region where more than 100,000 households depend on cocoa farming for their livelihoods.
According to the Wildlife Conservation Society, the area contributes almost one third of Nigeria's cocoa exports.
The Cross River State contains Nigeria's largest remaining rainforest and serves as the country's most important cocoa-producing region. This concentration of production makes the region strategically important for maintaining stable cocoa supply chains.
Addressing supply chain vulnerabilities
The partnership between Hershey and WCS will focus on improving traceability across the cocoa supply chain to prevent deforestation. According to Tricia Brannigan, Vice President and Chief Procurement Officer for The Hershey Company, "The long-term resilience of cocoa depends on thriving farming communities and healthy landscapes."
The global cocoa sector faces production challenges including climate pressures and livelihood constraints for farmers. These factors could put pressure on forests and biodiversity, which could affect supply stability. Supply chain disruptions in key producing regions can have significant impacts on global cocoa availability and pricing.
The collaboration comes at a time when emerging market requirements, including EUDR, are creating
new compliance demands
for cocoa producers. The partnership will help farmers prepare for these requirements while reducing the risk of cocoa-driven deforestation.
“Nigeria is committed to building a sustainable cocoa sector that balances economic growth with forest protection," says Balarabe Abbas Lawal, Nigeria’s Federal Minister of Environment.
Balarabe Abbas Lawal, Nigeria’s Federal Minister of Environment. Credit: Federal Ministry of Environment
"This partnership between WCS and Hershey directly supports our national policy objectives by promoting deforestation‑free cocoa, improving farmer livelihoods and protecting endangered species. It demonstrates the value of aligning private sector investment with government priorities to secure long‑term supply stability and safeguard our forests."
Building production resilience
The partnership will promote climate-smart cocoa production and agroforestry practices. WCS will work with communities, federal and state government agencies, supply chain actors and civil society organisations on a landscape-level collaboration to
support deforestation-free cocoa production
and supply.
Ethan Budiansky, Sustainable Commodities Lead at WCS, adds "investment in sustainable cocoa cannot stop at the farm. We need to work across landscapes and ecosystems to improve farmer livelihoods, build more resilient cocoa production and protect forests that provide critical habitat for wildlife like gorillas and elephants."
The initiative will help farmers improve productivity through regenerative agriculture practices. Hershey is committing to support one million hectares of
regenerative agriculture and restorative or protective practices
. These approaches are designed to enhance soil health and improve long-term yield stability.
The partnership will also strengthen forest protection and community-based natural resource management. These efforts could help ensure the long-term viability of cocoa production in the region while maintaining the ecological systems that support agricultural productivity.
Ethan Budiansky, Sustainable Commodities Lead at WCS
Landscape-level supply chain approach
WCS builds on more than 20 years of conservation work in Cross River State through this partnership. The organisation works with communities and government agencies to protect wildlife habitats, strengthen natural resource governance and support livelihoods.
According to Inaoyom Imong, Country Director at WCS Nigeria, "Through a landscape-scale approach, we will help farmers improve productivity, build climate resilience and access new market opportunities while safeguarding the globally important forests and wildlife of the Cross River landscape."
The Cross River landscape supports rich biodiversity, including Cross River gorillas, Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzees, drill monkeys and forest elephants. All species are listed as critically endangered.
Joe Walston, Executive Vice President of WCS Global Program, explains, "Too often, wildlife conservation and agricultural production compete. But when we get it right, we can achieve both."
The initiative is designed to be refined and expanded into other cocoa regions in Nigeria and beyond. The partnership will demonstrate how farming communities,
resilient cocoa supply chains
and healthy forests can co-exist.
Angela Tejada Chavez, Director of Sustainable Sourcing Cocoa for The Hershey Company
Angela Tejada Chavez, Director of Sustainable Sourcing Cocoa for The Hershey Company, adds Hershey "is working alongside farmers, communities, government stakeholders and supply chain partners to improve livelihoods, protect forests and help create a more resilient future for cocoa and the communities that grow it."
The partnership includes efforts to promote climate-smart cocoa production and agroforestry, strengthen forest protection and community-based natural resource management and improve
traceability across the cocoa supply chain
to stop deforestation.
Ethan has spent much of his career working with cocoa and chocolate companies and developing landscape collaborations across West Africa. According to him, "our partnership with The Hershey Company will drive action on the ground and demonstrate how cocoa and conservation can thrive in the same landscape."
Key partners
The Hershey Company
Kirk Tanner
Pennsylvania, US
The Hershey Company is a leading North American chocolate and confectionery manufacturer, founded in 1894 by Milton Hershey. The company produces iconic brands including Hershey's, Reese's, Kit Kat, and Kisses. Beyond candy, Hershey has expanded into snacks and beverage products. The company emphasizes sustainable cocoa sourcing and community development, maintaining strong ties to its Pennsylvania hometown where it operates Hersheypark and supports various philanthropic initiatives.
Wildlife Conservation Society
Adam F. Falk
New York, US
Founded in 1895, the Wildlife Conservation Society manages the Bronx Zoo and works globally to save wildlife and wild places. Operating in over 60 countries, WCS combines zoo management with field conservation, protecting species from gorillas to marine life. The organization conducts scientific research, manages protected areas, and partners with local communities. WCS's integrated approach connects urban wildlife education through its New York facilities with critical conservation work worldwide.

title: How Manufacturers are Automating Procurement with AI and EDI
content:
How Manufacturers are Automating Procurement with AI and EDI
Prioritise Us
on Google
The use of AI and automation in manufacturing is increasing. Credit: Getty Images
JAGGAER, GDP and Groves explore how manufacturers can use AI and EDI to reduce manual procurement work and progress toward greater autonomy
In today's market, procurement and supply chain operations are changing.
Manufacturing leaders have moved away
As demand and risk increase, modern tools help create greater efficiency and productivity throughout processes. With increased visibility and resilience, organisations are able to increase supplier adoption and undertake a wider business transformation.
Michael Mihalik, Director of Professional Services at Groves & Company, Michael Rösch, SVP Global Direct Advisory at JAGGAER and Wolfgang Winstel, VP of Sales at GDP offer insights into how manufacturers are seeing results form the integration of AI and EDI.
Why has procurement automation become a priority for manufacturers?
Michael M:
What we often see is that procurement teams simply have too much manual work. They are dealing with more suppliers, more data and more internal requests, but many processes still run through emails, spreadsheets and manual follow-ups. Usually the pressure to change comes when this starts slowing the business down. Automation helps standardise the process, reduce manual work and gives the team more time to focus on suppliers, risk and the actual business needs.
What does the journey from manual to autonomous procurement look like?
Michael R:
It is a progression, not a single switch. An AI assistant can first help users find information and navigate processes. Task-specific agents can then support or perform defined activities with human oversight. As organisations build confidence, they can consider greater autonomy for appropriate use cases. The pace depends on data readiness, controls, business value and risk.
Why do manual order confirmations remain a problem when many manufacturers already use EDI?
Wolfgang:
EDI works well for established, high-volume connections, but suppliers differ in size and digital maturity. On average,
manufacturers have 15% of their suppliers use EDI
, and 30% use a supplier portal. That leaves 55% of low-volume suppliers sending order confirmations by email, as PDFs, spreadsheets, scans or messages in the email body. Procurement teams must interpret and check these responses before updating the purchasing process, creating a sizeable manual workload.
Wolfgang Winstel, VP of Sales at GDP
How do JAGGAER and GDP combine AI and EDI to address that gap?
Michael R:
JAGGAER provides the procurement and supplier collaboration environment. GDP's EDI capability and AI Plugin help interpret unstructured supplier responses and turn relevant information into structured data for validation and onward processing. The aim is to extend automation to suppliers who do not have a conventional EDI connection while retaining checks and exception handling.
How does this approach differ from traditional OCR?
Wolfgang:
Traditional OCR typically extracts text and requires templates and training for different document layouts, which is a tedious process because it always needs to be adapted to changes in format and new suppliers. GDP's AI Plugin interprets information from a broader range of supplier formats, including PDFs, scans, spreadsheets and email bodies, without any training or templates. This allows for a quick setup and rollout and low maintenance once in production.
What is the potential business impact of automating emailed documents?
Michael R:
The value depends on document volume and the effort required to process each one. For illustration, 40,000 order confirmations at five minutes each amount to roughly 3,333 hours of manual work per year. At an assumed labor cost of US$30 per hour, that represents about US$100,000 in annual handling time. Automation can reduce routine processing and direct employees toward exceptions that require judgment.
Faster turnaround and more consistent data
may also improve supplier communication.
Michael Rösch, SVP Global Direct Advisory at JAGGAER
Most companies already use AI solutions or are going to in the near future. How does the GDP AI Plugin differentiate?
Wolfgang:
It would be very easy to use a generic AI solution and have it extract the content of a document. Our solution is embedded in a procurement environment and understands the context of the data fields. Also, we download every related PO from Jaggaer and compare the values in order to flag all changes to the original order. This way we can ensure that Jaggaer's "exception handling" and all attached processes still work.
Where should a manufacturer start, and how should it choose a pilot?
Michael M:
We normally start by looking for a process that causes a lot of manual work and where the impact is easy to measure. Good pilots are usually processes with enough volume, clear pain points and a manageable number of suppliers or users. Before starting, we look at the current process, the available data and the integrations that are needed. We apply what we call rapid prototyping. We start with an initial design, build a first version and let users test it in a realistic scenario. Based on their feedback, we adjust and improve the automation step by step.
This repeated cycle of development, testing and improvement helps the solution mature quickly and makes sure it works in practice, not just on paper. The pilot should be small enough to control, but large enough to show whether the solution really improves cycle time, quality or manual effort. A good pilot does not need to be big. It needs to solve a real problem, deliver a measurable result and give the business confidence to take the next step.
Michael Mihalik, Director of Professional Services at Groves & Company
What role do people play as procurement becomes more autonomous?
Michael M:
Change management is just as important as the automation itself. A good solution will not create value if users are not involved, informed and clear on how the new process works, who owns it, who makes decisions and when someone needs to step in. In marketing, there is the well known “Rule of 7”, the idea that people need several touchpoints before they take action. We experience the same in our transformation projects. A single training at the end is not enough. The more users are involved through communication, prototypes, testing and feedback before go live, the more familiar they become with both the process and their role in it, and the higher the chance they will actually adopt it.
How should manufacturers measure whether the transformation is working?
Michael R:
Start with a baseline, then track the share of documents processed without intervention, exception rates, handling and cycle times, data accuracy, supplier coverage and employee time spent on routine work. Pair these measures with user and supplier feedback. The result should be a
faster, more reliable process
that lets procurement spend more time on higher-value work.

title: Culina Announces New CEO After Brand Unification
content:
Culina Announces New CEO After Brand Unification
Prioritise Us
on Google
Fabian Koehler (right) is set to become Culina Group CEO on 1 February 2027, succeeding Liam McElroy (left) following the completion of the unification of Culina's subsidiaries under Culina branding
Liam McElroy set to be replaced as Culina Group CEO shortly after announcing unification of subsidiaries under Culina branding
Culina Group has announced that current Chief Executive Officer Liam McElroy will be succeeded by Fabian Koehler, the Deputy CEO, with effect from 1 February 2027.
The announcement of the executive appointment follows shortly after Culina group announced that it was unifying its subsidiaries under a single brand: Culina.
The announcement in mid October affected established logistics brand names including Culina Logistics, IPS, Stobart, Great Bear, Fowler Welch, Warrens, CML, Stobart Europe, IRF and iForce.
Culina will operate through five specialist divisions: Chilled & Fresh Logistics, Contract Logistics, Transport Logistics, Integrated Packing Services and International Logistics.
Fabian Köhler, Deputy Group CEO at Culina Group Limited (Credit: LinkedIn)
New CEO brings European road haulage experience
Fabian joined Culina in November 2024, when he first served as an external advisor, before moving into the Deputy CEO role in January 2025.
Before joining Culina, Fabian occupied senior leadership roles in Kuehne+Nagel's European road logistics division.
As Deputy CEO, Fabian has played a key role in shaping and delivering the One Culina three-year strategy and the group’s recent transformation journey.
The strategy has helped create a more unified and streamlined company by strengthening collaboration across the organisation and building a powerful platform for growth as one of the UK's leading independent and specialist supply chain partners.
As part of this leadership change, Liam McElroy will continue to support the group in a non-executive capacity.
As Non-Executive Director, Liam McElroy will continue to support the delivery of the company’s commercial priorities, providing strategic insight and guidance during the company’s continued transformation.
In October 2026, Culina announced that the company was unifying its subsidiaries under a single brand: Culina.
Incoming and outgoing CEOs on Culina’s transformation
Culina is one of the UK’s largest privately owned logistics supply chain partners, providing specialist expertise to deliver market-leading service, capacity and value for several globally-recognised brands.
Operating across chilled and fresh logistics, contract logistics, transport, specialist co-packing and international operations, Culina supports a diverse range of goods across multiple industries.
Committed to sustainable, efficient and innovative logistics, the company aims to set the benchmark for integrated
supply chain
excellence across the UK and beyond.
Discussing his appointment as lead executive, Fabian says: “I am honoured to take on the role of CEO and look forward to working with our colleagues, customers and partners as we continue to build on the strong foundations that have been created.”
He adds that Culina is a “remarkable business with exceptional people” and praises its “deep expertise and an unrivalled customer proposition”.

title: Sykeruns X7 electric dirt bike review: A lot of power for surprisingly little money
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Electric Dirt Bikes
Micah Toll
| Oct 27 2026 - 8:56 am PT
The mini electric dirt bike market has exploded over the last few years, with seemingly countless new brands offering everything from pint-sized electric pit bikes to surprisingly powerful off-road machines. The Sykeruns X7 falls somewhere in the middle, offering enough power to get into some serious trouble while keeping the price relatively approachable.
I’ve spent some time now riding the X7, and while it certainly isn’t the most refined electric dirt bike I’ve tested, there’s enough to like about what you’re getting for the money.
In fact, if you’re looking for a reasonably powerful electric dirt bike for recreational trail riding without spending several thousand dollars, this might be worth a closer look.
Sykeruns X7: What are we working with here?
The Sykeruns X7 is a compact electric dirt bike featuring a 5,500W peak-rated motor, which translates to around 7.4 horsepower. That’s quite a bit of power for a bike at this
price point of $1,699
, especially considering that many similarly priced electric two-wheelers are significantly less powerful. Oh, and for our readers, we’ve gotten you set up with a 20% discount. Just use code ELECTREK20 to drop the price down to an impressive $1,359!
Sykeruns claims a top speed of 57 mph (92 km/h), though since this is an off-road only bike, you’ll rarely get the chance to put that claim to the test. I certainly didn’t, as I didn’t have a long enough and flat enough stretch of trail where I felt comfortable hitting nearly highway speeds on a low-cost e-moto.
The battery is a 60V 27Ah pack, providing 1,620 Wh of capacity. Sykeruns claims up to 60 miles (96 km) of range, though as with virtually every electric dirt bike, your actual range will depend heavily on how aggressively you’re riding. Fast trail riding, steep climbs, and repeated hard acceleration can eat through battery capacity much more quickly than leisurely cruising. Suffice it to say that you’ll likely not see the 60 mile figure in real world scenarios, but that’s still a fairly large battery.
The bike rolls on a 17-inch front wheel and 14-inch rear wheel, both wrapped in knobby off-road tires. Hydraulic disc brakes handle stopping duties, while an inverted suspension fork and rear monoshock help smooth out the bumps.
At 143 lb (65 kg), the X7 isn’t exactly featherweight, but it’s also far from being a full-size electric motorcycle.
How does the Sykeruns X7 actually ride?
The first thing I was surprised about with the X7 is that it offers a pretty decent amount of performance for the money. There’s enough power here to have some real fun, and the bike doesn’t feel like one of those underpowered mini electric motorcycles that struggles once you get beyond casual neighborhood speeds.
That said, I wouldn’t describe the acceleration as mind-blowing, either. We’re not talking about the kind of explosive power delivery you’d get from a high-end electric dirt bike costing several times as much. Instead, the X7 delivers a healthy amount of acceleration that feels appropriate for a recreational off-road machine.
And let’s be real here, that’s probably what most people shopping in this budget category are looking for.
The suspension is another area where the X7 earns a passing grade without necessarily winning any awards. The front fork and rear shock do their jobs, absorbing the bumps and ruts you’d expect to encounter on typical trails. It’s nothing I’d call plush, but I could see it doing light jumps with minimal air time.
Would I want to take this thing to a motocross track and start launching it off massive jumps? Not particularly. The suspension doesn’t have the premium feel or sophisticated damping of more expensive machines.
But for general trail riding, exploring dirt roads, and the occasional overlanding shenanigans, it’s perfectly serviceable. Not every electric dirt bike needs to be a competition-ready machine, and the X7 seems comfortable occupying that more recreational category.
I was also pleasantly surprised by the tires, which seem well suited to the bike’s intended purpose. The knobby tread offers a reasonable amount of grip for off-road riding, and I didn’t find myself immediately wishing for a tire upgrade.
The overall size is worth mentioning, too. This isn’t a particularly large electric dirt bike, but at my modest 5’7” (170 cm) height, I felt comfortable on it. The riding position didn’t feel overly cramped, and the bike was manageable enough that I didn’t feel like I was wrestling with an oversized machine.
Taller riders might find it a bit more compact than they’d prefer, but for average-height riders, the proportions seem reasonable.
Build quality: Good enough, but nothing extraordinary
If there’s one area where the X7 reminds you of its budget-friendly $1,699 price tag, it’s the overall level of refinement.
Nothing about the bike struck me as particularly premium. The components, finishes, and general construction are more in line with what I’d expect from a relatively inexpensive electric dirt bike.
But that’s not necessarily a criticism. There’s a difference between something feeling inexpensive and something feeling inadequate, and the X7 generally stays on the acceptable side of that line.
The controls are straightforward, the digital display provides the basic information you need, and the overall package feels focused on delivering usable performance rather than impressing riders with fancy features.
The grippy hydraulic brakes are also a welcome inclusion, especially considering the speeds this bike is capable of reaching. With a machine that can approach highway speeds, having proper motorcycle-style braking hardware is important.
Of course, long-term durability is a separate question. Budget electric dirt bikes don’t always have the same track record, parts availability, or established dealer networks as the more recognizable motorcycle brands. That’s something worth considering before purchasing, particularly if you plan to ride hard or frequently.
One important warning: This is NOT a street-legal e-bike
One thing I appreciate about the Sykeruns X7 is that the company makes its intended use fairly clear.
There’s a large red warning sticker on the bike explaining that it’s intended for off-road use only. That’s a good thing, especially in today’s market, where the lines between electric bicycles, electric dirt bikes, and electric motorcycles are becoming increasingly blurred, despite laws existing to keep these types of bikes out of the bike lane and off of public roads.
The X7 is absolutely not an electric bicycle. It doesn’t have pedals, it produces several thousand watts of power, and it’s capable of speeds far beyond anything permitted under electric bicycle regulations.
It’s an off-road electric motorcycle, plain and simple.
Interestingly, though, Sykeruns has equipped the bike with features like a tail light and turn signals, which could potentially give some riders the wrong impression.
Those are certainly useful features on a motorcycle, but they don’t magically make a vehicle street legal. Without the necessary certification, registration, and other road-use requirements, the X7 remains an off-road-only machine.
I worry that some buyers might see those lights and assume they can ride the bike around town like a small electric motorcycle. That’s not the case, and it’s important to understand that distinction before buying one.
Electrek’s Take
After spending time with the Sykeruns X7, my biggest takeaway is that this is a reasonably capable electric dirt bike at a pretty compelling price.
It’s not the best electric dirt bike I’ve ever ridden. The suspension is fairly basic, the build quality is unremarkable, and there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about the design.
(or $1,359 if you use the code ELECTREK20 to take 20% off!), you’re getting a 5.5 kW peak-rated electric motorcycle with a sizable battery, proper off-road tires, hydraulic brakes, and enough performance to have some genuine fun on the trails.
That’s not a bad deal.
I wouldn’t say that the X7 here is trying to compete with
more up-market electric dirt bikes
And that’s really where I think the X7 makes the most sense.
If you’re an experienced dirt bike rider looking for a highly refined machine with excellent suspension and premium components, you’ll probably want to keep shopping.
But if you’re someone who wants a fun electric dirt bike for exploring private property, cruising around trails where motorized riding is permitted, or just enjoying some recreational off-road riding without spending a fortune, the Sykeruns X7 offers a pretty reasonable package.
It doesn’t need to be amazing at everything. At this price, being pretty good at most things is already an accomplishment.

title: Korean police book 80 Tesla drivers over illegal FSD unlock devices
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Fred Lambert
| Oct 27 2026 - 8:43 am PT
Seoul police have booked 80 people for using aftermarket devices to switch on Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” in cars that aren’t allowed to run it in South Korea. Officers also seized 21 of the devices.
The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency announced the case on Tuesday. It’s the largest enforcement action yet against the FSD “jailbreak” hardware that has spread through China, Europe, and Korea over the past year.
Police say the suspects either imported the unlock modules from Europe and China or made their own. One plugged a European-made unit into his own Tesla. Another, an IT worker, built his device with information he found on GitHub.
Suspects also swapped advice online on how to unlock FSD and how to stop the car from keeping any record that it had been activated.
They’re charged under Korea’s Motor Vehicle Management Act, which bans unauthorized software changes that can affect a vehicle’s safety. The penalty is up to two years in prison or a fine of up to 20 million won (about $15,000).
The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport asked police to look into it back in April after finding signs of unauthorized activation. A police official told
Korea JoongAng Daily
that “safety risks were confirmed,” including the possibility of FSD misreading driving conditions. The investigation is ongoing, with police consulting the ministry and the Korea Transportation Safety Authority on the technical side.
Most Korean Teslas can’t legally run FSD
Tesla launched FSD (Supervised) in South Korea in late 2025, but only on US-built vehicles: Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck. Those cars are exempt from Korean safety certification under the Korea-US free trade agreement. The Model 3 and Model Y, which Tesla ships to Korea from Giga Shanghai, haven’t cleared Korea’s safety standards for the feature.
And those two models are the bulk of the fleet. Citing Carisyou Data Lab, Korea JoongAng Daily reports that 47,458 of the 229,311 Teslas on Korean roads as of August, or 20.7%, can legally use FSD.
That number doesn’t match the government’s own count from a few months earlier. In May, data released by lawmaker Park Yong-gap showed just 4,292 of 180,684 registered Teslas (2.4%) were eligible: 2,708 Model X, 1,193 Model S, and 391 Cybertruck. Either way, the vast majority of Korean Tesla owners can’t legally use FSD, and some of them
paid over $6,000 for it anyway
The hardware is the same, which is why the hack works. The modules plug into the car’s CAN bus and get around the regional software lock.
Tesla has been fighting the devices itself. In April, it started remotely detecting them and stripping FSD from affected cars, warned owners they’d be fully liable for any crash and could lose warranty coverage, and permanently banned some Chinese owners from FSD.
Electrek’s Take
It’s easy to see why people do this. Picture a Korean owner of a Shanghai-built Model Y who paid for FSD, watching the Model X next door run the same software on the same computer. That’s frustrating.
Tesla sold FSD to owners of cars it had no regulatory path to enable in Korea, the same way it sold “Full Self-Driving” in Europe for years while approval kept slipping. It only
dropped the name there this month
after Germany pushed back. Sell a feature people can’t legally use and you create the market for the jailbreak.
Korea has now shown it will actually prosecute. So will Tesla refund the Korean owners who bought a feature their cars may never be allowed to run?

title: Musk declares Tesla Robotaxi win over Waymo, but Waymo still drives 7x more
content:
Tesla Robotaxi
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Oct 27 2026 - 7:21 am PT
Waymo vs Tesla driverless miles per week, all markets (Credit: Robotaxi Tracker)
Elon Musk says Tesla’s Robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest” after Tesla’s driverless fleet logged 438,000 miles in Austin in a single week, edging past Waymo’s 406,000 weekly average in the city.
That’s one city, one week, and a Waymo figure that’s four months old. Across the US, Waymo still drives about seven times more driverless miles than Tesla every week.
Where the chart comes from
The chart going around comes from
Robotaxi Tracker
, a community project that pulls driverless mileage from each company’s own reports: Tesla’s weekly Robotaxi safety report and Waymo’s quarterly Safety Impact data hub.
Jason Scharf posted the Austin view on X with the comment that “the battle for Autonomous Austin might already be over.” Musk replied overnight: “It was never a real contest.”
The Austin data is real –albeit with some caveats. In the week ending October 18, Tesla reported 438,000 miles with no safety monitor aboard in Austin, up 30% from the week before. Waymo averaged about 406,000 miles a week in Austin in the second quarter.
But the tracker’s own caption explains the catch. Tesla’s figure is its latest week. Waymo’s is an average of April through June, because Waymo publishes about three months after each quarter ends. So Musk is comparing Tesla’s best week ever to Waymo’s spring.
The national picture isn’t close
Switch the same chart to “All markets” and the story flips.
Waymo averaged 3.90 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026. Tesla did 558,000 miles in its best week. Waymo’s Phoenix, Bay Area, and Los Angeles markets each drive more miles per week on their own than Tesla’s entire network.
Cumulative numbers are even more lopsided. Waymo has logged 271.3 million rider-only miles since 2020, including 50.7 million in Q2 alone, as we covered when
Waymo released its latest safety data
. Tesla has 3.11 million driverless miles since January 22, 2026. Waymo drove more than that in a single week.
And Tesla’s total leans almost entirely on one city:
Tesla Robotaxi market
Driverless miles, week to Oct 18
Austin accounts for 79% of Tesla’s weekly driverless miles. Houston, Tampa, Orlando, and Miami combined did about 25,000 miles. Waymo’s smallest tracked market, Atlanta, averaged 250,000 a week in Q2.
Tesla flooded Austin with Cybercabs
The Austin surge has an obvious cause. Tesla launched public Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3.
According to Robotaxi Tracker’s count of the Texas DMV automated-vehicle list, Tesla now has 463 Cybercabs registered in Texas, 337 of them added in the last 30 days. That’s 48% of the 970 autonomous vehicles Tesla has registered in the state.
Tesla isn’t hiding the strategy. On the Q3 earnings call last week, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI software, said the company wants to “swarm Austin with Cybercabs everywhere.” Musk said the Austin Cybercab fleet had grown “by a factor of 10” in about a month.
So Tesla dumped hundreds of new, company-owned cars into one metro and the miles went up. That’s fleet deployment. It doesn’t show the software can do what Waymo does in 15 cities, and Tesla can’t repeat it everywhere at once.
Still limited by safety, by Tesla’s own admission
The bigger problem is what the cars are allowed to do.
On the same earnings call, Elluswamy described the service as constrained by the software, not by regulators. He said that if there’s “the slightest possible risk at all,” Tesla doesn’t take it on, and that the limits are “technology driven” for now. Service hours only recently stretched from 9 p.m. toward 2 a.m., and he listed highways, “higher speed roads,” 24/7 operation, and more weather conditions as things Tesla still has to unlock.
You can see those limits in the rides. Tesla Robotaxis don’t take highways, and riders report they avoid at-grade railroad crossings. In September, a rider
had a 10-minute Cybercab trip in Austin turn into a 70-minute detour
because the car drove south through East Austin until it found a bridge over the rail line, instead of taking MoPac.
That matters for this comparison, too. Miles is a flattering metric when your car takes the long way. A trip that should cover a few miles and instead loops across town logs a lot more mileage for the same rider.
Waymo, meanwhile, has been taking riders on freeways in Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles since November 2025.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due: Tesla’s driverless miles are growing fast, 30% in a single week, and Austin now has a real Tesla fleet carrying the public without anyone in the driver’s seat. A year ago, that wasn’t the case.
But “never a real contest” is a strange thing to say when you’re behind by 7x on weekly miles and 87x on cumulative miles, and your one win depends on comparing your newest week to your rival’s data from last spring.
What stands out to us is the type of autonomy Tesla is deploying. In 2020, Musk wrote that “Waymo is impressive, but a highly specialized solution,” and that Tesla’s approach was “a general solution.” For years, Tesla fans dismissed Waymo as a geofenced system that only worked in mapped areas with lots of restrictions.
Now look at Tesla’s Robotaxi: geofenced, no highways, avoiding railroad crossings, taking 70 minutes for 10-minute trips, and limited by hours because the software isn’t ready for anything with “the slightest possible risk.” By Musk’s own old definition, that’s a highly specialized solution. Waymo is the one driving on freeways now.

BYD is better known for its low-cost electric cars, like

The Chinese auto giant has greatly expanded its portfolio over the past few months and years. BYD now offers everything from entry-level EVs to three-row flagship SUVs, pickup trucks, electric supercars, and just about everything in between.
BYD has three sub-brands: Denza, FangChengBao, and Yangwang. It also has two main families under the BYD brand: the Dynasty and Ocean series.
Yangwang sits at the top of BYD’s brand hierarchy and showcases its latest breakthrough technologies.
Previously, Yangwang vehicles debuted on BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering a whopping 1,300 horsepower and featuring its
intelligent body control system, which enables the vehicle to “dance,” jump, and drive on three wheels.
BYD Yangwang flagship sedan prototype (Source: Hu Xiaoqing)
For its next model, BYD is pushing further into the elite segment to take on ultra-luxury brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Maybach.
BYD revealed the name of its flagship ultra-luxury EV for the first time on Tuesday: the Yangwang Altior, along with a new teaser of the partially uncovered executive sedan.

Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing said the name was chosen as an independent Chinese-English naming scheme. In China, it goes by DingYao. The “Ding” symbolizes stability and endurance, while “Yao” signifies radiant brilliance, or shining brightly like a star in the sky.
The English name Altior comes from Latin for “higher,” representing Yangwang’s relentless pursuit of ever-greater heights.
The new teaser comes after Hu

of the new Yangwang executive sedan testing for the first time last month.
BYD Yangwang flagship sedan prototype (Source: Hu Xiaoqing)
Although it was disguised, it appeared to be about the same shape and size as the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom. Local reports indicate it will be around 5,500 mm (216″) long.
HU confirmed for the first time last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China.
BYD has not yet revealed a specific launch date, but the Yangwang sedan could make its first appearance as early as next week. According to
CarNewsChina
, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD is aiming to reveal the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5.
Yangwang flagship electric sedan (Source: Zheng Yu)
Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said the new model will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” but didn’t reveal specifics.
Although details are still limited, the ultra-luxury sedan was shown at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it will support megawatt flash charging.
It also features rear-hinged coach doors, a first for BYD. The flagship EV will reportedly be the first to feature BYD’s solid-state batteries.
BYD executive vice president Stella Li said during an interview with
last month that the company’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027.
Li said BYD is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery technology and its commercialization, and the company plans to prove it next year.
BYD Yangwang executive sedan prototype testing (Source: Zheng Yu)
BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, plans to begin production of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in 2027. It will initially be produced in limited batches, then scale to mass production closer to the end of the decade.
While BYD has yet to confirm it, introducing the new battery tech in a flagship model would make sense.
The executive sedan is expected to debut around November 5. Prices are rumored to start in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000.
Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The brand also sells the U8 (and U8L), a plug-in hybrid luxury off-road SUV, and the U9, a fully electric super-coupe.
The extended U8L is Yangwang’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

title: Ford's new sub-$30K electric truck can power your home for a lot less
content:
Bidirectional Charging
virtual power plant
Ford Fathom
Michelle Lewis
| Oct 27 2026 - 6:00 am PT
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
Ford wants to make powering your home with an EV a lot cheaper. Its upcoming sub-$30,000 Fathom electric truck will feature a new bidirectional charging system that ditches the need for an expensive external inverter.
Arriving in 2027, the Fathom will be the first EV from a US automaker priced below $30,000 that can deliver more than 10 kW of AC power to a home without a separate wall-mounted inverter.
And Ford says it’s cutting the cost of the other equipment needed for home backup power, too.
How Ford’s cheaper bidirectional charging works
EV batteries store electricity as direct current (DC), but our homes use alternating current (AC). To send power from an EV battery into a house, traditionally, that meant installing a pricey external inverter.
Ford has come up with a different approach for its new Universal EV Platform, which will underpin the Fathom.
After acquiring startup Auto Motive Power in 2023, Ford redesigned its bidirectional charging system from the ground up. Instead of relying on a separate wall-mounted inverter, it built one directly into the truck’s E-box, one of the vehicle’s five main modules.
Fewer parts mean lower costs, and Ford says the savings will extend to the home charging equipment, too.
Fathom owners will have two ways to use the truck’s battery to power their homes.
Ford’s Home Power Station and Home Backup Panel. Photo: Ford
Home Power Management
will let owners charge their truck when electricity rates are low, then use that stored power at home when rates are higher. That could mean real savings for households on time-of-use electricity plans. They’ll need Ford’s new Home Power Station, which the company expects to cost about half as much as its first-generation bidirectional charger.
Home Backup Power
will let the truck keep the lights on during an outage. For that, owners will need both the Home Power Station and Ford’s Home Backup Panel. Ford says the backup hardware should cost at least 60% less than its first-generation equipment.
Ford hasn’t released prices for either piece of hardware, so we don’t yet know what a complete home installation will cost.
But pairing a sub-$30,000 electric truck with substantially cheaper home power equipment could make bidirectional charging a lot more appealing.
Ford is getting utilities involved early
Making the hardware cheaper is one thing. Making sure utilities can handle thousands of EVs that send electricity back into homes and potentially the grid is another.
Ford formed a working group in July with American Electric Power, BC Hydro, Consumers Energy, Exelon, and Pacific Gas and Electric. They’re working on making it easier for customers to connect bidirectional EVs before the Fathom arrives next year.
For example, someone using their truck solely for home backup power during an outage shouldn’t have to go through the same approval process as someone sending electricity to the grid.
The group is also looking at how to update utility procedures to accommodate newer bidirectional charging standards and make it easier for EV owners to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs). In other words, the batteries in parked EVs could become a useful source of electricity when the grid needs it most.
Ford says the Fathom’s system is designed to meet applicable UL 1741 requirements and IEEE 1547 interconnection standards. It also uses SAE J3068 communications technology, which Ford says helps reduce charger costs.
The idea is to get the technical requirements and utility processes sorted out before affordable bidirectional EVs start arriving in much larger numbers.
Electrek’s Take
Affordable EVs already offer some form of bidirectional power. Two of the cheapest electric cars in the US, the Chevy Bolt and Nissan Leaf, are both available for under $30,000.
The Bolt supports
vehicle-to-home
(V2H) power through GM Energy equipment, while the Leaf offers
vehicle-to-load
(V2L) capability through an external device plugged into its charging port.
Ford’s system takes things much further. It can deliver more than 10 kW of AC power to a home without an expensive external inverter, and Ford says the rest of the equipment will cost considerably less, too.
That’s a pretty compelling proposition, especially for people who live in areas prone to power outages or have electricity plans with higher peak-hour rates.
There are still some unknowns. Ford hasn’t announced the final hardware prices, and installation costs will vary. Plus, utility rules need to catch up if EV owners are going to take full advantage of bidirectional charging.
But this seems to be going in the right direction. If automakers can bring costs down and the industry can agree on consistent standards, having an EV that doubles as a home battery could eventually become a normal part of EV ownership rather than an expensive bonus feature.

title: Lectric launches XP Lite3 e-bike, the new best low-cost model in the US
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 27 2026 - 5:30 am PT
Lectric eBikes, the largest electric bike company in the US by just about any metric you can measure, has just unveiled its latest model: the
Lectric XP Lite3
. And with a starting price of just
, the new lightweight folding electric bike is continuing the company’s tradition of packing surprisingly impressive features into remarkably affordable e-bikes.
The XP Lite2 had been widely considered the best bang-for-your-buck option in the ultra-budget category, offering an affordable yet punchy Class 2 e-bike for a song, despite still coming from a reputable US-based company with strong reputation for warranty and support.
Now, the third-generation model builds on what has become one of the most successful budget e-bike platforms in the country, bringing a long list of upgrades designed to make the bike easier to ride, fold, transport, and live with.
And perhaps most importantly, Lectric has managed to keep that familiar
$799 starting price
that debuted on the original XP Lite1 all the way
back in 2022
The Lectric XP Lite3 gets a major upgrade
The new Lectric XP Lite3 weighs just 49 lb (22.2 kg), making it one of the lighter options in Lectric’s extensive lineup of folding electric bikes. That’s still no featherweight, partly due to Lectric’s insistence on not neutering the bike’s performance, but it’s still a solid 10-20 lb lighter than the average direct-to-consumer e-bike these days.
The bike retains the compact folding design that made its predecessors popular with everyone from college students to RV owners, but introduces a redesigned frame with improved ergonomics and a reinforced folding latch borrowed from the company’s
flagship XP4 model
New quick-release pedals further reduce the bike’s storage footprint, making it easier to squeeze into a car trunk, apartment closet, or RV storage compartment.
Despite its compact dimensions, the
XP Lite3
can support a maximum payload of 275 lb (125 kg) and accommodates riders ranging from 4’8” to 6’2”.
The bike reaches speeds of up to 20 mph (32 km/h) and offers up to 40 miles (64 km) or 80 miles (128 km) of range in Eco mode, though expect significantly less range when using higher-power pedal assist or throttle-only riding. The range discrepancy comes from two different battery offerings. The base model features a 374 Wh battery, while the long-range version has nearly twice the capacity at 672 Wh.
Power comes from Lectric’s Stealth M24 motor, which is rated at 300W continuous but over 800 peak watts. The motor combines with Lectric’s pedal assist selector to offer five levels of pedal assist that are personalizable, letting riders dial in exactly how much boost they’d like on their ride. Riders also get a twist throttle, a more comfortable style of throttle enabled by the lack of shifters crowding the bars on this single-speed e-bike.
Several other upgrades help the XP Lite3 punch above its weight class, including integrated rear turn signals, a bright 3.5-inch full-color display brought over from other recently launched models in the Lectric lineup, and a redesigned LevelUp Lite rear rack with new mounting possibilities.
Stopping power comes from Star Union 602 hydraulic disc brakes with thicker 2.3 mm rotors, another welcome feature on a bike at this price point.
Lectric is also offering a Gates Carbon Belt Drive version of the XP Lite3, giving riders a cleaner, quieter, and virtually maintenance-free alternative to a traditional chain drivetrain. That Gates belt drive model fetches a $100 premium, but is likely worth it for those who value the cleaner, maintenance-free alternative that is likely to outlast the bike itself.
The chain-drive version comes in Arctic White, Blue Mist, Matte Grey, and Matte Lavender, while the belt-drive model is offered in JW Black and Ballerina Pink.
Lectric continues to redefine affordable e-bikes
It’s difficult to overstate just how much Lectric has changed the American electric bicycle industry.
The Phoenix, Arizona-based company has grown into the country’s largest e-bike brand by both sales volume and the total number of e-bikes on the road. In doing so, it has become one of the most recognizable names in affordable electric transportation.
But Lectric didn’t get there by simply building cheap electric bikes.
Instead, the company helped revolutionize what consumers should expect from a budget-friendly e-bike, combining capable hardware, practical designs, and aggressive pricing with something that has historically been missing from much of the low-cost e-bike market: a real American company standing behind the product.
While countless inexpensive e-bikes sold online come from little-known overseas brands with questionable long-term support, Lectric has built its reputation around US-based customer service, accessible replacement parts, and a company that riders can actually reach when something goes wrong.
That’s a big part of what has made the XP Lite series so important.
Since its introduction, the XP Lite series has arguably set the standard for what an entry-level electric bike should be. It isn’t necessarily the most powerful, fastest, or fanciest e-bike on the road, but it delivers the essentials at a price that opens electric cycling to an entirely new audience.
And importantly, it does so without requiring riders to gamble on an unknown brand.
The XP Lite3 continues that formula, adding features like hydraulic disc brakes, integrated turn signals, and a color display that would have been difficult to imagine on a $799 e-bike just a few years ago.
Electrek’s Take
I’ve been following Lectric since the company’s earliest days, and it’s been fascinating to watch how the brand has consistently raised the bar for affordable electric bikes. I rode one of Lectric’s first 10 bikes off their nascent production line all the way back in 2019, and I think they’d agree that few people outside the company know the brand better than I do. So I can say that, without a doubt, this is one of the company’s most important launches to date because of how it revolutionizes how much bike someone can get without stretching their budget farther than they have to. And at a time when inflation is still rising unchecked and fuel prices are through the roof, this is what the industry needs more than ever.
Keep in mind that the
$799 price tag
for the XP Lite3 announced today is the same price that the original XP Lite carried back in 2022, despite that value ballooning to $939 in 2026 dollars due to rising inflation.
$799 in 2022 would be equivalent to $939.19 today, meaning Lectric has effectively been decreasing its prices over the last few years to maintain affordability for consumers (Source:
US Bureau of Labor Statistics
What impresses me most isn’t necessarily any single feature on the new XP Lite3. It’s the combination of all those features at a price that remains accessible to so many riders.
Hydraulic brakes, a color display, integrated turn signals, a refined folding mechanism, and even the option for a Gates belt drive? That’s quite a lot of bike for the money. And remember, the performance is still there. This is still a 48V e-bike with a legit 20 mph (32 km/h) top speed on throttle and pedal assist.
Sure, there are lighter e-bikes out there, and there are certainly more premium models with fancier components. But that’s not really the point of the XP Lite.
The point is to make electric biking accessible without making it feel like a compromise at every turn.
And when you consider that you’re getting all of this from the biggest e-bike company in the country, complete with US-based support and a proven track record, it’s hard to argue with the value proposition.
The original XP Lite helped establish what a good affordable electric bike could be. The XP Lite3 looks ready to move that benchmark forward once again.
And on a personal note, not only do I want my own
Lectric XP Lite3
now, but I think my wife’s new e-bike will soon be an XP Lite3 in Ballerina Pink with a Gates belt drive. Remember, “Happy wife, happy life!”

title: Algeria inaugurates 300 MW solar project - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The 300 MW solar plant, located in the eastern province of El Oued, is Algeria’s largest operational PV project to date.
Patrick Jowett
27 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
Dr. Mourad Ajal, Minister of Energy and Renewable Energy Resources
A 300 MW solar project has been switched on in Algeria.
According to a social media post published by the country’s Ministry of Energy and Renewable Energy, the El Oued Foullia solar energy station, located in the El Oued province, is Algeria’s largest operational solar project to date.
The project is owned by Sonelgaz, Algeria’s state-owned electricity and gas utility. Open-access platform GEM lists China State Construction Engineering Corporation as the operator.
The site forms part of the first phase of the Algerian government’s national program for the development of renewable energy, which is targeting the rollout of around 3.2 GW of renewables capacity. The ministry’s latest update says this phase will be distributed across 21 plants and 14 provinces. Longer term plans are targeting the deployment of
15 GW of solar by 2035
A government statement says the inauguration of the 300 MW project reduces reliance on traditional energy sources and supports economic and local development. It is the third large-scale solar project to be commissioned in Algeria this year, following the inauguration of the Tendla and El-Ghrous projects, both with a capacity of 200 MW.
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has tracked 2.87 GW of operational solar in Algeria, according to figures available in its project database, 1.7 GW of which is listed as commercial and industrial projects. The database identifies a further 220 MW of solar at various stages of development.

title: Bangladesh moves to cut tariffs for long-delayed solar projects - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Bangladesh is seeking lower tariffs on solar power purchase agreements (PPAs) signed years ago for projects that are still not generating, a move investors warn could raise contract risk across the market.
Syful Islam
27 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Power purchase agreements
Bangladesh is renegotiating PPAs with solar developers that signed high tariffs years ago but never built their plants, prompting investor warnings about contract risk.
A government committee formed in April has already held talks with several project owners and is scheduled to meet two more on Oct. 27 and Oct. 29, with the aim of lowering tariffs agreed when project and equipment costs were higher.
The projects were approved under the Quick Enhancement of Electricity and Energy Supply (Special Provisions) Act, 2010, during the previous government’s tenure. Most were approved on the basis of unsolicited proposals from investors and have not been completed despite repeated extensions of their approvals.
Government officials said the PPAs were signed at high tariffs that reflected project and financing costs at the time. Construction costs and solar equipment prices have since fallen significantly, they said, so the projects’ tariffs should be brought in line with current rates for other projects.
Committee Chairman Mahfuzar Rahman, a joint secretary at the power division of Bangladesh’s Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, said the government is revisiting existing contracts with projects that failed to come online on time.
“Actually, we need to check the issues involving their power tariff and implementation delays and revisit them,” Rahman said. He said the government will act on the outcome of the review.
Project owners and private investors have raised concerns about the renegotiation. They said the government’s concern over utility-scale solar projects that signed PPAs and implementation agreements several years ago but have made limited progress is understandable. However, they said projects should be held to their contractual milestones, and investors that fail to perform should face the remedies already set out in their project agreements rather than tariff changes.
The investors said the tariff is a fundamental assumption behind an independent power producer’s financial model, debt sizing, lender due diligence and equity investment decision. If investors and lenders perceive that agreed tariffs can be revisited after signing, they said, it adds a further layer of contractual and regulatory risk to the market. For long-delayed or non-performing projects, they called for a transparent, project-specific review based on the obligations and remedies in each project’s agreements.
Mostafa Al Mahmud, president of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association, said tariffs for projects that have failed to make progress can be renegotiated, but that renegotiating tariffs for projects at an advanced stage of construction is not acceptable.
“Any such steps will lower the confidence of investors in Bangladesh which require substantial domestic and international investment to achieve renewable energy ambitions,” said Mahmud.

title: Australian state targets 75% renewables for main grid - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Western Australia has committed to a renewable energy target of 75% by 2030-2031 for its main electricity grid as it prepares for the retirement of state-owned coal-fired power stations by the end of this decade.
David Carroll
27 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
The Western Australia government aims to achieve 75% renewable electricity on the South West Interconnected System (SWIS) by 2030-31, supported by large-scale solar, wind, and battery energy storage projects.
The target doubles the previous goal of 40% and comes as the state prepares to exit coal-fired power by 2030.
The state government said the renewable energy target (RET) is complemented by a Made in WA Energy Affordability Investment Program that will provide low-interest loans of up to AUD 15 million ($10.5 million) to help manufacturers install solar and battery systems and upgrade equipment to take advantage of cheaper energy.
WA Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the new 75% target is a “statement of intent” that is designed to encourage private sector investment.
“We know that renewables, backed by storage and gas, is the cheapest and most reliable
energy mix for Western Australia
,” she said. “That’s why we’re powering ahead with our support for the energy opportunities of the future and encouraging businesses to invest in WA.”
The government’s commitment has been welcomed by climate advocacy collaborative Solutions for Climate WA and its alliance of business, industry, investors, unions, and advocacy bodies.
Solutions for Climate WA Director Jessica Panegyres said the new target is a key step forward for the state’s energy future.
“[This] makes it clear that the future of our electricity system is renewables,” she said. “A renewable energy target sends an important signal to the businesses, investors, workers and communities who will deliver WA’s next generation of energy infrastructure.”
Western Australia has some of the best renewable energy resources in the world and a strong industrial base and Panegyres said setting a target provides the certainty required to turn that potential into
investment
on the ground.
Panegyres said the next task is making sure WA has a credible pathway to achieve its goal.
“That means continuing to accelerate investment in renewable energy generation, storage and the transmission infrastructure needed to connect it, while ensuring communities and regional areas share in the benefits,” she said.
Smart Energy Council (SEC) State Manager John Welch said WA’s new renewable energy target will advance the rate of growth for the state’s renewable energy industry
“Our members across solar, wind and battery storage are ready to build in WA, and a target gives them a clear goal to build towards,” he said, adding that transmission will be critical to achieving the target. “The priority now is to keep the grid build moving and lock in dates for its next stages.”
