title: Lula targets data center investment using Brazil’s renewable energy potential - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Brazil’s newly re-elected president wants to attract data centers and develop domestic AI, linking digital infrastructure investment to renewable energy availability, grid capacity and workforce training.
Alessandra Neris
27 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Artificial Intelligence
Utility-scale
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said this week he plans to use the country’s renewable energy potential to attract data center investment, outlining the proposal in his first public address after winning re-election.
“We have to take advantage of the energy potential of a country that may have the greatest capacity for renewable energy to bring here the data centers needed to store our data in Brazil,” Lula said.
He also called for some data center capacity to be reserved for Brazilian information, linking digital infrastructure expansion to national technological sovereignty.
For the electricity sector, the proposal could create opportunities for long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), self-generation and new renewable energy projects. Project viability will also depend on grid connections, supply reliability, and transmission and distribution infrastructure.
Brazilian AI
Lula also advocated developing domestic artificial intelligence to reduce dependence on foreign technologies.
“I don’t want to keep depending on Chinese or American artificial intelligence; I want to create a Brazilian one,” he said, linking the ambition to training professionals in fields such as mathematics and engineering.
Expanding computing infrastructure for AI could increase electricity demand and the importance of renewable power supply, storage and energy management. Lula did not detail specific regulatory mechanisms or requirements for data center investors.
In September, the government enacted Redata, a special tax regime for data centers. The incentives require operators to meet their electricity demand through supply contracts or self-generation using renewable or low-emission sources.
Six areas of Lula’s address with potential implications for electricity
Beyond attracting data centers, other priorities mentioned by Lula could affect the energy market.
1. Digital sovereignty and infrastructure
Expanding domestic data storage and processing capacity could stimulate investment in digital infrastructure. The proposal also aligns with Redata, which aims to encourage data center development in Brazil.
2. Renewable energy expansion
Lula presented the availability of clean energy as a competitive advantage for attracting data centers. This could create opportunities for solar projects and bilateral power contracts, although he announced no specific measures to increase generation for the sector.
3. Grid capacity and electricity supply
Large new electricity loads require assessments of connection capacity, necessary grid upgrades and supply reliability. These factors could influence where data centers are built and whether projects are viable.
4. Workforce training and innovation
Lula highlighted mathematics and engineering as important to developing domestic technology. A skilled workforce is also important for expanding renewable energy, battery storage, automation and digitalized electricity networks.
5. Climate policy and deforestation
Lula said he intends to keep climate policy among the government’s priorities and highlighted the reduction in deforestation over the previous four years. He announced no new specific decarbonization targets for the electricity sector during the address.
6. Digital economy and electricity demand
Lula identified the digital economy as an investment priority for his next term, alongside the green and creative economies. Growth in AI and data processing could increase electricity demand and create opportunities for storage, energy management and renewable power supply.
Investment in the digital and green economies
Attracting data centers through Brazil’s energy resources would link digital infrastructure expansion to the availability of renewable electricity. Delivering the strategy will depend on incentives, power contracting conditions and adequate infrastructure to serve new loads.
Lula said he plans to meet with business leaders, educators and scientists over the following two months to discuss the new government’s priorities. His address did not detail additional electricity-sector measures tied to the proposals.

title: German solar developers seek €70/MWh auction ceiling for 2027 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Fifteen solar developers warn that planned changes to Germany’s renewable energy law, grid connection rules, and network charges could raise ground-mounted solar costs by up to 30%, prompting calls to increase the auction ceiling from €59 ($65.91)/MWh to at least €70/MWh.
Ralph Diermann
27 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Fifteen photovoltaic project developers, including RWE, Enertrag, BayWa r.e., Belectric, Juwi, and GP Joule, have called for a higher auction price ceiling for ground-mounted solar projects in Germany from 2027, warning that planned policy and regulatory changes could undermine project economics.
The companies argue that the current ceiling of €59/MWh may no longer allow economically viable bids. More frequent negative wholesale electricity prices and the planned shift to two-sided contracts for difference would reduce revenues, including during periods of high electricity prices.
Further cost pressures could come from new capacity charges under the German Federal Network Agency’s AgNes process. Under the regulator’s proposal, operators of new generation plants with capacities above 30 kW would pay a grid feed-in charge from 2029. A rate of around €4/kW to €7/kW per year is under discussion.
The developers cite a Prognos study commissioned by the German Association of Energy and Water Industries (BDEW), which estimates that the planned changes to the Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG), grid connection package, and AgNes network charging system could increase the levelized cost of electricity from ground-mounted solar by up to 30%. The resulting costs would be €13/MWh to €15/MWh above the current auction ceiling of €59/MWh.
The companies want the ceiling for auctions held in 2027 raised to at least €70/MWh. From early 2028, they propose a sliding ceiling based on the results of the three most recent auctions. The limit would be calculated from the average of the highest-priced successful bids, plus an 8% buffer, subject to a proposed cap of €70/MWh.

title: Stellantis plans 21.56 MW of solar for Mexican auto complex - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Stellantis has submitted plans for two solar plants totaling 21.56 MWp at its Saltillo industrial complex in Mexico, with annual generation of 51.68 GWh for on-site consumption.
Luis Ini
27 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Stellantis México has submitted an environmental impact assessment to Mexico’s Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) for two solar plants with a combined capacity of 21.56 MWp at its industrial complex in Saltillo, Coahuila. The project is named PS 360E Stellantis Saltillo Complex.
The installations will supply electricity to the automaker’s industrial facilities. Stellantis, which manufactures vehicles under brands including Ram, Jeep, Fiat, Peugeot, and Citroën, operates Ram truck assembly and engine manufacturing facilities at its industrial complex in the Derramadero area.
According to the submitted documentation, the project will occupy 61.21 hectares within the industrial property, approximately 15 kilometers southwest of Saltillo.
The two plants, PS 360E Stellantis Saltillo Complex I and II, will each have a capacity of 10.78 MWp, with 9 MWac and a net capacity of 8.8 MW. The first will supply the load center at the Saltillo truck plant, while the second will serve the load center associated with the Saltillo Sur engine plant and the Chrysler Camión facilities.
The project will use approximately 33,696 monocrystalline bifacial solar modules rated at 640 W each, mounted on 216 single-axis solar tracking structures. The trackers will be oriented north to south, with a tilt range of up to 60 degrees in either direction.
Annual electricity generation is estimated at 51.68 GWh, comprising 25.60 GWh from the first plant and 26.08 GWh from the second.
Both plants will operate as grid-connected self-consumption facilities without exporting surplus electricity to Mexico’s National Electric System. All generated electricity will be consumed within the automotive complex, with each plant connected independently to its respective load center.
The electrical infrastructure will include four transformer centers and four independent medium-voltage circuits operating at 13.8 kV. The circuits will connect the solar installations to an existing substation through underground sections and approximately 1.1 kilometers of overhead lines.
The proposed schedule includes site preparation and construction, with commissioning planned for month 24 after the project begins. The installations are expected to have a 30-year operating life. Public documentation does not disclose the investment amount.
The project builds on the relationship between Stellantis and Argentine energy company 360Energy, in which the automaker acquired a 49.5% stake in 2024.
The companies are already developing renewable electricity projects for Stellantis industrial facilities. In April 2026, they commissioned an 8 MWp solar plant at the Córdoba Industrial Hub in Argentina, expected to generate 16.7 GWh annually for Stellantis’ automotive factory.

The Czech government has proposed changes to its new capacity mechanism, which is open to battery storage, including moving two supplementary auctions from 2026 to 2027, a year later than prospective participants had planned for.
Brian Publicover
27 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
he Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade (MPO) has published a draft amendment to a general measure it issued in August introducing the country’s capacity mechanism. The draft also proposes a related obligation on Czech transmission system operator ČEPS.
The ministry said the changes are intended to clarify the mechanism’s conditions, strengthen legal certainty for participants, ensure transparent and nondiscriminatory procedures and adapt the rules to practical implementation. Anyone whose rights or interests may be directly affected can submit written comments until Oct. 30.
According to Czech energy news site

, the draft changes 20 provisions of the original measure and moves two extraordinary supplementary auctions, held four and five years before delivery, from 2026 to 2027. Auction timeline

The first delivery period runs from Nov. 1, 2030, to Oct. 31, 2031.

Individual contracts can last up to 15 years. Existing and new generation, electricity storage, cross-border capacity and demand-side response are eligible to participate.

title: China's new catalyst could help astronauts make fuel from Mars air
content: China-based scientists have developed a catalytic process that converts thin Martian atmosphere into versatile methanol. The team at the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory (Hefei) developed a dual-site catalyst that combines copper and sodium on a porous crystalline support to convert carbon dioxide and hydrogen (derived from local ice) into methanol fuel.In testing, the sodium-boosted catalyst produced 245 grams of methanol per kilogram of catalyst per hour. This output is reportedly “11 times” higher than using copper alone. The material also reduced unwanted by-products and maintained stable performance throughout 12-hour trials.Methanol offers a solution for sustaining off-world bases. It could serve as a reliable energy source for electricity generation, heating, and powering planetary rovers.“The optimized catalysts, especially MOF-808-NaCu, showed markedly enhanced CO2 hydrogenation performance, delivering a methanol space-time yield of 245 g·kgcat–1·h–1,” the researchers wrote in the study paper. “These findings clarify the promoting role of neighboring alkali-metal sites in dual-site catalysis and offer a material-design strategy for efficient CO2 conversion toward future Mars exploration applications,” it added. The chemical secretEstablishing a human settlement on Mars is the ultimate dream for off-world living, but the logistics present a huge challenge. Over 95 percent of the Martian atmosphere consists of carbon dioxide, making survival difficult.Transporting thousands of tons of fuel from Earth across millions of kilometers of deep space is far too expensive to be practical. So future settlers would need to produce essential supplies directly on the Red Planet. And that future begins from extensive research on Earth first. Researcher Zhang Zhe and his team synthesized a dual-site catalyst known as MOF-808-NaCu. Built on a porous metal-organic framework (MOF-808), the material pairs copper atoms directly with neighboring sodium promoters.The sodium acts like a chemical magnet. It attracts incoming carbon dioxide molecules and alters their electronic structure, holding them in position so the adjacent copper sites can drive a hydrogenation reaction using hydrogen split from local Martian water ice.Space agencies like NASA and private contractors like SpaceX have long relied on Sabatier reactors to generate methane fuel. Methane serves as a potent rocket propellant, but storing it requires complex cryogenic cooling systems to keep it liquid at -257.8 degrees Fahrenheit (-161 degrees Celsius).Why methanol beats methaneMethanol offers a far more practical alternative because it remains liquid at ambient temperatures and normal atmospheric pressure.Producing a liquid chemical that stays stable without massive refrigeration equipment gives a future Martian base an instant, multipurpose reserve for power, heating, ground transportation, and industrial manufacturing.Aside from its use as a fuel, methanol could also serve as a chemical raw material for manufacturing antifreeze, construction supplies, and various essential products on Mars.China’s space program has gathered fast momentum since its Tianwen-1 rover touchdown in 2021. With the upcoming Tianwen-3 mission scheduled to attempt humanity’s first Mars sample return, developing in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) technology is the logical next leap.However, certain engineering challenges remain before this catalyst can be deployed off-world. Chiefly, engineers will need to design lightweight compressors that can capture and pressurize the whisper-thin Martian air.But all said, scientists are proving that the key to surviving on Mars could just be learning to live off the land for all the resources already there.

title: US tests 2-version cleanup system against chemical, biological agents
content: Sensitive military equipment exposed to chemical or biological warfare agents could be cleaned and returned to service through a transportable system being developed for US special operations forces.Ohio-based defense contractor BLADE, formerly HDT Global, announced on October 26 that it had won a contract to continue developing the large variant of the Critical Equipment Decontamination System (CEDS). Designed for use in austere and contested locations, the system aims to help operators recover valuable equipment without sending it back to a depot or replacing it.The company did not disclose the contract’s value, duration, or number of systems covered. It also did not specify whether the award advances the program toward production.Two versions for sensitive equipmentCEDS is intended to decontaminate low-density, high-value equipment, allowing troops to reuse items that might otherwise have to be discarded. Equipment processed through the system is meant to be safe enough for reissue without requiring operators to wear additional protective gear.The program includes two configurations. The small variant is an inflatable, soft-walled shelter developed by Integrated Solutions for Systems in Huntsville, Alabama.The large variant resembles a medium-sized metal shipping container. It was developed by the former HDT Expeditionary Systems unit in Fredericksburg, Virginia, according to the US Army.Both configurations address the challenge of recovering sensitive equipment after contamination. BLADE said the large system is intended to reduce the logistical demands of replacing gear and return mission-essential equipment to operators faster.Tests use real warfare agentsPrototyping began in fiscal 2022. Testing has involved actual equipment exposed to real chemical and biological agents at the Czech military’s research institute, known as VVU, rather than relying on simulants.The small variant completed operational testing at the facility in December 2024. The large variant was scheduled to follow in 2025, although BLADE’s latest announcement did not provide an update on that testing.Earlier program plans targeted delivery of the first systems to US Special Operations Command units in fiscal 2027. The newly announced contract did not confirm whether that fielding target remains unchanged.The program is managed by the Joint Project Manager for CBRN Special Operations Forces under the Pentagon’s Portfolio Management Executive for Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defense.Recovering equipment closer to operators“Through the CEDS program, we are advancing critical decontamination capabilities that enable Special Operations Forces to recover essential equipment, sustain operations and maintain their advantage in contested environments,” said Tim Stickler, BLADE’s senior director of CBRN integrated protection and bio and chemical security. “We are proud to support this mission and provide the reliable solutions our warfighters depend on,” he added. Special operations forces are also receiving a separate capability, the Forward Area Mobility Spray System, for washing down contaminated vehicles and equipment in the field.That system includes backpack and vehicle-mounted versions. Its man-portable version reached full operational capability in May 2025, nearly three years ahead of schedule.All three spray-system variants are due to be fielded by fiscal 2028, while the latest CEDS award supports continued development of its larger equipment-decontamination configuration.

title: US method identifies radioactivity from 100-feet above in seconds
content: U.S. researchers have found a new method that aids faster and more accurate radioactive material detection from the air.​According to the University of Michigan Engineering and Paul Scherrer Institute study, the system is capable of accurately locating a radioactive source within 6.6 feet (two meters) and measuring its activity within two percentage points of its true value.​The study demonstrated that, using a specialized physics-based math framework (Bayesian inference), the system could recognize both single and mixed radioactive sources during a six-second helicopter flyover equipped with airborne detectors.​Microsecond detections from nearly 100 feet​The research team recently conducted the first field test of the method in Switzerland. They placed known radiological sources on the ground, including mixed sources, and later flew a military helicopter nearly 98.43 feet (30 meters) over it. The aircraft, installed with a radiation detector in the cargo bay area, detected the  identity, activity, and location of the radioactive source using the Bayesian method. The detection happened despite a weak and heavily distorted signal during a single-pass flyover, the study reported.​Researchers noted that these detections were achieved within seconds, unlike the conventional techniques, which take hours or days to evaluate radiological emergencies.​The stark reduction in response time, from hours or days to microseconds, was made possible by recognizing the physics happening in the backdrop of events rather than enhancing the computing power of the system, highlighted the lead author of the study.​”I was surprised how much efficiency we could gain by reorganizing the physics rather than simply using more computing power,” said David Breitenmoser, a postdoctoral research fellow of nuclear engineering and radiological sciences at the University of Michigan.​Splitting gamma ray journey​Conventionally, a radioactive material is identified by recognizing the gamma ray pattern emitted by each material, which acts as a unique fingerprint. However, the method poses problems for air detection. These rays, while making their way up to the airborne detectors, shift energy levels due to collisions with air and aircraft and generate distorted or blurry signals.The problem is worsened because, during the single flyover, the aerial detectors only pick up a small fraction of these emitted gamma rays. As a result, interpretation using these minimal signals requires a full spectrum analysis that takes longer to match the blurry signals to the simulated energy spectra for specific radioactive sources under given flight conditions.​Using the new method, Breitenmoser tried to reduce the time taken by existing methods. He cut down simulation time by splitting the gamma rays’ journey into two parts: scattering in the air and scattering within the aircraft.He factored in air temperature and humidity for atmospheric scattering calculations, while using precomputed mathematical functions specific to the helicopter model used during testing to calculate the aircraft scattering part. By integrating these values, he reduced computation time, thereby improving the response time.​“Once we separated transport through the atmosphere from the helicopter response, simulations that had taken hours or days could be evaluated in microseconds,” said Breitenmoser.The study further reported that to locate the radioactive source below, the Bayesian framework constantly updates its statistical confidence by quickly comparing thousands of pre-existing spectral templates with blurred aerial data.​Beyond radiological emergencies​Aided by the new methods, aerial detection of radioactivity could help first responders respond faster and make more informed decisions during a radiological emergency, such as a reactor meltdown or the detonation of a nuclear weapon.​This vital airborne data helps emergency teams decide who needs to be evacuated, where people should take shelter, and who should receive potassium iodide pills to protect their thyroids.​“What excites me most is the combination of speed and quantitative detail that could make airborne measurements substantially more useful in both emergency response and routine monitoring,” said Breitenmoser in a statement.​He added the technique could be applied to routine radiological monitoring around nuclear plants, environmental assessment and cleanup, and mineral exploration.​The findings were published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: China Zorrilla: World’s largest electric ship starts commercial runs
content: Ocean transportation is entering its green era. The world’s largest battery-electric ship has begun carrying passengers between Argentina and Uruguay, putting a 130-meter (426 feet), fully battery-powered vessel into commercial service.China Zorrilla, built by Incat Tasmania for ferry operator Buquebus, completed its maiden commercial voyage between Buenos Aires and Colonia across the River Plate (55 km or 34-mile journey). It can carry up to 2,100 passengers and 225 vehicles.The first passenger crossing followed an official launch ceremony in Buenos Aires on October 21.Incat Managing Director Craig Clifford, Buquebus representatives, and maritime authorities from both countries attended the event, which marked the completion of years of engineering and construction at the shipbuilder’s Hobart yard.More than 40 MWh of battery storageChina Zorrilla carries more than 250 tonnes of batteries and has an energy storage system exceeding 40 megawatt-hours. The system supplies electricity to eight electrically driven waterjets that propel the vessel.Its passenger facilities include a duty-free retail area covering about 2,300 square meters, along with accommodation for travelers making the crossing.For Incat, the vessel represents the culmination of one of its most technically complex construction projects. Chairman Robert Clifford credited the Tasmanian workforce with overcoming the engineering challenges of building a battery-powered ship of this size.“This is a truly historic day for Incat, for Tasmania and for the global maritime industry,” Clifford said.The vessel also extends the relationship between Incat and Buquebus, the operator that commissioned the ferry for its South American service.A quieter passenger crossingCraig Clifford traveled aboard China Zorrilla during its first commercial voyage. He said the absence of familiar machinery sounds and vibration was among the most noticeable differences for passengers.“What really stands out is the passenger experience. When you’re aboard a vessel of this size, you naturally expect to hear and feel the machinery working beneath you. On Hull 096, that familiar engine noise and vibration simply aren’t there,” Clifford revealed. Robert Clifford said the vessel’s operation demonstrated that large passenger and vehicle ferries could use electric propulsion in commercial service.“This ship proves that large, high-capacity commercial vessels can operate on electric power, and that passengers can enjoy a completely different experience in the process, without the traditional diesel-engine noise, vibration or exhaust emissions,” he said.The comments describe the onboard experience as the ferry moves from construction and commissioning into regular passenger operations.More electric ferries under constructionIncat is also building three 129-meter battery-electric ferries for Danish operator Molslinjen at its Hobart shipyard. Two additional 78-meter hybrid-electric vessels are under construction there.Those projects add to the shipbuilder’s work on electric propulsion, with China Zorrilla now carrying passengers after years of construction at the same yard.For Buquebus, the milestone places the battery-electric vessel on the Buenos Aires–Colonia route, carrying both travelers and vehicles across the River Plate.“To be here in South America and travel aboard this vessel with passengers for the first time is something very special,” Clifford said in the press release.

title: MIT builds 23-foot metal structure using origami-inspired method
content: MIT researchers have developed a scalable, origami-based construction system. It uses modular building blocks folded from flat metal sheets to construct lightweight, hyper-rigid 3D structures without requiring interior support columns or heavy welding equipment. Using pattern-based geometry, the team developed software that turns complex building designs into flat, easy-to-cut pieces that snap together naturally using basic hand tools.This fast and sustainable approach is ideally suited for rapidly deployable disaster relief shelters, aerospace components, and modular architectural facades.“This work shows that folding metal is a method that is ready to be used for building structures. We can do it big enough and strong enough, now that we can bring it out of the lab and to the construction site,” said Neil Gershenfeld, director of MIT’s Center for Bits and Atoms.Alfonso Parra Rubio, a graduate student in the Center for Bits and Atoms (CBA) at MIT, works on a foldable metal sculpture. Credit: Vikram ValluriGenius of modular foldingPaper origami is delicate. Architectural origami hasn’t been much stronger until now. The usual single-sheet folds tend to wobble and lack the strength needed to support real-world weight.MIT researchers have designed a scalable construction method that uses origami principles to turn flat metal sheets into strong, load-bearing structures. Lead author Alfonso Parra Rubio and his team re-engineered tessellation patterns from the 1960s, pioneered by artist Ron Resch. Rather than folding one giant, unwieldy sheet, the MIT team broke the problem into smaller, individual building blocks. Joining two tripod-shaped cells into a single modular block creates a structural unit with zero degrees of freedom. It locks dead stiff.When connected into an interwoven lattice, these unit cells form a cavernous 3D shell. It requires no central support pillars, cuts material use by a third, and delivers 3.5 times the stiffness of previous origami methods.Works outside the labBuilding complex geometry usually triggers a nightmare of miscommunication between architects, structural engineers, and site laborers. MIT overcame that chaos with software.An automated solver breaks down complex architectural visions into individual, foldable design files. A CNC milling machine cuts these precise shapes from flat metal sheets, then they can be packed tightly into flatbed trucks or air-dropped directly into crisis zones.The assembly process on-site is designed to be simple. Modular cells fit together in only one correct orientation, eliminating positioning errors during construction. Workers require nothing more than basic hand screwdrivers to connect the units, skipping the need for heavy welding equipment or specialized tools. This streamlined approach makes building faster, quieter, and far less expensive than standard methods.To prove it works outside the lab, the team constructed a massive 23-foot folded aluminum sculpture suspended from the ceiling of the Boston Public Library. A crew with zero formal construction background built the entire room-sized structure in just a few days.While rapid-deployment disaster shelters remain the most immediate application, the implications span far beyond relief zones. Aerospace engineers could adapt this technique to build lighter airplane and spacecraft hulls, as the system produces exceptionally lightweight yet rigid components.Urban architects are eyeing the method for sound-dampening interior panels, modular robotics, and striking, eco-friendly building facades that slash manufacturing carbon footprints.

title: Right-handed neutrinos could help explain the Big Bang, says study
content: Physicists at the University of Southampton in the UK and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur have proposed that the largely neglected ‘ghost’ particle called a right-handed neutrino could have been a dominant force in the universe right after the Big Bang and may have played an important role in how the universe shaped up to the way it is today. Neutrinos by themselves are known as ghostly particles since they do not typically interact with anything. A neutrino released from our Sun could travel for an entire light year (5.9  trillion miles or 9.5 trillion kilometers) through matter before striking any atom. The Standard Model of Particle Physics suggests that neutrinos should be massless. Yet, they exist in three different types – electron, muon, and tau- each differentiated only by differences in their mass. Like other particles, neutrinos have their own spins, which scientists use to define them as either left-handed or right-handed. But every neutrino scientists have detected so far has been a left-handed one. What are right-handed neutrinos? Right-handed neutrinos are hypothetical particles with no electric charge and are thought to be heavier than their left-handed counterparts. While they do not feel the weak nuclear force, right-handed neutrinos likely interact with the left-handed neutrinos, which might explain why the latter have differences in their mass. Quantum physicists use a theoretical framework called the seesaw mechanism to explain this. According to this framework, ordinary neutrinos carry traces of the right-handed neutrinos, which give them mass. The mass of the right-handed neutrino and the trace are inversely related. So a heavier right-handed neutrino leaves a fainter trace and makes the ordinary neutrino lighter. This is much like a playground seesaw, where the ends move in opposite directions. The role after the Big BangWhen the Big Bang occurred, matter and antimatter were generated in equal amounts. Their interactions should have annihilated everything and the universe would not be what we see it as today. However, according to Rishav Roshan, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southampton, UK, right-handed neutrinos played a crucial role in preventing this from happening. Working with Sudipta Show, a physicist at IIT Kanpur, Roshan suggests that the heaviest neutrino was 100 trillion times heavier than a proton and would have zipped at nearly light speed after the Big Bang. After losing some energy, it would have spread out and moved to weaker wavelengths as the universe expanded. The cooling cosmos would have slowed the neutrino and locked its energy into mass, increasing its share of cosmic energy. The particle would have remained dominant until it decayed into other particles. Such a universe dominated by a heavy neutrino would have expanded faster, but its interaction would have only begun only after it outpaced the expansion of space. In this scenario, the decay neutrinos would leave behind an excess of leptons that formed the matter that we see in the universe today. The researchers suggest that a lighter right-handed neutrino about 100 billion times as heavy as a proton could have been involved in the process. However, since it is not possible to generate something this big in a particle accelerator, the researchers plan to look for the signs of its existence in gravitational waves. The research findings were published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

title: Chinese firm delivers 10,000 robotic arms as humanoids enter factories
content: A Chinese robotics firm has delivered its 10,000th humanoid force-controlled robotic arm, marking a milestone in its industrial robotics business. ROKAE said the unit left its production line in September, and the announcement also identified five Helios wheeled humanoid robots operating at Schaeffler’s factory in Taicang, China. The robots are equipped with ROKAE’s AR Series arms and deployed on a component-assembly line. The announcement highlighted the growing role of robotics suppliers in Schaeffler’s efforts to use automated systems in its factories while manufacturing components for the emerging humanoid robotics industry.Scales force-controlled roboticsROKAE has delivered its 10,000th humanoid force-controlled robotic arm, marking a production milestone for its industrial automation technology. It also reported that five of its Helios wheeled humanoid robots, equipped with AR Series arms, are operating at Schaeffler’s manufacturing facility in Taicang, China, a German industrial supplier. The robots perform tasks including parts handling, assembly, and inspection on a production line for humanoid robot components.The company announced the milestone on October 26, stating that the 10,000th arm rolled off its manufacturing line in Shandong Province in September. The figure refers specifically to its humanoid force-controlled arm product line, rather than the total number of complete humanoid robots it has produced or delivered.Force control is a central feature of the technology. Unlike systems that rely solely on predetermined movements, force-controlled robotic arms can regulate the forces applied during physical interactions. This capability is relevant to tasks that require robots to handle components, make contact with objects, and perform assembly operations with controlled pressure.ROKAE’s AR Series arms provide force control at each joint, according to the company. This allows the system to manage physical interactions throughout the arm’s range of movement. The technology is designed for applications where precise and responsive handling is required, including industrial assembly and inspection.The arms use the company’s MAC controller, a compact unit measuring 213 × 145.5 × 45 millimeters. Depending on the configuration, the controller can manage all seven joints of a single arm, all 14 joints of a two-arm system, or more than 20 joints across a humanoid robot. This arrangement allows the control system to coordinate multiple joints within a robotic platform.Humanoids enter factory productionROKAE said more than 80 industrial partners have integrated its humanoid force-controlled arms into production applications. Its broader portfolio also includes HSA Series integrated force-controlled joints, the iNex embodied AI control system, and Helios wheeled humanoid robots.At Schaeffler’s Taicang facility, the Helios robots combine wheeled mobility with the manipulation capabilities of the AR Series arms. According to ROKAE, the machines support parts handling, assembly, and inspection on a component-production line. Their deployment shows how mobile robotic platforms and force-controlled manipulators can be combined for manufacturing tasks.The installation is part of Schaeffler’s wider effort to use humanoid robots in its own manufacturing operations while producing components for the robotics industry. The company previously described six humanoids working across five stations at the Taicang facility, which produces components including linear and rotary actuators. ROKAE’s latest announcement identifies five Helios robots specifically, but does not explain the difference between the two reported counts.The companies have not disclosed detailed operating figures for the ROKAE deployment, including production rates, human intervention requirements, or quantified productivity improvements. These measurements would help establish how effectively the robots perform in sustained industrial operations.

title: 12.5-mile range interceptors built to counter mass drone attacks
content: German defense technology company Helsing has unveiled Contra, an AI-controlled air defense system designed to coordinate responses to large-scale drone and missile attacks. The system combines sensor data, automated command-and-control software, and multiple weapons, alongside two new interceptors developed to counter faster aerial threats.Announced on October 26, Contra is built around Helsing’s Altra command-and-control platform. The company says it can detect and engage hundreds or thousands of incoming threats simultaneously by combining information from different sensors into a unified air picture. According to Helsing, human operators retain control over decision-making and target prioritization. The launch comes as European militaries seek more affordable ways to counter mass drone attacks, particularly as newer jet-powered attack drones become harder to intercept using conventional low-cost defenses.AI coordinates multiple air defense systemsContra is designed to connect radar, electro-optical, infrared, and acoustic sensors with different defensive weapons. Rather than relying on a single interceptor, the platform can coordinate a mix of existing and new systems, letting defenses respond to different threats within one network.Helsing says the system can integrate third-party equipment, including interceptor missiles, counter-drone lasers, guns and net-based systems. The company claims it can integrate be hardware within days, although the announcement does not provide independent test results demonstrating this capability at scale. AD-1 Inferno targets fast-moving dronesThe first new interceptor, AD-1 Inferno, uses a jet engine and is designed to counter fast-moving aerial threats, including jet-powered attack drones. Helsing says it can travel at speeds exceeding 700 km/h (435 mph) and has a range of at least 20 kilometers (12.4 miles).Unlike a conventional interceptor that must engage a target immediately, Inferno is designed to loiter in the air, operate in swarms, and make repeated engagement attempts. It receives mid-course guidance from ground-based radar stations, while an onboard radar seeker guides it during the final stage of an interception.These features are intended to help defend against targets that are too fast for slower interceptor drones but may not justify the expense of traditional high-end air defense missiles. AD-2 Ambush provides a faster interception optionThe second interceptor, AD-2 Ambush, uses a solid rocket motor for rapid engagements against high-speed, high-altitude threats. Helsing says it can reach speeds above Mach 2 and has a range of at least 20 kilometers.Today we are unveiling Contra, an AI-controlled autonomous air defence system designed to protect countries from scaled drone and missile attacks.Alongside Contra, two new interceptors:AD-1 Inferno to counter jet-powered threats. AD-2 Ambush to counter high-altitude threats. pic.twitter.com/Z9HE2UB2ft— Helsing (@HelsingAI) October 26, 2026The company positions Ambush as a complementary system for targets that exceed Inferno’s intended engagement envelope, including fast attack drones and subsonic cruise missiles. Like Inferno, it uses ground-based mid-course guidance and an onboard radar seeker for terminal guidance in different weather conditions.Both interceptors are designed for containerized launch and mass production at Helsing’s Resilience Factories. The company says their unit costs will be significantly lower than those of existing missile interceptors, but it has not published specific prices. Designed for large-scale productionHelsing says Contra and its interceptors are intended to address a growing imbalance between inexpensive attack drones and the cost of shooting them down. The company cited intelligence reports estimating that Russia was producing 4,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones per month. However, the system remains in development and testing. If the company can deliver its promised performance and production volumes, Contra could offer European forces another way to coordinate air defenses against large, mixed attacks.

title: Lockheed Martin targets 621-mile range with ramjet-powered missile
content: Lockheed Martin has been selected to develop and test a longer-range version of the US Army’s Precision Strike Missile (PrSM), designed to strike targets at least 621 miles (1,000 kilometers) away.The PrSM Increment 4 variant is intended to engage moving maritime targets and relocatable land targets when launched from the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS).The missile will use an advanced propulsion system supplied by L3Harris, which Lockheed Martin says could roughly double the range of the baseline PrSM.Flight competitions planned for 2027 and 2028 will evaluate the competing designs, with Lockheed Martin developing prototypes and investing in propulsion, sensors, and manufacturing capabilities.Ramjet-powered strike missileThe missile is intended to engage moving maritime targets and relocatable land targets from existing launch systems. Its development focuses on extending range through advanced propulsion while retaining compatibility with current launchers and established guidance and control systems.PrSM Increment 4 uses an advanced propulsion system supplied by L3Harris. Lockheed Martin says the technology could roughly double the standoff range of the baseline PrSM, allowing the missile to engage targets at significantly greater distances.The design incorporates ramjet propulsion alongside guidance and control subsystems developed for the PrSM family. Ramjet technology is intended to sustain high-speed flight by using the missile’s forward motion to compress incoming air, supporting propulsion during the powered flight phase.Developing the propulsion system also requires manufacturing components to precise tolerances. Lockheed Martin has invested more than $300 million with industry partners to mature technologies intended to extend missile range.The company has also brought a $300 million additive-manufacturing and automation line online. The facility produces airframe and propulsion components while maintaining the dimensional precision required for ramjet performance.Increment 4’s sensor package is another key part of the development effort. The system is designed to support engagements against both moving ships and relocatable ground targets, requiring the missile to detect and track targets that may change position before impact.Lockheed Martin has invested $250 million in its Strigo Product Center, which develops radio-frequency sensors, missile datalinks and seeker technologies. Work at the center contributes to elements of the Increment 4 guidance package.Expands missile productionThe Increment 4 design is intended to retain the transport container and fire-control interface used by the baseline PrSM Increment 1. This would allow the missile to operate from the M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) and M270A2 launcher without requiring changes to existing training or logistics arrangements.Maintaining compatibility with established launch systems could simplify the introduction of the longer-range missile. It would also allow the Army to build on its existing PrSM infrastructure rather than introduce an entirely separate launch system.Lockheed Martin is developing prototypes ahead of the scheduled flight competitions, which will assess designs for the next phase of the Army’s precision-strike capability. The company says its work combines existing missile technologies with advances in propulsion, sensing and manufacturing.Production is expected to build on Lockheed Martin’s manufacturing operations in Camden, Arkansas, where the company already produces PrSM Increment 1 and Increment 2. The facility is expanding with robotics and advanced automation to increase production capacity.The upgrades are intended to support the transition from low-rate manufacturing to full-rate production while maintaining consistent quality.The Army’s upcoming competitions will determine how the competing designs perform as development progresses. Lockheed Martin’s Increment 4 effort focuses on extending missile reach while maintaining compatibility with existing launch systems and incorporating the propulsion and sensor technologies needed for longer-range engagements.

title: Tesla Semi rival cuts diesel use by 36.5% and lowers charging costs
content: Diesel trucks could cut fuel consumption without swapping their engines for batteries. Range Energy said its electric trailer cuts tractor fuel use by 36.5 percent on the miles it assists, while also powering the trailer’s refrigeration unit.The California-based company released a white paper on October 26 comparing its eTrailer with conventional diesel equipment and a Tesla Semi. Targeting grocery and foodservice refrigerated fleets, the analysis models seven years of operation to assess fuel savings, charging costs, and financial returns.Across 1,000 simulated futures, the eTrailer delivered better financial results than a Tesla Semi with its own depot charger in 61 percent of cases. The findings come from Range’s modeling, and production deliveries are scheduled to begin in late 2027.Electrifying the trailerRange’s approach adds an electric powertrain to a Class 8 semi-trailer, allowing fleets to retain their existing tractors rather than purchase electric replacements.According to the company, the eTrailer connects to any tractor without modifications or special driver training. Once its battery is depleted, the truck can continue its route using diesel.For refrigerated fleets, the system addresses two sources of diesel consumption: the tractor’s engine and the refrigeration unit, commonly called a reefer.The reported 36.5 percent reduction in tractor fuel consumption applies specifically to assisted miles. That translates to approximately 57 percent better fuel economy over those miles, while the reefer runs on electricity.“Fleets need to see the most fuel savings for every dollar they invest, with equipment that fits how they already operate, yet the path off diesel has largely been framed as a choice between staying put and buying a new electric truck,” said Kyle Foley, CEO of Range.Modeling seven years of costsRange’s engineering team used a Monte Carlo analysis, which tests different combinations of uncertain inputs rather than relying on one forecast.Its 1,000 scenarios varied diesel and electricity prices, charger installation costs, insurance, resale values, and eTrailer fuel savings drawn from pilot data.The base case assumed diesel at $5.07 per gallon and excluded purchase incentives for both options. Under those assumptions, the eTrailer and a Tesla Semi with a dedicated depot charger both paid back their investment in under six years.Over seven years, the analysis estimated that the eTrailer avoided 387 gallons of diesel per $1,000 invested, compared with 358 gallons for the Semi configuration.Charging at the loading dockThe eTrailer uses a standard 480-volt dock circuit. Range estimates a typical installation costs about $5,200 and takes roughly a month, compared with an average installed cost of $51,500 for a Tesla Semi depot charger.The study also models existing depot power supporting about eight eTrailers, versus approximately three Semis on individual chargers, before additional utility service is needed.Range said the trailer can also work with electric tractors, adding at least 100 miles of range while powering refrigeration independently of the truck’s battery.For fleets considering the system, the white paper provides modeled costs and pilot-based savings ahead of the planned 2027 production deliveries.

title: 7,800-ton USS Colorado nuclear submarine picked for AUKUS rotation
content: Australia will host USS Colorado, the first U.S. nuclear-powered attack submarine under the AUKUS (Australia-UK-U.S.) defense pact, strengthening military cooperation among the three allied nations.The deployment marks a step toward establishing a regular American submarine presence in the country and expanding the three nations’ collective deterrence capabilities in the Indo-Pacific. The agreement aims to strengthen Australia’s naval capabilities while deepening defense ties with the United States and the United Kingdom. The move comes amid growing regional security concerns over China’s military expansion and reflects the allies’ efforts to maintain a strategic balance in the region. Expands submarine presenceAustralia will host the USS Colorado, a U.S. Navy Virginia-class fast-attack submarine, from late 2027 as the three AUKUS partners expand their undersea warfare capabilities. The deployment will establish the first submarine assigned to Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West), a planned rotational force based at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia.The arrangement is designed to strengthen submarine operations in the Indo-Pacific while helping Australia develop the technical expertise and infrastructure required to operate and maintain its own nuclear-powered submarines. It will also expand regional maintenance and support options for American and British submarines.The USS Colorado (SSN 788) is a 115-meter (380-foot) Virginia-class fast-attack submarine designed for undersea warfare, surveillance, and land-attack missions. It carries land-attack missiles and sophisticated torpedoes, giving it capabilities to engage targets both underwater and on land.The U.S. Navy commissioned the submarine in March 2018. Its assignment to SRF-West represents a significant step in establishing a regular rotational presence of American nuclear-powered submarines at an Australian naval facility.Under the plan, HMAS Stirling will eventually host up to four U.S. fast-attack submarines and one British fast-attack submarine on a rotational basis. The submarines will not be permanently based at the facility but will rotate through it as part of the three countries’ broader defense cooperation.The deployment will also build on Australia’s preparations to support allied submarines. A U.S. Submarine Maintenance Period is scheduled to begin later this week, demonstrating the country’s growing capacity to sustain American and British nuclear-powered fast-attack submarines.Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles said the initiative was on track, with American personnel already at HMAS Stirling preparing the site.Boosts sonar productionSRF-West aims to help Australia develop the expertise and infrastructure needed to operate, maintain and regulate its own nuclear-powered submarines. Although the submarines will carry conventional weapons, their nuclear propulsion systems require specialized technical skills, trained personnel and dedicated facilities.The rotational force will also expand maintenance options for AUKUS partners, supporting submarine deployments and helping sustain advanced undersea platforms in the Indo-Pacific. Australia’s wider submarine program could cost up to U.S. $235 billion over 30 years, according to government forecasts.The three partners said SRF-West activities would comply with their international obligations, including the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. Australia will also adhere to the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty, known as the Treaty of Rarotonga.Meanwhile, Australia is strengthening its domestic naval technology industry. French defense group Thales has opened a sonar facility in Rydalmere, western Sydney, to manufacture and maintain towed-array sonar systems for military submarines, ships and other maritime platforms.Jointly funded by Thales Australia and the Australian government, the facility will supply sonar systems for Hunter-class frigates, Collins-class submarines and the BlueSentry autonomous system. Towed-array sonar uses sensors deployed behind a vessel to detect and track underwater acoustic signals, supporting maritime surveillance and submarine detection.Local production and maintenance are expected to reduce reliance on overseas facilities, shorten offshore servicing periods and extend deployment times.Thales owns approximately 35 percent of Naval Group, the French defense contractor that lost Australia’s submarine contract in 2021 after Canberra canceled the program in favor of AUKUS.

title: Google Beam could help deployed US troops feel closer to loved ones
content: Google is partnering with the USO to bring its Google Beam 3D video communication technology to 20 USO locations worldwide, helping service members experience those moments with their families.The rollout will use HP Dimension with Google Beam systems, which create lifelike conversations without requiring glasses or headsets. A pilot earlier this year connected Trzebień, Poland, with Fort Bliss, Texas. The program is now expanding to include Grafenwöhr, Germany, and Fort Hood, Texas.Google has also released a docuseries directed by military veteran and filmmaker Kyle Hausmann-Stokes. It follows four soldiers from the 2nd Battalion, 37th Armored Regiment during their deployment in Poland, showing how they used Beam to reconnect with loved ones back home.Bringing depth to video callsOriginally developed as Project Starline, Google Beam uses artificial intelligence and specialized display technology to give remote conversations a sense of physical presence. The HP Dimension system features a 65-inch screen and six cameras built into its frame. The cameras capture the participant from multiple angles, while an AI model uses those images to construct a three-dimensional representation in real time.The display sends different images to each eye, creating depth without wearable equipment. Head tracking adjusts the perspective as participants move, while spatial audio helps position voices where the person appears on screen.Together, these features are designed to preserve eye contact, gestures, and other nonverbal cues that help people communicate naturally.Sharing milestones across deploymentsFor Sergeant Amoy Brown and his wife, aviation logistics specialist Tiyanna Orane, an eight-hour time difference complicated opportunities to celebrate together. During their Beam session, Brown celebrated Orane’s military promotion and interacted with their young son, Azeal.Army Chaplain Roland Kassales, who spent 15 months deployed during his first two years of service, listened as his daughter Blythe read stories she wrote.“Being able to incorporate feeling and body language — all those things that make communication meaningful — will go a long way towards overall well-being for soldiers,” Kassales said. Kassales’ comments reflect the program’s focus on helping families communicate through expressions and movement, alongside speech. The sessions gave participants opportunities to share everyday activities and major milestones.A closer view of family lifeSergeant First Class Matthew Jennings used Beam to see how much his newborn daughter, Lilly, had grown and watch one of his sisters play guitar. His wife, Mayra, manages a blended household of seven while working 12-hour shifts.For Major Michael Rodriguez, an armor battalion operations officer with 12 years of service, the connection offered a chance to watch his one-year-old daughter, Kathryn, practice taking her first steps. His wife, Jessica, works as a pediatric physical therapist while caring for their four young children.The expansion to 20 USO locations will extend the program beyond its initial Poland–Texas connection. Google’s accompanying docuseries documents what those calls have already allowed four deployed soldiers and their families to share.

title: 220-second X-ray scan delivers images 27 times faster than conventional method
content: Researchers have demonstrated a new X-ray technique that can produce detailed images and reveal a material’s chemical properties using a single optical component, possibly making advanced X-ray experiments faster and simpler.​The study showed that the approach could image circular samples about 27 times faster than a conventional point-by-point scan while collecting a complete spectroscopy dataset in about 220 seconds.​Instead of relying on multiple optical elements, the researchers used a reflection zone plate (RZP). This precisely nanostructured reflective optic can reflect, focus, and separate soft X-rays at the same time.​The international team from Germany, Switzerland and Japan carried out the experiments at the P04 beamline of the PETRA III synchrotron radiation source at DESY in Hamburg.​Narrow X-ray beam creates 2D imageStandard X-ray imaging shows the shape and location of features within a sample, while spectroscopy reveals information about its chemical composition, electronic structure and molecular bonding. Combining both techniques typically requires multiple optical components that must be carefully aligned, the researchers noted. In the new approach, the RZP performs all of these functions in a single compact system.​To test whether the system could produce clear images, the researchers first examined standard test patterns containing Siemens stars, star-shaped targets commonly used to measure image sharpness, and the letters “RIXS.”​Rather than scanning one tiny point at a time, the team lighted the sample with a narrow X-ray line. The team then moved the sample in small steps across the beam, like a document passing through a scanner. A computer stitched the individual image strips together to create a complete two-dimensional image.​The technique resolved features measuring about 14 to 24 micrometers (μm), several times smaller than the width of a human hair. Because the system scanned an entire line instead of individual points, it imaged circular objects about 27 times faster while maintaining comparable image quality.Distortion-free imagesThe researchers said the achievement was notable because such imaging was previously thought to be unworkable due to the Abbe sine condition. This optical principle predicts image distortions under certain conditions. They overcame the problem by operating the reflection zone plate in the paraxial regime, allowing it to collect only X-rays traveling within a narrow angular range. This lowered optical distortions and enabled sharp imaging of larger objects.​”The strong dispersion of the RZP allows several spectroscopic features to be measured simultaneously,” said Dr. Christoph Braig. “Importantly, both the elastic and inelastic signals can be recorded in the same optical configuration.”After testing the imaging method, the team replaced the test pattern with a thin jet of acetonitrile dissolved in ethanol to demonstrate chemical analysis. Instead of lighting the sample with a single X-ray energy, they used a beam containing many energies at once, creating what the researchers described as an X-ray “rainbow.”​The RZP measured the energies of incoming and outgoing X-rays at the same time, allowing the researchers to capture a complete two-dimensional resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) map without changing the experimental system. The system recorded emitted X-rays between 388.6 and 401.8 electron volts (eV), resolving elastic, inelastic, and vibrational features near the nitrogen K-edge. The entire dataset was collected in about 220 seconds, considerably faster than standard methods.​”Our experiments show that a RZP can provide both spatial and spectroscopic information using a compact optical arrangement,” said Jens Rehanek. “This could make advanced soft X-ray measurements more efficient and easier to implement.”​Last and corresponding author Zhong Yin of the Synchrotron Radiation Instrumentation Science Laboratory (SRIS) at Tohoku University said combining reflection, focusing, imaging and spectral dispersion into a single optical element offers “a compact and efficient route to soft X-ray spectromicroscopy” and could open new opportunities to study materials at the atomic scale.​The findings were published in Optics Express.

title: Hybrid-electric aircraft makes aviation first with 150-foot landing
content: Electra has demonstrated a way to bring fixed-wing air travel into urban spaces that conventional airplanes cannot use. Its hybrid-electric demonstrator recently took off and landed at Downtown Skyport in Lower Manhattan, marking what the company describes as the heliport’s first such operation by an airplane without vertical takeoff capability.The flight points to a potential new role for compact aviation sites across the United States. Electra wants to use existing infrastructure to establish shorter regional air routes without requiring conventional airport runways.Engineering shorter takeoff distancesElectra’s Ultra Short aircraft combines hybrid-electric propulsion with blown-lift technology to operate within remarkably short distances. The system directs airflow over the wings to generate additional lift at low speeds, helping the aircraft take off and land in approximately 150 feet.That capability could expand the number of locations suitable for regional air travel. Heliports, small fields, and other compact sites could serve as access points without the expense of constructing new runways.The demonstration also advances Electra’s broader Direct Aviation concept. The approach aims to connect passengers with destinations closer to their starting points, reducing dependence on major airports and congested ground transportation.According to Electra’s market outlook, travelers could save approximately three hours and 45 minutes on trips between New York City and Boston. The company estimates savings of three hours and 30 minutes for Washington, D.C., and 45 minutes for Philadelphia.Those figures represent projected journey-time savings, not measured results from the Manhattan demonstration.Existing sites, new flight routesElectra has tested its EL2 technology demonstrator at several locations, including downtown Charleston, Bader Field in Atlantic City, and Snowshoe Mountain Resort. Each demonstration explores how short takeoff and landing performance could open unconventional access points.The company is also participating in the Federal Aviation Administration’s advanced air mobility integration pilot program. Its work has included demonstrating helicopter-style instrument flight procedures at Roanoke-Blacksburg Regional Airport.Electra says more than 60 airline operators intend to operate regional Direct Aviation routes. Its partners also include airport authorities, aviation service providers and developers interested in establishing new urban and residential access points.Marc Allen, Electra’s CEO, said the Manhattan flight showed how operators could expand aviation access without building additional runways. He added that existing sites across the country could support a more distributed regional transportation network.Commercial and defense applicationsShort-field performance could also prove useful beyond passenger transportation. Electra says military operators could use compact landing areas to move personnel and supplies when conventional runways become unavailable, damaged, or too dangerous to use.The aircraft’s hybrid-electric system and short operating requirements could offer flexibility for logistics missions. However, the Manhattan demonstration alone does not establish the aircraft’s operational readiness for commercial or military service.Electra plans further demonstrations as it advances its larger EL9 aircraft toward certification, production, and service. The company’s longer-term goal is to connect smaller aviation sites into a regional network that complements existing airports.Whether that network becomes practical will depend on aircraft certification, operating economics, and the availability of suitable sites.

title: Companion humanoid robots get lifelike silicone skin, 100 languages
content: Realbotix is putting a hefty price tag on physical AI companionship, with its new Echo humanoid robots starting at $11,950. The lineup combines lifelike silicone skin, articulated movement, and integrations with popular conversational AI platforms. The most expensive configuration costs $59,950 and offers 39 degrees of freedom for upper-body movement.The Canadian robotics company plans to manufacture just 250 units in its initial production run. That allocation includes 225 tabletop robots and 25 full-body models, with deliveries scheduled for the second half of 2027. Customers can reserve a unit with a $199 deposit, although the purchase also carries a mandatory monthly software subscription.Two configurations, distinct capabilitiesThe $11,950 Echo Tabletop measures 32 inches tall and weighs approximately 25 pounds. Its 17 degrees of freedom allow movement across its articulated structure. Silicone-based synthetic skin covers its face and neck, giving the robot a more lifelike exterior. Realbotix positions this configuration for individual interactions involving education, therapy, and personal wellness.The $59,950 Echo Full Body stands considerably taller. The female configuration measures 72 inches, while the male version reaches 77 inches. Both measure 28 inches wide and deep, with a listed weight of approximately 88 pounds. Its 39 degrees of freedom support more extensive upper-body movement.Neither configuration offers a fully articulated human body. Realbotix describes fluid upper-body motion on the full-body model, so buyers should not confuse its joint count with unrestricted humanlike mobility. Both models feature advanced facial expressions and chest-mounted speakers for spoken interactions.Vinci adds on-device visionEcho supports integrations with ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, giving users access to different conversational systems through subscription tiers. Four characters offer distinct personalities and voices: Aria, Mila, Dave, and Amar. The robots can communicate in more than 100 languages and respond in the language used by the person addressing them.Realbotix’s optional Vinci system adds computer vision and on-device processing. Its capabilities include facial recognition, gaze tracking, emotional-cue detection, and spatial and temporal awareness. Realbotix claims subsecond latency for local processing, which could help the robot recognize returning users and maintain eye contact during conversations.The company also plans digital AI twins for 2027. Subscribers will be able to interact with their selected character through a computer, tablet, or phone when away from the physical robot. Realbotix says encrypted memories and preferences will carry across digital and physical versions of the same character.Cloud AI raises privacy questionsRealbotix says conversation histories, saved memories, and facial-recognition data remain on the robot or a paired device. The company claims it neither receives nor reviews those records. It also says it does not use locally stored information for advertising, analytics, or model training.Cloud-based features follow a different path. When Echo uses external AI, speech, or avatar services, the information required to deliver those features may reach third-party providers. Realbotix receives service-usage logs but says it cannot directly access conversation content processed by those providers.Operating the robots requires a subscription to the Robot Configuration App, with plans starting at $19.99 per month. That recurring fee adds to an already substantial purchase price, particularly for the full-body model. Organizations ordering at least 10 units can contact Realbotix for volume pricing.The initial production limit makes Echo a tightly constrained launch, not a mass-market humanoid release. Whether its lifelike exterior and conversational abilities justify the price will depend on how reliably the hardware performs outside demonstrations.

title: OpenAI claims major proofs in math, computing and quantum physics
content: OpenAI says its models have produced mathematical proofs that challenge established theories in harmonic analysis and computer science. The work also includes a claimed existence proof for quantum field theories, including quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Researchers will now examine the results, verify their implications and explain their significance to the wider scientific community.The company has adopted different release strategies for the three projects. It has published the mathematical and computing proofs, while an external physics group will prepare its own account of the research.Math results challenge established theoriesOne proof addresses the local smoothing conjecture, a problem in harmonic analysis proposed by Christopher Sogge in 1991. It describes how waves behave when they concentrate, suggesting that extreme focusing cannot persist for long periods.OpenAI says its models proved the conjecture across every spatial dimension. The result also resolves the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture, according to the company.Previous research established important milestones in this area. In 2019, Larry Guth, Hong Wang and Ruixiang Zhang proved the local smoothing conjecture in two spatial dimensions. Wang and Zahl subsequently proved the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture in 2025.OpenAI generated its new proof on Oct. 18, 2026, and formalized it in Lean the following day. Lean is a proof assistant that helps mathematicians verify arguments with computer-based checks. The company has published both the natural-language proof and its formal counterpart on GitHub.Computing theory faces fresh scrutinyOpenAI also says its models disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture in computational complexity. The hypothesis concerns the difficulty of solving Boolean satisfiability problems and underpins conditional hardness results across numerous research fields.Researchers have used ETH in hundreds of papers covering graph theory, computational biology, databases, and computational geometry. If the new result withstands scrutiny, it could force researchers to reassess assumptions behind those studies.The models produced the disproof on Oct. 16, 2026, before formalizing it in Lean the following day. However, refuting ETH would not automatically deliver faster algorithms for existing computing problems. Researchers must still determine what the result means for practical computation.Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego will lead the review alongside Ryan Williams of MIT. OpenAI has agreed to fund a conference examining the claim and released its proof materials for independent evaluation.Quantum field theory proof awaits reviewThe physics work concerns the mathematical foundations of quantum field theory. OpenAI says its models produced existence proofs for interacting theories involving gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions. The results include QCD, which describes the strong force governing interactions between quarks and gluons.The work also addresses pure Yang-Mills theory, a key component of a Millennium Prize problem from the Clay Mathematics Institute. That problem concerns the mathematical existence of quantum Yang-Mills theory and the presence of a mass gap.Physicist David Gross will lead an external group that includes Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov and Nikita Nekrasov. The team plans to develop its own explanation before releasing the model-generated physics materials.OpenAI says all three collaborations will operate independently, with participants free to publish their findings. The company has also pledged support through a previously announced $5 million contribution to the Simons Foundation. That funding will help researchers organize workshops and conferences to examine the work and assess its broader implications.

title: Apple's new iPad mini gets 8.5-inch OLED, A20 Pro and ray tracing
content: Apple has given the iPad mini a major hardware overhaul, bringing OLED technology, a faster processor, and water resistance to its smallest tablet. The redesigned model measures just 5.4 millimeters thick while fitting a larger screen into the same footprint as its predecessor. It also gains a landscape-oriented front camera and improved audio hardware.The new iPad mini arrives with Apple’s A20 Pro chip, which promises substantial gains in graphics performance and on-device AI processing. Preorders open October 28, with availability starting November 6. Apple has yet to disclose pricing in the announcement.OLED comes to miniThe new 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display marks one of the biggest changes to the iPad mini. Apple has trimmed the bezels by 24%, creating more screen space without making the tablet larger. OLED technology also gives the display better control over individual pixels, producing deeper blacks and a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio.Brightness gets a substantial boost, too. The screen reaches 1,200 nits at peak brightness, more than twice the previous generation’s maximum. Full-screen brightness reaches 600 nits for SDR and HDR content, while the display can dim to just one nit for comfortable reading in dark rooms.Apple is also offering an optional nano-texture finish to reduce glare in bright environments. That could make the tablet more practical for photographers, designers, and technicians who regularly work outdoors. Support for the P3 wide color gamut should also help deliver more accurate colors.A20 Pro delivers more powerApple built the A20 Pro using a 2-nanometer manufacturing process and a chip package inspired by its M-series processors. Its seven-core GPU includes Neural Accelerators in every graphics core, giving the tablet additional hardware for demanding AI workloads.According to Apple, the new iPad mini delivers up to 4.5 times the AI performance of its predecessor. Graphics performance can reach 2.7 times the previous model’s level, while multithreaded CPU performance improves by up to 60%.The GPU also supports dynamic caching, hardware-accelerated mesh shading, and ray tracing. These features could benefit graphically demanding games and applications that handle complex 3D scenes.Apple reserves a Dual 16-core Neural Engine for the 512GB configuration. The 32-core setup doubles the previous generation’s neural processing capacity, according to the company. Increased unified memory bandwidth should also help with demanding applications that run models directly on the device.Slimmer tablet gains protectionThe new iPad mini measures 5.4 millimeters thick and comes in midnight and starlight finishes. Apple has also added an IP67 rating, which protects against dust and water exposure under specified laboratory conditions. The rating does not make the tablet waterproof.A 12-megapixel Center Stage camera now sits along the landscape edge, making video calls more natural when holding the tablet horizontally. Apple has also introduced an Acoustic Display designed to improve the audio experience, alongside faster wireless and cellular connectivity.The tablet runs iPadOS 27, bringing Apple’s next-generation Intelligence features and Siri capabilities. Apple says these tools can draw on personal context, answer questions, and understand information displayed on the screen.The hardware upgrades give the iPad mini more screen space and processing headroom without sacrificing its compact size. Independent testing will reveal how much those improvements translate into everyday performance and battery life.
