title: World's largest scooter rolls out after 7 years of development
content: Measuring about 8 feet (2.4 meters) long, riding on oversized fat tires, and standing tall with towering handlebars, SuperfastMatt’s giant Razor-style scooter is impossible to ignore.​The oversized two-wheeler, designed to resemble a scaled-up Razor scooter, has finally reached the finish line after a seven-year journey marked by delays, relocations, and countless side projects.​The project dates back to the earliest days of Matt Brown’s YouTube channel, SuperfastMatt. ​Aluminum-clad wooden bodyBrown originally bought a standard Razor scooter, recreated it in CAD software, and scaled every dimension up. His first design stretched well beyond 20 feet, making it impractical to store or maneuver. He eventually redesigned the project around the dimensions of an existing fat-tire electric scooter wheel, settling on an 8-foot deck that conveniently matched standard lumber lengths.The scooter’s frame is primarily wooden. Before installing a half-inch plywood deck, Brown reinforced the structure with full-length two-by-fours. The electric drivetrain, including the rear hub motor, came from a used fat-tire scooter, while the electronics were mounted between the wooden rails. He initially rebuilt the battery pack himself, then replaced it years later after the original cells deteriorated from long-term storage.​To replicate the appearance of an oversized Razor scooter, Brown wrapped the wooden frame in aluminum sheeting and added a center tread strip. The result closely resembles the familiar kick scooter, only scaled to extraordinary proportions.​The project, however, repeatedly took a back seat. Brown shifted his attention to other ambitious builds, including motorcycle engine swaps, a Tesla-powered 1950s Jaguar, a land-speed car, and an off-road Dodge Viper. Multiple house moves required storing the unfinished scooter, while the COVID-19 pandemic canceled the desert event where it was originally supposed to debut.​When Brown eventually returned to the scooter, the battery had failed after years of inactivity. Replacement battery packs brought it back to life, but the giant machine proved awkward to steer at low speeds, requiring an exceptionally wide turning radius. Installing shorter handlebars borrowed from a standard Razor scooter significantly improved handling.3D-printed parts​Modern 3D-printing also helped complete the project. Brown printed fork covers, decorative tubes, and a functional telescoping handlebar clamp that allows the bars to extend and lock securely. Foam exercise rollers serve as handlebar grips, while the fork covers intentionally face the opposite direction of the original Razor design.​After the platform cracked during a beach outing, Brown fixed it with heavy steel angle brackets and finished the scooter with button-head bolts designed to resemble the rivets found on a real Razor scooter.​Wherever it goes, the scooter attracts attention. Passersby routinely stop to photograph it, and many ask for a chance to ride it. At the desert event where it finally made its public debut, the giant scooter became a popular photo attraction.​Brown also addressed smaller reliability issues that surfaced during testing. Dust and moisture had affected the brake lever switch, while the telescoping handlebars occasionally slipped after hard jolts. He even mounted two standard Razor scooters on the rear deck so passengers could ride along, though the extra riders made tight-space navigation more challenging.​According to Brown, the build is the largest two-wheeled Razor-style scooter he has encountered.

title: OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra matches GPT-6 Astra at 10% of the token cost
content: OpenAI has released GPT-6.1 Terra, a new model built to handle complex computer-based work at a lower cost. It focuses on tasks that require visual reasoning and interaction with desktop applications. The release also brings substantial gains in factual accuracy and coding performance over GPT-5.6 Terra.Terra targets practical workloads that businesses want to automate without paying premium prices for every task. These include processing invoices and interpreting technical drawings. OpenAI says the model can also tackle demanding professional tasks at a fraction of the cost of its more expensive alternatives.Faster performance at lower costsGPT-6.1 Terra delivered a significant improvement on Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark covering complex professional tasks. Challenges include converting architectural drawings into 3D models and documenting individual film shots for restoration teams.At medium reasoning effort, Terra scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra. OpenAI achieved that improvement at roughly one-third of the cost. Terra also matched GPT-6 Astra’s performance on the benchmark at approximately one-tenth of its price per token.GPT-6.1 Terra: delivering fast and capable computer use at a lower price.GPT-6.1 Terra understands what’s on screen, takes action across apps, writes naturally, and is a more capable model for your whole workday with the efficiency to take on more of it. pic.twitter.com/8JTN1yonmV— OpenAI (@OpenAI) October 26, 2026Speed offers another advantage. OpenAI says Terra completes tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. At maximum reasoning effort, it also achieves roughly nine times lower task costs than Claude Opus 5.5.The results extend to desktop automation. OSWorld 2.1 evaluates how well models operate desktop applications through multistep workflows. Terra surpassed GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at medium reasoning effort while costing substantially less per task.Terra also performed strongly on MMMU-Pro, which tests visual reasoning. It outperformed GPT-5.6 Terra at every tested reasoning setting. Its scores came close to those of GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, despite its lower cost.Fewer errors, better codingOpenAI has also worked to reduce factual mistakes, which can undermine automated workflows. Its internal benchmark uses prompts designed to expose weaknesses in model responses.At low reasoning effort, Terra recorded an error rate of 16.7 percent. GPT-5.6 Terra scored 53.6 percent on the same evaluation. That represents a reduction of 36.9 percentage points.The improvement continued at maximum reasoning effort. Terra’s error rate fell to 4.3 percent, down 18 points from its predecessor. That brings its performance close to the levels reported for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.Coding performance has improved considerably, too. Terminal-Bench 4.0 measures how well coding agents solve command-line problems. One example involves fixing a webpage whose layout shifts as it loads.At maximum reasoning effort, Terra solved 50.3 percent of the benchmark’s tasks. GPT-5.6 Terra recorded a score of 21.5 percent, giving the new model more than twice its predecessor’s success rate. OpenAI still recommends GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra for its most complex coding challenges.Availability and API pricingGPT-6.1 Terra became available on October 27 to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users through ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API using the model identifier gpt-6.1-terra.Standard API pricing starts at $1 per million input tokens. Cached input tokens cost $0.05 per million, while output tokens cost $5 per million. OpenAI says these rates are 50 percent lower than those for GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol.Terra retains the safeguards developed for GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI reports stronger resistance to prompt injection and better disclosure of limitations. Its preparedness evaluations also place the model at the Critical threshold for cybersecurity.The lower price could make complex computer automation more accessible to developers and businesses. However, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the stronger options for the most demanding coding work.

title: Prismatic batteries to supercharge US power grid with 17% more energy
content: South Korean battery giant Samsung SDI has signed a new agreement to supply the US with one gigawatt-hour (GWh) of batteries that feature 17 percent higher energy density and a 25-year lifespan.As part of the collaboration, the Yongin-based company will provide its Samsung Battery Box (SBB) 1.7 to Houston’s battery energy storage system (BESS) specialist Alpha Omega Power (AOP). The fully integrated ESS solution integrates nickel-cobalt-aluminum (NCA) batteries According to Samsung SDI, the systems will reportedly be used in energy projects across the Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) and Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) power markets. The construction is set to begin in 2027. All battery cells and modules will be manufactured at the StarPlus Energy plant in Kokomo, Indiana. The site is a joint venture between Stellantis N.V. and Samsung SDI. Deliveries scheduled for completion by the end of 2026. Higher energy densityThe 6.14-megawatt (MW) containerized system delivers 17 percent higher energy density than its predecessor, the SBB 1.5. It moreover maintains the same 20-foot container footprint, and relies on high nickel-cobalt-aluminium oxide (NCA) cells. The upgrade is expected to increase the storage capacity without taking up more space. Samsung SDI said that the system features Enhanced Direct Injection (EDI) technology, which sprays fire-extinguishing agents directly into battery modules. It also incorporates AI-based algorithms to spot potential faults early and predict battery lifespan, and uses the company’s prismatic battery technology, known as PrismStack, which is designed to provide strong durability and safety.The Samsung Battery Box (SBB) 1.7.Credit: Samsung SDIPrismatic batteries are housed in rigid rectangular cases that provide structural protection for the battery cells. Samsung SDI noted its prismatic technology has helped the company meet the strict safety and performance requirements of US energy companies.The SBB 1.7 is also built for 25 years of continuous use, which makes it suitable for long-term grid storage applications. “With our differentiated technology and local production capabilities, we will continue to expand our business foundation and strengthen our position in the North American ESS market,” said Fabrice Hudry, president of Samsung SDI America’s ESS division.Expanding storage capacitySamsung SDI highlighted that the system has met major safety requirements. This includes the NFPA 855, that covers stationary energy storage installations, as well as the UL 9540, a safety standard for energy storage systems.The latest deal builds on an earlier agreement between Samsung SDI and Alpha Omega Power signed in late 2025. Together, the two contracts cover 1.5 GWh of energy storage systems, all of which will be manufactured at the Indiana facility.The batteries will help AOP meet the nation’s growing energy needs. “American-made ESS from SAMSUNG SDI will play an important role in AOP’s continued growth,” Paul Choi, AOP CEO, stated. “This second agreement strengthens our domestic supply chain supporting the next generation of energy infrastructure.”“Alpha Omega Power is one of the fastest growing independent power producers in the country, and the kind of sophisticated operator we want to partner with to tackle grid reliability challenges,” Hudry concluded in a press release.

title: Unexpected Discovery of Abnormal Antibodies Could Help Explain Childhood Cancer
content:
Researchers have discovered an unusual immune response in children that may interfere with the body’s ability to repair damaged DNA. Credit: Shutterstock
Laboratory experiments show that antibodies associated with childhood cancer can enter cells and bind DNA repair proteins, suggesting a possible route by which the immune system could weaken genetic safeguards.
Years before some children were diagnosed with cancer, their blood already contained antibodies directed against proteins that normally repair damaged DNA. Researchers in Norway have found that these antibodies were much more common among children who later developed cancer than among those who did not, raising the possibility that the immune system itself may interfere with a cell’s ability to protect its genetic material.
Childhood cancers, including leukemia, myeloma, neuroblastoma, and osteosarcoma, differ from adult cancers in their causes, locations, and responses to treatment. Children have had far less time to accumulate DNA damage from environmental exposures, lifestyle factors, and aging. Their tumors therefore tend to contain fewer mutations and often arise from immature cells, such as stem cells or progenitor cells that can develop into more specialized cell types.
Cells rely on hundreds of proteins to identify and repair damage or errors in their DNA. The Norwegian researchers suspect that this protective machinery may sometimes be disrupted by auto-antibodies, antibodies that mistakenly target the body’s own proteins rather than foreign threats. If these antibodies interfere with DNA repair, genetic damage could accumulate even without inherited defects in the genes responsible for maintaining the genome.
Antibodies target six DNA repair proteins
To investigate this possibility, Serguienko, Dr Ola Myklebost, and their colleagues analyzed the proteome, or collection of expressed proteins, in tumor and blood samples from 175 adults and children with sarcoma or acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The samples were collected between 2014 and 2017 through the NoSarC Norwegian Sarcoma Study, the Norwegian Childhood Cancer Biobank, and the Oslo University Hospital Cancer Research Biobank. The team compared them with samples from anonymized healthy individuals, including blood donors, children participating in the Bergen Growth Study, and children visiting a clinic in Bergen.
Children with cancer between the ages of two and 19 had substantially more circulating IgG antibodies targeting DNA repair proteins than young adults or older individuals. These antibodies primarily recognized proteins associated with six genes: RAD52, NUMA1, ALKBH7, APBB1, UNG, and MGMT. Although these genes are closely involved in DNA repair, they were not significantly mutated in the cancers studied. This raised the possibility that the proteins could be disrupted by the immune system even when the genes encoding them remained largely intact.
Antibodies found years before diagnosis
Finding these antibodies in children who already had cancer, however, could not establish whether they appeared before the disease or developed in response to it. The researchers therefore examined blood samples collected years earlier from 59 school-age children who participated in two long-term British studies, the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children and Born in Bradford.
Roughly half of these children subsequently developed cancer before turning 30, while the others did not. Comparing the two groups allowed the researchers to investigate whether antibodies targeting DNA repair proteins were present before cancer was diagnosed.
“Although this cohort is small, it was the best we could find internationally,” said Myklebost, an emeritus professor of molecular oncology at the University of Bergen. “Even so, we were able to show that indeed, children who later got cancer (on average six years after blood sampling) were about eight times more likely than their healthy peers to have antibodies to at least one core antigen involved in DNA repair.”
The findings, published in
Frontiers in Immunology
, suggest that these antibodies can appear well before cancer develops. Their presence alone does not establish that they cause the disease, however. To explore whether they might actually interfere with DNA repair, the scientists conducted additional experiments using living cells.
How antibodies may disrupt DNA repair
Those experiments showed that the auto-antibodies could enter cells, particularly during the stage when cells finish growing and prepare to divide. Once inside, the antibodies appeared to concentrate around a cellular structure called the TIGER organelle, where transcription factors and other short-lived but essential proteins are produced and modified.
“We showed that many children with various types of cancer have antibodies against some of their own DNA repair proteins. We also demonstrated that such ‘auto-antibodies’ can enter live cells and bind to – and probably inhibit – the activity of these essential proteins,” said corresponding author Myklebost.
The researchers propose that antibodies entering a cell or its nucleus could attach to DNA repair proteins and prevent them from working normally. By binding to these proteins, the antibodies might immobilize them or directly interfere with their activity, leaving the cell less capable of correcting genetic damage.
Such interference could produce effects resembling those caused by inherited defects in DNA repair genes that increase cancer susceptibility. The difference is that the repair machinery would be impaired by antibodies rather than by mutations in the genes encoding its components.
“[These results] together provide a plausible mechanism for increased cellular damage that could lead to cancer development,” concluded the authors.
An important question remains unanswered: Why would a child’s immune system begin producing antibodies against proteins needed for DNA repair?
“They could be triggered by infections, by crossreacting to some microbial proteins or overstimulation of the immune response, or by some imbalance in immune tolerance,” hypothesized Myklebost.
Antibody screening needs stronger evidence
These possibilities remain unconfirmed, but the findings suggest a potential approach to identifying children who may face an increased risk of cancer. If further research establishes that the antibodies contribute to cancer development, screening for them could eventually help identify susceptible children years before diagnosis, potentially allowing earlier detection or even preventive interventions.
For now, the researchers are working to determine whether the antibodies directly impair DNA repair and whether that interference can cause cancer. Demonstrating those effects would provide much stronger evidence for the proposed mechanism.
“At present we are investigating the effect of patient antibodies on the repair of induced mutations in cultured cells. Ultimately, we hope to clone white blood cells that secrete such auto-antibodies, and test for any cancer-causing effects in mice to definitively prove our hypothesis,” said Myklebost.
Reference: “Pathogenic autoantibodies targeting DNA repair proteins are shared by cancer patients and healthy children later diagnosed with cancer” by Anastassia Serguienko, Jeetesh Sharma, Ronas Shakya, Monica Cheng Munthe-Kaas, Kjetil Boye and Ola Myklebost, 25 August 2026,
Frontiers in Immunology

title: Scientists Discover a Surprising Dental Benefit of Cranberry Juice
content:
Natural compounds in cranberries may influence how harmful oral bacteria behave. New findings point to a surprising potential benefit that warrants further investigation. Credit: Shutterstock
In a small human study, unsweetened pure cranberry juice was linked to slower plaque regrowth and lower acid production, hinting at a possible oral health benefit.
Cranberry juice has a reputation for being tart, acidic, and often sugary, qualities that might seem poorly suited to protecting teeth. A small human study from the University of Illinois Chicago, however, found that unsweetened pure cranberry juice was associated with slower dental plaque regrowth and lower acid production.
UIC College of Dentistry researcher Christine Wu examined whether compounds naturally found in cranberries could affect dental plaque bacteria, which feed on sugars and produce acids that contribute to enamel decay. Cranberries contain proanthocyanidins, anti-inflammatory compounds known for their ability to interfere with the attachment of bacteria such as E. coli to cells.
“Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I’m interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health,” Wu said.
Testing pure juice against sweetened cranberry drinks
Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds in the laboratory, Wu and her colleagues used commercially available beverages. Fourteen children and eight adults were randomly assigned to drink either unsweetened pure 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice with added sugar, or water.
Christine Wu. Credit: Christine Wu
“It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children,” said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry.
Participants arrived on the morning of the study with plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first used cotton swabs to collect plaque samples from one side of each participant’s mouth. After rinsing with water, participants drank three small portions of their assigned beverage, swishing each several times before swallowing.
Thirty minutes later, researchers collected plaque from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. This allowed them to compare plaque collected before and after exposure to the beverages.
Cranberry juice reduces plaque acid production
Plaque exposed to pure cranberry juice appeared to regrow more slowly than the samples collected before the experiment. Swishing with pure cranberry juice was also associated with lower acid production in both children and adults. That matters because acids produced by plaque bacteria can contribute to the breakdown of tooth enamel.
The findings raised the possibility that cranberry juice could eventually be considered a “functional beverage” with potential oral health benefits. Wu noted that other commonly consumed juices, including orange and apple juice, had not shown the same promise in her work.
“Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar,” she said.
Promising results need larger tests
The results are preliminary. The study included only 22 participants and measured short-term effects, so additional experiments will be needed to determine whether the findings hold up in larger groups and over longer periods.
For now, Wu said she would not rule out occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth cleanser.
“But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute,” she said, “to make it a bit more palatable.”
Reference: “In vivo exposure to cranberry juice suppresses dental plaque regrowth and acid production in adults and children: a PGRM study” by Christine D. Wu, Wei Li, Monique Luu, Evelina Kratunova and Qian Xie, 23 June 2026,

title: Scientists Discover That Eating Peanuts Every Day May Help Protect the Aging Brain
content:
A small clinical trial suggests that a common food may improve how the aging brain responds to insulin in regions involved in memory. Credit: Shutterstock
A daily serving of peanuts may improve insulin sensitivity in the aging brain, potentially supporting memory.
Peanuts may offer more than a convenient source of protein and healthy fats. New research suggests that eating them regularly could help the aging brain respond more effectively to insulin, a hormone that plays an important role in memory, learning, and communication between nerve cells. As people grow older, the brain can become less sensitive to insulin, a change linked to age-related cognitive decline.
In a small clinical trial, researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands found that eating unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions involved in memory. The study, conducted by the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM), was published in
Food & Function
How Peanuts Affected The Aging Brain
“The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline,” says Dr. Peter Joris, the study’s senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center.
The trial included 31 healthy adults aged 60 to 75. Each participant completed a 16-week period of eating peanuts and a control period without them. This randomized, controlled crossover design allowed researchers to compare each person’s results under both conditions.
Insulin-induced changes in regional cerebral blood flow (CBF; mL/100 g/min). Whole-brain analysis revealed one cluster in the right hemisphere where CBF responses to intranasal insulin were beneficially affected after the peanut intervention compared with the control period (-5.4 ± 5.4 mL/100 g tissue/min). This cluster encompassed parts of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, thalamus, and posterior cingulate gyrus. The color map corresponds to Z-values. Credit: Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) at Maastricht University Medical Center, Maastricht, Netherlands
During the peanut period, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings), or about 2.1 ounces, daily. Premeasured packets helped them follow the prescribed amount, which they could eat in one sitting, divide throughout the day, or add to meals. They were instructed to consume the peanuts in the morning or afternoon.
The changes in insulin responsiveness appeared in a cluster on the brain’s right side, encompassing parts of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus. These regions are involved in memory.
Measuring Insulin’s Effects on the Brain
To assess the brain’s response, researchers administered insulin through the nose and measured the resulting changes in regional cerebral blood flow (CBF). They used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), combining advanced imaging with a controlled dietary intervention lasting several months.
Earlier results from the 16-week peanut intervention, published in 2025 in
Clinical Nutrition
, showed a 3.6% increase in global cerebral blood flow, which supplies the brain with oxygen and nutrients, alongside a 5.8% improvement in verbal memory.
The team also assessed cognitive performance using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) and measured intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content, or liver fat, with abdominal MRI.
“Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults,” says Dr. Peter Joris, the study’s senior author and an associate professor at Maastricht University Medical Center. “These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake.”
“Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals, and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits,” adds Joris. “Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance.”
Reference: “Daily consumption of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts beneficially affects regional brain insulin responsiveness in older adults: results of a longer-term randomized controlled trial” by Kerkhof, Lucia, Mensink, Ronald P., Plat, Jogchum, Nijssen, Kevin M. R. and Joris, Peter J., 30 September 2026,
Food & Function
DOI: 10.1039/d6fo03208g
The NUTRIM study was supported by funding from The Peanut Institute Foundation. The funder did not have a role in the study design, implementation, analysis, or interpretation of the data or the writing of the manuscript.

title: From 54% to 100%: Scientists Reveal a Potential Breakthrough in Quantum Technology
content:
The photon changes shape during propagation. Credit: Oliver Diekmann / TU Wien
Scientists have proposed a surprisingly simple way to improve photon absorption using specially engineered waveguides, potentially making future quantum technologies far more efficient.
Quantum technologies depend on a process that remains surprisingly unreliable: transferring a single photon between two quantum bits, or qubits. With conventional methods, the receiving qubit successfully absorbs the photon only about 54 percent of the time. This inefficiency creates a major obstacle for quantum computers, secure quantum communication, and future quantum networks.
Researchers at TU Wien have proposed a way to overcome this limitation by changing the shape of a photon’s wave as it travels between qubits. Their calculations and computer simulations suggest that the method could achieve 100 percent absorption under ideal conditions.
Why the Shape of a Photon Matters
Two qubits (two atoms, for example) can exchange quantum information when one emits a photon and the other absorbs it. But photons do not behave simply like tiny particles moving between two points. Their wave properties determine how efficiently they can be transferred.
“When a qubit emits a photon, you must not picture the photon as a tiny particle that is simply shot out,” says Dr. Zeyu Kuang from the Institute of Theoretical Physics at TU Wien. “The photon is a wave, and a wave has a certain shape and a certain extension.”
The researchers compare photon emission to striking a bell. The sound begins strongly and gradually fades, much like the wave emitted by a qubit. Unfortunately, this waveform is poorly suited to absorption by another qubit. A pulse that gradually increases in strength before reaching its peak would work much better.
Stefan Rotter, Zeyu Kuang, Oliver Diekmann and Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero (from left to right) Credit: TU Wien
Reversing a Photon’s Waveform
The solution relies on time-reversal symmetry, a fundamental principle of quantum mechanics. Under ideal conditions, a quantum process can run in reverse, meaning a photon emitted with a particular waveform can be perfectly absorbed if that waveform is reversed in time.
“This follows from time-reversal symmetry in quantum mechanics,” Oliver Diekmann explains. “Under ideal conditions, quantum dynamics are reversible. If a qubit perfectly emits a photon with a particular waveform, the time-reversed process tells us which waveform that qubit can absorb perfectly.”
To achieve this reversal, the researchers propose using a specially engineered optical waveguide. Unlike light traveling through a vacuum, different frequency components of light inside a waveguide can move at different speeds. This behavior, known as dispersion, can be controlled to reshape the photon pulse during transmission.
A Potential Breakthrough for Quantum Communication
“We calculated how this goal can be achieved and simulated the process on a computer,” says Prof. Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero. “Our results indicate that the required setup should be technically feasible. This passive approach could significantly improve the absorption of photons by qubits and thereby increase the efficiency of many quantum technologies.”
Although the approach has not yet been demonstrated experimentally, the simulations suggest that carefully designed waveguides could make photon transfer substantially more reliable, potentially improving the performance of future quantum computers and communication networks.
Reference: “Passive Quantum State Transfer in a Dispersion-Engineered Waveguide” by Zeyu Kuang, Oliver Diekmann, Lorenz Fischer, Stefan Rotter and Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero, 4 September 2026,
Physical Review Letters
DOI: 10.1103/m2md-rxkv

title: After 150 Years, Scientists May Have Solved the Mystery of Westminster Abbey’s Roman Coffin
content:
Skeleton: the skull, as repaired in 1869. Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd.
Radiocarbon dating and traces of a vanished wooden coffin suggest that a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey became the final resting place of a medieval abbot.
A Roman stone coffin at Westminster Abbey bears the name of a wealthy Briton who lived nearly 1,700 years ago. Yet the skeleton found inside appears to belong to someone who died centuries later. After more than 150 years of uncertainty, new archaeological evidence has narrowed the mystery to two medieval monks who once led the monastery.
The limestone sarcophagus carries an inscription commemorating Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in the city around AD 300 to 400. Its lid, however, features a large Latin cross dating to approximately the 10th or 11th century. The difference in dates suggests that the Roman coffin was reused for a much later burial, leaving the identity of its occupant unresolved.
A new analysis by Professor Warwick Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey, concludes that the remains most likely belonged to a high-ranking medieval monk. His findings, published in the peer-reviewed
Journal of the British Archaeological Association
, identify two possible occupants.
Interior of the sarcophagus. Detail of the western part, prior to in situ cleaning of the skeletal remains. Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd.
The leading candidate is Aelfwig, who died around 1020 after serving as Abbot of Westminster Abbey, which was then a Benedictine monastery. Another possibility is his successor, Wulnoth, who died in 1049. Both men are believed to have been buried at the Abbey.
“We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus,” says Rodwell.
A broken lid and a hidden coffin
The coffin’s complicated history has made identifying its occupant particularly difficult. Workmen first accidentally uncovered it in 1820 while working in the area of King Henry III’s original sacristy on the north side of Westminster Abbey. During that encounter, the stone lid was broken into six pieces. The damage was repaired when the sarcophagus was officially rediscovered in 1869.
Skeleton: pathology. A. Left tenth and eleventh ribs, showing well-healed fractures. B. Left tibia and fibula, showing evidence of a non-specific infection. Scales of 10 cm. Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd.
The burial site has since undergone several investigations. In 2009, Channel 4’s Time Team examined the archaeology and structure of the medieval sacristy. More recently, Pre-Construct Archaeology (PCA), one of the UK’s largest commercial archaeological and heritage practices, carried out an excavation completed in 2025. That work was needed to enable construction of the King Charles III Sacristy, which is scheduled to open in 2027.
One of the most revealing developments, however, came in 2016, when the Roman sarcophagus was sent to a conservation studio. Although the skeleton had long been believed to be lost, PCA researchers lifted the lid and discovered that an almost-complete set of human remains was still inside.
The researchers also noticed a rectangular outline marked by white residue on the interior of the stone coffin. The residue came from lime, a substance traditionally used in burials, and its shape suggested that a wooden coffin had once rested within the sarcophagus.
Interior of the sarcophagus. Image shows as it was found upon opening in 2016. Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd.
“Although no physical traces of that feature remained, it can only have been a timber coffin, which has completely decayed over the course of the seven centuries that the sarcophagus was buried in the sacristy courtyard,” writes Rodwell.
This evidence helps explain how the Roman burial container was reused. The medieval occupant appears to have been placed inside a wooden coffin, which was then enclosed within the older stone sarcophagus. Its lid was re-carved with a prominent Latin cross, adapting the Roman monument for a Christian burial.
Interior of the sarcophagus. After the removal of rubble and superficial dirt on the bones. Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd.
Rodwell describes the surviving outline of the wooden coffin as a “remarkable new discovery.” He also believes the deceased was “honored” with a “fine sarcophagus,” suggesting that the burial was intended for someone of considerable religious standing, potentially an abbot.
Bones date the burial to Saxon England
Further evidence came from a detailed examination of the human remains. James Young Langthorne, a human bone specialist with PCA, determined that the deceased was a man between 35 and 49 years old who stood approximately 5 feet 9 inches (175 centimeters) tall.
Interior of the sarcophagus. The empty coffin. Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd.
Those findings differ considerably from an assessment made in the 1800s, which described the skeleton as belonging to a “robust young man” who was no more than 30 years old and stood about 5 feet 7 inches (170 centimeters) tall.
A sample of bone was also sent to the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre for radiocarbon dating. The results placed the remains between AD 987 and 1052, a period that includes the deaths of both Aelfwig and Wulnoth.
“This confirms that the reuse of the sarcophagus, and the associated remodeling of its cover, occurred in the late Saxon period,” says Rodwell.
Two possible identities, no definitive answer
The new age estimate and radiocarbon results support the possibility that either abbot was buried in the sarcophagus. Neither man’s birth date is known, making it difficult to distinguish between them using the skeletal evidence alone.
Excavation of the sacristy site in progress, 2019. View west. The pit from which the sarcophagus was removed in 1869 is labelled ‘S’. Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd.
“We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to fifty when he died.”
Aelfwig may nevertheless have a slight advantage as a candidate because of his earlier connection to the monastery.
“The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.”
Although the evidence cannot yet establish which abbot occupied the coffin, the combination of radiocarbon dating, skeletal analysis, and archaeological discoveries has substantially narrowed the possibilities. The sarcophagus, originally created in Roman Britain and later adapted for a medieval Christian burial, is now on public display in the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.
Reference: “Westminster Abbey’s Roman Sarcophagus and its Afterlife” by Warwick Rodwell, 20 October 2026,
Journal of the British Archaeological Association

title: Scientists Discover Mysterious 150,000-Year-Old Bone From an Extinct Human Relative in Chinese Cave
content:
The Penghu 1 jawbone was discovered off Taiwan and previously identified as Denisovan through ancient protein analysis. Although not part of the new Bianfu Cave study, this fossil provided additional evidence of the geographic range and physical characteristics of these ancient human relatives. Credit: Chun-Hsiang Chang, Jay Chang
A search through more than 60,000 bone fragments uncovered the first confirmed Denisovan radius, a forearm bone offering rare clues to how these ancient human relatives were built.
A forearm fragment from a cave in southwest China combines features resembling those of Neanderthals and modern humans, yet it belonged to neither. Proteins preserved in the bone identify its owner as Denisovan, part of an ancient human group recognized through genetic evidence.
The fragment is the first, and so far only, confirmed Denisovan radius, one of the two long bones in the forearm. Denisovans are thought to have lived across much of Asia, but their fossil record is sparse, particularly for bones below the skull. That scarcity has left researchers with little evidence of the physical traits that helped them adapt to different environments.
The radius is among five remains from Bianfu Cave in Yunnan Province that a new study identified as Denisovan. Dating to the late Middle Pleistocene, the fossils fill a longstanding gap in the group’s known distribution in southwest China. Professor Qiaomei Fu of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) led the research in collaboration with multiple institutions. The findings were published in
on September 9.
Neanderthal and modern human traits combined
Cataloged as BFD771, the radius fragment preserves the end nearest the elbow. Its large dimensions at that end resemble Neanderthal radii, as does the likely inward orientation of its radial tuberosity, the bony projection where the biceps muscle attaches. Its overall external shape, however, is closer to that of modern humans. So is the geometry of a cross section through the middle of its neck, the narrowed region near the elbow end. The researchers interpret this combination as evidence of distinctive mechanical demands and behavioral adaptations in Denisovans, differing from those inferred for Neanderthals and modern humans.
The geographical location of the Bianfu Cave and the morphology of the two human teeth and three newly discovered Denisovan bones. Credit: IVPP
Two skull fragments, BFD767 and BFD769, provided another anatomical comparison. Both are pieces of parietal bones, which form part of the top and sides of the skull. Their skull vault thickness patterns most closely resemble those of
Homo heidelbergensis
and late Middle Pleistocene archaic
Bone shape narrows the search
Finding these bones required narrowing a collection of more than 60,000 fragments. Researchers increasingly use Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry, or ZooMS, to screen large fossil collections by examining protein signatures. The technique requires minimally invasive sampling and is simple, fast, and relatively inexpensive. Even so, hominin fossil recovery rates at sites such as Denisova Cave and Baishiya Karst Cave have been just 0.1%. Applying ZooMS to every fragment from Bianfu Cave would have been costly and inefficient.
The team instead developed a “morphological pre-screening + ZooMS identification” strategy, first examining bone shapes to select 22 potential hominin remains. ZooMS then confirmed that the two parietal fragments and the radius fragment belonged to hominins, the group that includes humans and our extinct close relatives. The combined approach substantially improved screening efficiency and provides a repeatable method for searching other Paleolithic sites with abundant bone fragments.
BFD767 and BFD771 came from Layer 7, dated to approximately 148,000 to 134,000 years ago. That layer also contained four hominin teeth, two of which the researchers included in the study: a lower fourth premolar, YHB3518, and a lower second molar, YHB3075. The other skull fragment, BFD769, came from the older Layer 9, dated to approximately 167,000 to 150,000 years ago.
Proteins identify five Denisovan remains
Identifying the bones as hominin remains did not reveal which ancient human group they belonged to. To find out, researchers analyzed proteins preserved in three bones and two teeth, recovering 6 to 16 proteins from each specimen. Protein fragments in the tooth enamel also indicated that both teeth belonged to males.
All five fossils carried the Denisovan-specific protein variant
R996K. Additional variants in the teeth supported this identification and helped distinguish the fossils from other ancient human groups, including
Homo erectus
The researchers also constructed evolutionary trees using the recovered protein sequences. All five specimens clustered with the Denisovan specimen Denisova 3, with 100% posterior probability, providing strong support for their identification.
These findings make Bianfu Cave the richest known source of Denisovan fossils outside Denisova Cave. Dating to a glacial period known as Marine Isotope Stage 6, the remains suggest that the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau’s relatively warm climate and abundant food resources may have provided a favorable habitat for Denisovans.
Reference: “Ancient proteins identify various Denisovan remains from Southwest China” by Huiyun Rao, Song Xing, Qijun Ruan, Fan Bai, Yuhao Zhao, Zhongyou Wu, Siyuan Tang, E. Andrew Bennett, Xiaotian Feng, Sungui Lin, Qingfeng Shao, Xiong Yang, Zitao Li, Kai Zhou, Feng Liu and Qiaomei Fu, 9 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10976-9

title: Scientists Trap a Rare-Earth Metal in a Molecular Cage, Unlocking a Strange New State
content:
Chemistry
Terbium is a silvery-gray rare-earth metal known for its unique magnetic and luminescent properties. Used in display screens, lighting, and advanced electronic devices, it also holds promise for emerging technologies such as quantum computing and highly sensitive sensors. Credit: Shutterstock
Molecular cages helped chemists remove one electron from terbium, making an unusual form easier to study for possible uses in quantum computing and advanced sensors.
Rare-earth metals are essential to modern technologies, from smartphones and high-performance magnets to advanced medical devices. Yet separating these valuable elements remains a major challenge because many share remarkably similar chemical properties. Terbium is particularly difficult to manipulate, as it strongly favors a stable electronic state that resists change.
Now, researchers led by the University of Iowa have found a way to overcome this barrier, trapping terbium inside specially designed molecular cages and stabilizing an unusual form of the metal under ordinary environmental conditions. The breakthrough could open new possibilities for rare-earth separation and technologies ranging from quantum computing to advanced sensors.
Terbium resists giving up an electron
Terbium usually favors the plus-3 oxidation state, as do the other lanthanides. Oxidation states track how many electrons an atom has formally lost or gained, and moving terbium from plus-3 to plus-4 requires removing one electron. The plus-3 state is terbium’s most stable and has been well documented, while its behavior in other states remains much less explored.
“You can compel it to give away or accept an electron,” explains Korey Carter, an assistant professor in the University of Iowa’s Department of Chemistry, “but it’s generally energetically unfavorable.”
Isolating terbium without an air-free lab
Carter led the study with Pere Miro, an associate professor in the same department. Their team built a molecular assembly of tungsten and oxygen called a polyoxometalate and added binding agents known as ligands. The resulting cage-like structures held terbium in place while the researchers changed its chemistry.
With a terbium atom sandwiched in these cages, the chemists added potassium persulfate, a chemical oxidant. The reaction removed an electron from terbium, changing its charge and shifting it into the plus-4 oxidation state. The team isolated this unusual form and described it in detail.
Chemists led by the University of Iowa have isolated the rare-earth metal terbium under normal environmental conditions, which could lead to greater uses. The illustration shows how the team devised a cagelike, molecular structure primarily composed of tungsten (gray) and oxygen atoms (red) that bound the terbium (brown), creating the conditions for the terbium atom to change its oxidation state and be separated. Credit: Korey Carter lab, University of Iowa
“One of the challenges with lanthanides is they prefer to be in the same oxidation state, and it’s tricky to change that state and thus separate one from another without it being performed in a tightly controlled environment, such as a lab,” says Carter, the study’s co-corresponding author. “But we devised a method to isolate, or separate terbium, by changing its oxidation state in an environment that doesn’t require specialized lab controls.”
Previous researchers had produced terbium in the plus-4 state in rigorous air-free environments, according to Carter. The Iowa team worked under ambient conditions, without special controls for temperature, humidity, or pressure.
“If you were in your house and you were setting up a chemistry experiment, it would be analogous to what we were doing in the lab,” he says.
The silvery-gray metal is mined primarily in China, though it is also found in the United States and a few other countries. It already supports a broad range of technologies. Terbium is central to the green phosphors that produce light in televisions, fluorescent lamps, and LED displays, and it plays a key role in solid-state devices and fuel cells. It has also improved the safety of medical X-rays by allowing the same image quality to be achieved with much shorter exposure times.
The new method provides a proof of concept for potentially easier, less expensive separation of terbium, with possible lessons for separating other lanthanides. Making these less familiar chemical states more accessible could also help researchers investigate properties relevant to quantum technologies, which use the unusual behavior of atoms and smaller constituents. Potential applications include computing and advanced sensors for navigation, medical imaging, and other fields.
Carter’s group now wants to apply what it learned from terbium to actinides, a group of highly radioactive elements. Members of this group are used in cancer-fighting treatments, to power cardiac pacemakers implanted in the body, and in smoke detectors.
“Our findings highlight the ability to do transformative research at the University of Iowa, and they provide a platform to extend the chemistry to the actinide series in UI Radiochemistry laboratories,” Carter says.

title: Why Do We Have Necks? Scientists Uncover a 380-Million-Year-Old Evolutionary Twist
content:
Reconstruction of the skeleton of Tiktaalik roseae, a 375-million-year-old fossil fish. New research using modern sturgeons as an analogue suggests that stem tetrapods, like Tiktaalik, and the earliest land animals had stiff necks, not the flexible necks that scientists have long believed. Credit: Tom Stewart, Penn State
The first necks may owe more to the beginnings of walking than to looking around, according to models showing how little our early ancestors could move their heads.
In fish, the shoulders attach directly to the skull, so looking left or right means turning the whole body. Some of the animals making the transition from water to land about 380 million years ago began to develop a separate neck. Yet new research suggests that this change did not give them much more freedom to move their heads.
Models combining new fossil evidence with mechanical tests on living fish indicate that these early necks remained stiff, challenging the long-standing idea that they evolved to let the head move more freely. The international study, which included Tom Stewart, an assistant professor of biology at Penn State, was published October 14 in
The presumed advantage of looking around
Fossils from the Devonian Period, about 420 million to 360 million years ago, capture animals with a mixture of aquatic traits and features associated with life on land. Some had robust fins that might have supported their weight, allowing them to prop themselves up or push along the bottom in shallow water. Distinct necks also began appearing in these transitional fish.
“This is a really interesting time in Earth’s history where some of the first forests are forming, and there’s a really radical reorganization of the Earth,” Stewart said. “So, understanding exactly when our lineage made that transition from water to land, how it was achieved, and which anatomical systems were changing is an important part of that story. What’s cool is that many of the changes that were occurring in the skeleton at this time, about 380 million years ago, are still reflected in our own bodies today.”
One of those transitional fish was Tiktaalik, whose fossils come from Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada, in the northern Arctic.
Illustration of a sturgeon, top, and an artist’s reconstruction of the fossil fish, Tiktaalik, one of the closest relatives to limbed vertebrates. New research used biomechanical studies in the sturgeon to model the flexibility of the neck in the first animals to venture out of the water and onto land. The research suggests that the earliest land animals may have had stiff necks, not the flexible necks that scientists have long believed. Credit: Vic Putinski
“The materials have been really important because Tiktaalik is one of the closest relatives to limbed vertebrates,” Stewart said. “It helps us to reconstruct a lot of intermediary steps in the transition to life on land, such as the move from suction feeding in water to biting on land or from swimming to walking.”
For the ancestors of four-limbed animals, known as tetrapods, the ability to look down or from side to side could have helped them find food and avoid predators in shallow water or on land. Scientists reasoned that these environments might make independent head movement more useful than it was in deeper water.
“Tiktaalik is one of these fossil fish, and it was first described in 2006,” Stewart said. “It has been reasonably assumed for decades that this separation of head and shoulders must have allowed the head to move more freely, so the hypothesis that neck mobility was an evolutionary driver for this change in the tetrapod body plan has prevailed, at least until now.”
Living fish help reconstruct ancient movement
Testing that explanation required reconstructing a backbone unlike those of most vertebrates alive today. Early tetrapods and their close relatives had a long rod of tissue called the notochord running through the entire vertebral column. Their vertebrae were small and arranged around this large core of soft tissue, which behaved differently from the joints between vertebrae typical of modern animals.
“The fish that were undergoing these changes had a vertebral column that was largely made up of soft tissue, which, unlike bone, is rarely preserved in the fossil record,” Stewart said. “In these cases, we can look to modern animals to serve as analogs for the past, like how living birds can teach us about now extinct dinosaurs.”
Backbones built around a notochord are rare today, although they were common throughout the history of life on Earth. Sturgeon, distantly related fish sometimes called living fossils because of their primitive features, retain this kind of backbone. That made them a useful way to investigate the mechanical properties missing from the fossils.
“We want to understand how these early tetrapods were living and how that is reflected in changes to their bodies,” Stewart said. “Trying to reconstruct where an animal lived, how it moved, what its behavior was, is a really difficult thing. The cool part of this story is that it combines data from fossils and studies of living animals in a mechanical, functional perspective to reconstruct what the changes we see in the animal’s anatomy mean for their behavior.”
A neck without much head movement
The researchers measured the stiffness of modern sturgeon notochords, then applied those material properties to models of the necks of early tetrapods and transitional relatives such as Tiktaalik. The models allowed them to test whether separating the shoulders from the skull would have freed the head to move despite the backbone’s structure.
“I undertook this study to find out how big of a difference this change in anatomy made for these animals,” said Dana Korneisel, a postdoctoral researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden and first author of the paper. “The vertebral columns of sturgeon are built a lot like those of early tetrapods, but they didn’t seem terribly stiff. So, after doing the modeling, the lack of significant head mobility for almost all of these animals was a huge surprise.”
The estimates considered only the backbone. Muscles, skin, and, in many of these animals, bones embedded in the skin could have restricted movement further, meaning the living animals may have had even less neck mobility than the models suggest.
“Head elevation in these animals was no more than what you would expect in fish and, sometimes, even less,” Korneisel said. “We found that the kind of head twisting that we can do when we shake our heads was not feasible in any of these animals.”
With little extra head movement available, the researchers suggest that a distinct neck likely arose instead from anatomical changes associated with using the front limbs for locomotion. Greater flexibility appears to have been a later benefit, rather than the advantage that initially drove the separation of head and shoulders.
“We know that tetrapods did eventually gain higher neck mobility,” Korneisel said. “Clearly it was advantageous eventually, but it was not an advantage available to these early tetrapods yet because of the limitations of their anatomy.”
Reference: “Early tetrapod neck mobility modelled using an extant analogue” by Dana E. Korneisel, Cassandra M. Donatelli, Linfang Han, Thomas A. Stewart, Andrew L. Traynor, Benjamin K. A. Otoo, Marcos Martinez, Tetsuto Miyashita, Emily M. Standen and Hillary C. Maddin, 14 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11158-3

title: Tiny Magnets Implanted in Muscles Are Giving Prosthetic Hands a Remarkable New Ability
content:
Technology
Graphical representation of the technology developed in the study. Credit: Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna
Tiny magnets implanted in muscles are helping a prosthetic hand feel like it is opening and closing naturally.
You can close your eyes, make a fist, or reach for an object without ever needing to look at your hand. That seemingly effortless ability depends on a hidden sense called kinesthesia, which tells the brain how muscles and limbs are moving. After an amputation, this vital stream of sensory information is disrupted, making even simple movements with a prosthetic hand more difficult and less intuitive.
Now, researchers led by the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa, in collaboration with Cleveland Clinic, have uncovered new clues about how the brain interprets these movement signals. Their findings, published in
Science Advances
, suggest that the brain perceives finger movements as coordinated patterns rather than isolated actions. The discovery could help scientists develop prosthetic hands that not only move more naturally but also restore the feeling of movement itself.
The team compared data from the world’s only two neural-machine interfaces designed to restore this sense in upper limb prostheses. Despite their different designs, both produced sensations of coordinated finger movements, suggesting that the brain organizes incoming muscle signals into grasp patterns known as “synergies.”
Implanted Magnets Create Movement Sensations
Vibrating a muscle can make someone feel that a limb is moving. But applying vibration from outside the body also stimulates the skin, mixing sensory signals in ways that can complicate feedback from a prosthesis.
Sant’Anna’s myokinetic kinesthetic interface (MKkI) targets the muscles through small magnets implanted in the remaining forearm. The magnets generate vibrations within the muscles without directly stimulating the skin. Researchers connected this bidirectional interface to the Mia Hand, a robotic hand developed by Sant’Anna spin-off company Prensilia.
Myokinetic Kinesthetic Interface. Credit: Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna
A 34-year-old Italian participant tested the system for six weeks. He experienced sensations of his hand opening and closing, with fingers appearing to move together in patterns closely resembling natural movement.
“The myokinetic kinesthetic interface is unique because it uses a simple, minimally invasive implant to stimulate muscles without touching the skin. This approach may be the key to better understanding how human motor control works but also how to restore movement sensation after amputation,” says Federico Masiero, Ph.D., the study’s first author. A former Ph.D. student at Sant’Anna, Masiero is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Munich Institute of Robotics and Machine Intelligence (MIRMI) of the Technical University of Munich (TUM).
Different Interfaces Reveal A Shared Pattern
The sensations reported in the Italian trial resembled those experienced by participants using a
kinesthetic feedback system developed at Cleveland Clinic
. That system combines surgical nerve redirection with robotics, whereas Sant’Anna’s approach uses implanted magnets. Both selectively vibrate deep muscles to generate movement sensations.
Across the two systems, users felt coordinated finger actions rather than isolated movements. Both teams also observed that some sensory information was processed without users immediately becoming consciously aware of it. The findings suggest that muscle feedback may be organized into coordinated movement patterns at a more subconscious level than previously understood.
“The ability to compare independently generated data from two very different interfaces makes these findings especially compelling,” says Professor Paul Marasco, Ph.D., who coordinated the study at Cleveland Clinic. “It gives us a stronger foundation for designing therapies and devices that work with the nervous system in a more natural way, with the ultimate goal of improving outcomes for patients.”
Understanding that organization could help researchers deliver feedback that better matches how the brain handles movement. Beyond prosthetics, the findings may eventually inform
stroke rehabilitation
, epilepsy, and pain treatment, although those applications remain possibilities for future research.
Combining Prosthetic Control With Sensation
The next challenge is to use the implanted magnets for control and sensation at the same time. Building on
earlier research
, the team plans to track the magnets’ positions to control the prosthesis while simultaneously applying vibrations to the same magnets to provide movement feedback.
The longer-term goal is a permanent implant that can be studied beyond the initial six-week trial. Together with the teams’ previous
collaborative studies
, this work lays a foundation for combining intuitive control with natural grasp sensations in a new generation of more human-like prosthetic hands.
“Our solution was implemented as a preliminary demonstrator: the implant was designed to last six weeks, a period we considered sufficient for an initial verification of the interface’s usefulness and effectiveness. The results were very promising and prompted us to explore a permanent implantable solution, which will allow us to study the interface over much longer periods and with a larger number of participants,” says Professor Christian Cipriani, who created the interface and coordinated the study.
Reference: “Coordinated hand movement sensation revealed through an implanted magnetic prosthetic kinesthetic interface” by Federico Masiero, Mattia Gentile, Marta Gherardini, Eliana La Frazia, Charles H. Moore, B. Ülgen Kilic, Valerio Ianniciello, Roberta Reho, Tommaso Mori, Flavia Paggetti, Lorenzo Andreani, Simon A. Whitton, Paul D. Marasco and Christian Cipriani, 24 June 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adx5046
The study, coordinated by The BioRobotics Institute of the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa, in collaboration with the Pisa University Hospital (AOUP) and Cleveland Clinic, was supported by European, Italian, and U.S. funding. These include the ERC projects MYKI and MYTI, the Fit For Medical Robotics and PROPRIOUSS projects funded by the Italian Ministry of University and Research, and US data originally collected under awards from the NIH Office of the Director and DARPA. The first author of the study is a researcher at the Technical University of Munich, funded by a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Action fellowship.

title: “Strangest of Its Kind”: Scientists Uncover a Bizarre Bacterial Self-Destruct Switch
content:
Scientists have uncovered an unusual bacterial immune system that overturns long-standing assumptions about how retrons defend against viruses. Credit: Shutterstock
An unusual bacterial defense uses DNA to switch on toxin production, suggesting a new way to build molecular tools that control genes.
An infected bacterium can protect its neighbors by destroying itself before the virus inside it has a chance to multiply. Bacterial immune systems called retrons trigger this sacrifice when they detect particular strains of phages, the viruses that infect bacteria.
Decades of research have established a familiar explanation for how this works. A toxin stays ready inside the cell, restrained by small, single-stranded DNA molecules. An invading phage disturbs that DNA, releasing the toxin to kill the cell and stop the infection from spreading through the colony.
Researchers at Gladstone Institutes have now discovered a class of retrons that reverses the relationship between DNA and the toxin. In type VI retrons, DNA switches toxin production on rather than holding an existing toxin in check. The study, published in
Molecular Cell
, comes from the team of Gladstone Investigator Seth Shipman, PhD, its senior author.
“The way we typically detect retrons inside uninfected cells is by looking for this single-stranded DNA,” says Karen Zhang, a PhD student in Shipman’s lab and lead author of the study. “But type VI retrons caught our attention because they didn’t appear to have this signature. It was very odd, and we wondered if they might be broken.”
Gladstone scientists, including Karen Zhang, uncovered a counterintuitive class of bacterial defense systems, known as type VI retrons, that can be adapted to engineer more efficient gene editing tools. Credit: Michael Short/Gladstone Institutes
Tests in bacteria carrying type VI retrons showed that the defenses still worked against phages, leaving the researchers to explain how a functioning system could lack its expected DNA signal.
“That kicked off a long molecular odyssey,” Shipman says. “Whenever we tried the experiments we normally use to study retrons, they would fail, so we kept having to think of new ways to figure out how these retrons work.”
The DNA that standard tests missed
One early breakthrough came from Spacer-seq, a tool previously developed in Shipman’s lab. It uses molecular components of CRISPR-Cas, another bacterial immune system, to create a record of gene activity inside a cell. After standard methods repeatedly failed to detect DNA made by type VI retrons in uninfected cells, the team turned to this alternative approach.
“We had just about given up hope that any DNA was being made when this approach finally revealed a very, very low level of production in uninfected cells,” Zhang says.
Seth Shipman (left) and Karen Zhang (right) discovered a new complex retron system, which they plan to use when developing future molecular technologies. Credit: Gladstone Institutes
That trace gave the researchers a reason to keep investigating. Further experiments showed that type VI retrons produced no noticeable levels of toxin in uninfected cells, either. Phage entry triggered single-stranded DNA production to rise to the levels needed for defense. As the DNA accumulated, it interacted with an RNA molecule that had been blocking toxin production. This interaction removed the block, allowing toxin production to ramp up.
The toxin appears to be a tiny protein that embeds itself in the membrane surrounding the bacterial cell. By destabilizing that membrane, it kills the infected cell.
“It’s almost the mirror-image version of how we traditionally view retrons, because the DNA switches on toxin production instead of inhibiting an already-produced toxin,” Zhang says. “It would be fascinating to explore how bacterial evolution could have resulted in such a complex molecular system—whether type VI retrons are older or newer than other retrons, or whether they’re a stepping stone between different types.”
Zhang (left), Shipman (right), and their colleagues had to concoct novel experiments to decipher the mechanism of type VI retrons and reveal that they operate in a mirror-image version of traditional retrons. Credit: Gladstone Institutes
Bacterial defenses inspire gene-control tools
Retrons can also efficiently modify and deliver single-stranded DNA, capabilities that have drawn the attention of researchers developing DNA-editing tools. Shipman and his team are working to harness those abilities to rewrite disease-causing mutations inside human cells with unprecedented precision. Understanding the machinery of different retrons provides molecular designs they could adapt for that work.
“This is, by far, the strangest of the retron systems that we or anyone else has come across,” Shipman says. “These retrons operate with Rube Goldberg-level complexity, using molecular mechanisms that we would never have thought to invent, but that we’ll use in future technologies.”
The unique machinery of type VI retrons could be used to build molecular sensors and switches, as well as new types of antimicrobial therapies. Seen here are Shipman (left) and Zhang (right). Credit: Gladstone Institutes
The type VI machinery is already inspiring work in Shipman’s lab on synthetic sensors and switches that could control gene activity.
“This system represents a unique way to potentially build a molecular sensor and switch encoded in DNA and RNA, that no one has thought of before,” Zhang says. “Synthetic sensors and switches have many possible applications, both in treating disease and in designing experiments to better understand how certain diseases operate.”
The tiny, highly potent toxins could have medical uses as well. The scientists are working on ways to incorporate them into new antimicrobial therapies that could target and kill bacteria responsible for human disease.
“This study highlights why it’s so important for a molecular technology development lab like ours to keep looking to nature for inspiration,” Shipman says. “We can use what evolution has given us as starting points to build complex machines that would have been tremendously hard to even conceptualize.”
Reference: “Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein” by Karen Zhang, Matías Rojas-Montero, Darshini Poola, Josepha M. Klas, Arturo Carabias, Dennis J. Zhang, Mario R. Mestre, Ruiliang Zhao, Ana Dávila-Hidalgo, Lieza Chan, Kliment A. Verba, Guillermo Montoya, Rafael Pinilla-Redondo, Alejandro González-Delgado and Seth L. Shipman, 13 October 2026,
Molecular Cell
DOI: 10.1016/j.molcel.2026.09.026
The work was supported by the National Science Foundation, the Robert J. Kleeberg Jr. and Helen C. title: Scientists Discover a Strange Insect in the Himalayas Where No One Expected It
content:
Scientists have identified a new species of giant wormlion in the Himalayas, challenging long-held assumptions about where these unusual insects can survive (Artist’s concept). Credit: SciTechDaily.com
A newly identified Himalayan wormlion challenges the idea that its genus lives only in the tropics, raising the possibility of undiscovered relatives on nearby mountain slopes.
In rain-sheltered patches of sand and soil on the southern slopes of the Himalayas, wormlion larvae build funnel-shaped pits to catch prey. Larvae belonging to this group were first collected in southern Xizang in 1978, but without adult flies to examine, scientists could not confirm their identity.
Adult specimens collected during a 2025 expedition to Yadong County have now helped resolve that 48-year mystery. A team led by researchers at Dali University in China has described the new species,
Vermitigris tsangyanggyatso
, in a recent paper published in the open-access journal
Wormlions belong to Vermileonidae, a family of brachyceran, or short-horned, flies. They are the only known family of flies whose larvae capture prey by constructing these pits. Their hunting strategy evolved independently of the similar traps built by antlions, an example of evolutionary convergence.
Nine years to identify a wormlion
The researchers’ search for adult wormlions had already taken years of patient work with another species. Asked what first drew them to the family, the team recalled:
“Well, it was probably an accidental discovery that first motivated us. In 2015, while searching for pit-building antlions on Cangshan Mountain in Dali, China, we discovered an unfamiliar larva that we found particularly interesting. However, because the adults have an extremely short lifespan, we failed for many years to determine its identity.
It was not until 2024 that we finally obtained adults through artificial rearing in the laboratory. It turned out to be a new species, which we named
Vermiophis cangshanensis
. This first discovery therefore took nine years. Since then, we have paid close attention to wormlions wherever we encounter them.”
Morphological characters of Vermitigris tsangyanggyatso sp. nov. Credit: Li-Xia Shan and Ji-Shen Wang
Unusual anatomy and versatile pit building
The adults collected in Yadong revealed a species that is unusually large for its group. Their bodies measure up to 19.5 millimeters, about three-quarters of an inch, with wings nearly 16 millimeters, or 0.63 inches, long. A uniformly yellowish-brown to reddish-brown abdomen distinguishes
Vermitigris tsangyanggyatso
Its mouthparts also offer a clue to how it lives as an adult. Some related lineages diversified during the Late Mesozoic while developing elongated mouthparts for feeding on nectar. The new species instead has a markedly shortened rostrum, or snout, suggesting that it may not feed at all during its final life stage.
Fully grown larvae are larger than the adults, reaching 20 to 28 millimeters, or about 0.8 to 1.1 inches, in length. They have a single semicircular proleg, a fleshy, leglike appendage, bearing a distinct row of five to seven spines. Yet their anatomy has not fully explained how they construct traps in the different materials available to them.
Habitats and habitus of Vermitigris tsangyanggyatso sp. nov. Credit: Li-Xia Shan and Ji-Shen Wang
The team found larvae in three types of rain-protected shelter: fine-grained soil beneath giant rocks, wood debris under a pavilion, and fine-grained river sand accumulated beside a river. Field observations indicated a strong preference for the river sand. These sheltered sites provide the stable conditions the larvae need to maintain their pitfall traps, although the physical features that allow them to work across such different textures remain uncertain.
“We honestly do not know yet. Perhaps future behavioral experiments will help answer this question,” the team said when asked which features make that possible.
Dry refuges in wet Himalayan forests
Wet forests have traditionally been shown to act as barriers to wormlion dispersal. Finding this species in protected pockets within such an environment shows how members of
Vermitigris
can live there despite the surrounding wet conditions.
The adult observations offered another piece of the dispersal picture. On sunny days, most flies rested quietly on leaves near the places where their larvae lived. One specimen, however, was found farther away around agricultural fields, which the researchers interpreted as evidence of strong flight and dispersal abilities.
Distribution of Vermitigris spp. Question mark (?) indicates an unconfirmed record from India (Oldroyd 1947). Credit: Li-Xia Shan and Ji-Shen Wang
The Himalayan location also broadens the climates in which researchers might expect to find the genus. As the team explained:
“The previously known species were first discovered in tropical Southeast Asia, and these insects were therefore thought to be restricted to tropical regions. The discovery of this species suggests that they may also be capable of adapting to subtropical climates. We hope that more unknown species will eventually be discovered in mainland Southeast Asia, such as Thailand, as well as in southwestern China, including Yunnan, Guizhou, and Sichuan Provinces.”
The species name honors Tsangyang Gyatso, the sixth Dalai Lama, a celebrated 17th-century Tibetan poet-monk from Xizang known for his romantic verse and unconventional life. Its description raises the number of
Vermitigris
species recorded in China from one to two and the genus’s worldwide total from four to five. There are now 67 known living species of wormlion flies.
Many neighboring areas along the southern Himalayan slopes remain unsampled, leaving room for further fieldwork to uncover additional members of this poorly documented group. For co-author Ji-Shen Wang, the work also reflects a curiosity that extends beyond his original research specialty:
“From the perspective of science communication, I would say that although my primary research interest is the insect order Mecoptera (scorpionflies), I have gradually expanded my interests into Diptera (flies) as well.
As a naturalist, I find the diversity of life on Earth endlessly fascinating, and this curiosity about nature continually motivates me to explore and wonder. I would like to quote Herman Melville from
Moby-Dick
: ‘As for me, I am tormented with an everlasting itch for things remote. I love to sail forbidden seas, and land on barbarous coasts.”
