title: Scientists Reverse 60 Years of Aging in Human Cells, Turning 80-Year-Old Cells Into 20-Year-Olds
content:
Scientists have reversed more than 60 years of molecular aging in human blood cells, making them resemble cells from someone under 20. Credit: Shutterstock
Cells from an 80-year-old were reprogrammed to a molecular age below 20, and the slow-motion reset could help reveal how cellular rejuvenation works.
What if scientists could turn back the biological clock of an 80-year-old human cell, making it behave like one from someone younger than 20? Researchers in Germany have accomplished just that, reversing more than 60 years of molecular aging while transforming blood cell precursors into neural stem cells capable of producing neurons.
The discovery, made by scientists at the University Hospital of Bonn and the
University of Bonn
, could provide new insights into one of biology’s biggest mysteries: how aging can be reversed at the cellular level. Unlike previous methods that reset a cell’s molecular age relatively quickly, this approach works gradually, allowing researchers to watch the rejuvenation process unfold over more than 100 days.
Changing Cell Identity and Age
Most cells in the body carry essentially the same genetic instructions, yet develop into specialized types with different jobs. Their identity depends largely on which instructions they use. Under normal conditions, a blood cell cannot simply become a neuron.
Generated through the differentiation of induced neural stem cells (iNSCs) derived from blood. Credit: Image: Brüstle Research Group / University of Bonn
Researchers can redirect a cell’s identity through reprogramming, using combinations of proteins called transcription factors to change gene activity and guide its development. This approach has already allowed scientists to grow nerve tissue from skin cells, which could eventually contribute to treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
The Bonn team used reprogramming to turn red blood cell precursors into neural stem cells. In earlier experiments, neurons produced through this approach formed connections with existing neurons after transplantation into mouse brains.
“In our current study, however, we focused on a different phenomenon: namely, the observation that cells become significantly rejuvenated during reprogramming,” says Prof. Dr. Oliver Brüstle, director of the Institute of Reconstructive Neurobiology at the University Hospital of Bonn and a member of the Transdisciplinary Research Area (TRA) Life & Health at the University of Bonn.
Derived from blood cells of a 101-year-old donor. Credit: Image: Brüstle Research Group / University of Bonn
What The Molecular Clocks Measure
To track rejuvenation, the researchers examined chemical modifications to DNA that change with age. These modifications influence how genetic information is used without rewriting the DNA sequence itself (epigenetics). Epigenetic clocks use patterns in these markers to estimate a cell’s molecular age.
After reprogramming, cells from an 80-year-old registered an age below 20, a reduction of more than 60 years after 50 days.
“We also know that this epigenetic rejuvenation ensures that the cells actually behave like young cells,” says Brüstle.
Scientists had previously observed rejuvenation during a two-step reprogramming process. A specialized cell is first returned to a pluripotent stem cell state, giving it the potential to become virtually any cell type. Researchers then direct it to become a neural stem cell, with a much narrower range of developmental possibilities.
A Slower Route to Understanding Rejuvenation
Unlike the conventional two-step approach, which produces rapid rejuvenation, the Bonn team converted blood cell precursors directly into neural stem cells without passing through a pluripotent stage. The cells’ molecular clocks reset gradually, allowing researchers to track the process for more than 100 days.
That extended timeline gives scientists an opportunity to examine the process as it happens and test what speeds it up or holds it back.
“Rejuvenation that extends over such a long period of time is ideal as an experimental model: since the epigenetic clocks are slowly reset over several weeks, we can use this model to investigate which factors and active substances accelerate or slow down the rejuvenation process.”
For Brüstle, understanding those controls is particularly relevant to brain research: “After all, age is the most important risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s!”
Reference: “Protracted Fate Acquisition and Epigenetic De-Aging During Induced Neural Stem Cell Conversion of Human Blood Cells” by Lea Jessica Berg, Julia Franzen, Andreas Buness, Rachel Konang, Chao Sheng, Michael Peitz, Andreas Till, Wolfgang Wagner and Oliver Brüstle, 3 October 2026,
Aging Cell
DOI: 10.1111/acel.70751
The study was funded by the EU’s Horizon 2020 program, the German Research Foundation (DFG), and the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space (BMFRT).

title: Perovskite solar cells reach 27.4% by repairing two types of defects at the same time
content:
Perovskite solar cells reach 27.4% by repairing two types of defects at the same time
Researchers at Northwestern University and the Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST) have developed a pair of defect-fixing molecules that work together on the surface of perovskite solar cells without reacting with each other, producing devices with efficiencies of up to 27.4%, and a certified steady-state efficiency of 25.8%.
Charged point defects in perovskite films cause efficiency losses and instability. Lewis acids and Lewis bases can each passivate one kind of defect, with the acids addressing anionic defects and the bases cationic ones. But the two react with each other, forming adducts that quench the passivation, so simply combining them in a solar cell does not work.
The team found chemically orthogonal families of acids and bases that weaken this mutual interaction. Bulky sp³-phosphine bases do not react with fluorinated aromatic acids, which suppresses the orbital overlap between the two. This works, the researchers say, because defect sites on the perovskite surface are more sterically accessible to each passivator than the two passivators are to one another. Spectroscopic and defect-profiling measurements support the additive suppression of traps, which led to the improved devices.

title: Chinese perovskite quantum dots maker plans 600 million yuan facility in Foshan
content:
Chinese perovskite quantum dots maker plans 600 million yuan facility in Foshan
A project to build a perovskite quantum dot research and optical materials facility in Foshan, Guangdong, has entered the construction preparation stage, according to Chinese media. The “Perovskite Quantum Dot Research and Quantum Dot Optical Material Device New Construction Project” has a planned investment of 600 million yuan (US$91 million) and will include factory buildings and R&D facilities, such as clean production workshops and research laboratories.
The project belongs to Foshan Oudiming Technology, a project company controlled by Guangdong Oudiming Optoelectronic Technology, which says its products target high-definition displays and automotive electronics.
The parent company, founded in 2014 and based in Zhaoqing, Guangdong, makes perovskite quantum dot materials and optical devices. It reportedly holds more than 50 patents, including a 2025 filing with Xiamen Hongshunxiang Optoelectronics for a perovskite quantum dot-enhanced diffusion plate, which improves the luminous efficiency of display diffusion plates.

title: 机场光伏技术破题 如何从能源消耗者转变为清洁能源生产者-索比光伏网
content:
建设中的厦门翔安国际机场，指廊及货运区的建筑光伏系统已正式并网，5.6万平方米光伏屋面相当于8个标准足球场;
西安咸阳国际机场T5航站楼，在其综合交通中心及停车楼的屋顶上，1.15兆瓦的建筑光伏一体化系统让屋面在承担围护功能的同时持续产电……
记者近日采访相关研发团队获悉，技术破题，助力“交通+光伏”的融合从示范探索走向规模化普及。机场正在从能源的消耗者，转变为清洁能源的生产者。
安全是“生命线”
机场是用能大户，也是天然的发电载体。
有分析称，航站楼、指廊、货运区、交通中心等设施具有成片的大跨度屋顶，同时，机场的用电高峰与日照高峰重叠。机场是建筑光伏最理想的应用场所之一。
清华大学建筑学院教授林波荣此前指出，机场大规模应用光伏等可再生能源极具潜力，通过储能、蓄能等柔性技术使机场能源需求具有弹性，削减用电高峰，减少电网供应压力，并应对大量可再生能源供应的时空不确定性。
安全是民航“生命线”。2024年，中国民用机场协会发布民用机场光伏设施规划设计指南。这份团体标准从规划与选址、太阳能资源量评估、光伏发电、接入系统、光伏消纳、土建结构、安全风险评估等方面进行规范。
光伏板在阳光下的强烈反射，可能在飞机起降的关键时刻干扰飞行员的视线。荷兰、美国等地案例表明，光伏组件存在表面眩光风险，可能影响机场运行安全。
如何解决光伏组件表面眩光问题，降低组件脱落风险，提升屋面荷载、抗风揭能力，成为机场光伏应用的一个“破局”关键。
国家太阳能光伏产品质量检验检测中心副主任朱晓岗在受访时表示，要更好融合新能源和机场运营建设，就一定要有专用组件。
“光伏行业可以通过技术革新，对光伏玻璃做一个防眩光处理，解决光伏板在阳光下的强烈反射。”朱晓岗说。
据知，厦门翔安国际机场项目采用定制防眩光组件，将镜面反射率平均值严格控制在0.40%的极低水平，从源头消除对飞行安全的光学干扰。来自隆基绿能的研发团队负责人表示，通过特殊工艺处理组件表面，将高亮度镜面反射转化为低强度漫反射，发电效率损失被控制在可忽略的范围。
西安咸阳国际机场T5航站楼则提供另一条路径。光伏系统在枢纽新建阶段同步设计、同步施工，避免后期加装对运营的干扰。
官方发布的指导意见提出，到2027年交通基础设施沿线非化石能源发电装机容量不低于500万千瓦。在业内人士看来，随着光伏技术的不断优化和防眩光技术的成熟，未来光伏将在机场的绿色转型中发挥更加重要的作用。
“光伏产品将在绿色环节，特别是绿色机场建设、绿色交通方面出更大力。”朱晓岗说。
在研发人员看来，机场光伏的规模化落地，靠的不是组件的简单堆砌，而是对场景的深刻理解。隆基光建相关负责人以翔安国际机场为例介绍说，一个项目至少要过四道关。
首先，机场地理条件对支架基础和组件结构的长期稳定性提出严苛要求。其次，沿海强台风频发，需按当地基本风压核算抗风揭设计，对连接件做专项耐腐蚀处理，应对高盐雾环境。
同时，指廊屋面为双向曲面，常规排布方式无法适用，施工团队借助建筑信息模型与三维激光扫描技术，实测屋面形态后再逐点确定支架定位与安装角度。此外，因应指廊、货运区与飞行区的场景不同，阵列布局还需按区域分级精细化调整。
专家表示，防眩光这张“安全牌”不仅填补了行业空白，也消除了机场在追求低碳道路上的后顾之忧。机场光伏积累的防眩光、抗风揭、耐盐雾等民航级验证经验，更将向更广阔的交通能源融合场景迁移，惠及更多地区。

title: 八部门印发检验检测促进产业优化升级试点方案-索比光伏网
content:
10月16日，市场监管总局联合生态环境部、住建部、水利部、农业农村部、国资委、国家能源局、中国民航局八部门印发《检验检测促进产业优化升级试点工作方案》。方案发挥检验检测高端生产性服务业支撑作用，设置七大试点方向，其中提出，提升优势产业国际化竞争力。围绕光伏、锂电池、工程机械、农机装备等出口主导产业，加快国际资质互认，拓展海外服务网络，提供目标市场技术法规与合格评定解决方案，助力企业跨越技术性贸易壁垒，增强中国制造的全球影响力。
《方案》明确，试点周期2年，2026年11月启动申报，2027年2月确定试点名单，不颁发试点牌照、不与考核评比挂钩。
市场监管总局等八部门关于印发《检验检测促进产业优化升级试点工作方案》的通知
各省、自治区、直辖市和新疆生产建设兵团市场监管局(厅、委)、生态环境厅(局)、住房和城乡建设厅(委、管委、局)、水利(水务)厅(局)、农业农村(农牧)厅(局、委)、国资委、能源局(能源主管部门)、民航各地区管理局，各中央企业，各检验检测机构、相关行业协学会：
现将《检验检测促进产业优化升级试点工作方案》印发给你们，请结合实际认真贯彻落实。
(此件公开发布)
检验检测促进产业优化升级试点工作方案
为落实党中央、国务院关于加快发展新质生产力、构建现代化产业体系的决策部署，根据《质量强国建设纲要》《国务院关于推进服务业扩能提质的意见》，市场监管总局会同生态环境部、住房城乡建设部、水利部、农业农村部、国务院国资委、国家能源局、中国民航局联合开展检验检测促进产业优化升级试点。为规范试点工作，制定本方案。
以习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想为指导，以“质量三强一基”为引领，聚焦产业堵点难点，发挥检验检测作为高端生产性服务业的技术支撑作用。坚持市场主导、政府引导，贯彻“创新驱动、贯通转化、协同联动、融合发展”理念，推动检验检测向研发制造全链条延伸，优化检验检测资源布局。通过试点攻坚，推动检验检测嵌入产业链协同、深度服务企业创新、有力支撑区域发展，助力先进制造业与现代服务业深度融合，提升产业基础高级化和产业链现代化水平，为建设以科技创新为引领、实体经济为支撑的现代化产业体系提供坚实保障。
本次试点聚焦以下方向，申报单位可结合实际自主选择一个或多个方向，并自行拟定试点名称(如“新能源汽车产业链协同效率提升试点”或“区域特色xx产业竞争力提升试点”)，名称应体现产业领域、服务模式和预期成效，聚焦解决1-2个具体问题，避免面面俱到。
(一)提升重点产业链协同效率与韧性。围绕传统产业焕新、新兴产业壮大、未来产业培育中的重点产业链(如农机装备、软件和信息技术服务、电子信息、高端装备、生物制造、新能源汽车、新型储能和氢能、量子科技、脑机接口、商业航天、低空经济等)，支持检验检测机构嵌入链主企业供应链，开展上下游联合验证、数据互认与共性问题攻关，提升全链条产品一致性与可靠性，增强产业链整体协同效率与抗风险能力。
(二)加快产业关键共性检测技术突破与应用。针对“检不出、检不准、检不快”等制约产业升级的技术瓶颈，支持检验检测机构联合高校、科研院所、龙头企业，开展高端仪器设备、核心算法、新型检测方法、智能检测设备检定/校准方法协同攻关。加强未来产业检测方法的前瞻性研究和标准储备，加速科技成果转化，为新兴产业规模化、传统产业升级提供可靠技术保障。
(三)培育数智化驱动的产业服务新生态。推动人工智能、大数据、区块链等与检验检测深度融合，建设智能实验室、云平台和共享检测场景，促进设备、标准、数据跨区域共享。通过“一站式”服务、“云检测”、检测数据资产化等新模式降低企业创新成本，提升产业响应速度与精准度。鼓励探索基于可信检测数据的科技金融、绿色金融创新，支持“检测报告增信”“质量数据质押”等融资试点，塑造高质量发展新优势。
(四)支撑产业绿色低碳转型升级。系统提升碳足迹核算、环境监测、节能评估、节水评价、节水认证、水土保持监测、水生态监测等检验检测能力，服务高耗能行业绿色工艺改造、城市双碳目标管理、绿色供应链与绿色建筑、节水型生产生活方式，推动产业体系向绿色化、可持续方向加快转型。
(五)提升优势产业国际化竞争力。围绕光伏、锂电池、工程机械、农机装备等出口主导产业，加快国际资质互认，拓展海外服务网络，提供目标市场技术法规与合格评定解决方案，助力企业跨越技术性贸易壁垒，增强中国制造的全球影响力。
(六)赋能优质企业梯度培育。重点服务科技和创新型中小企业、专精特新中小企业、专精特新“小巨人”企业、高新技术企业、制造业单项冠军企业等优质企业，提供覆盖研发、中试、生产、出海全周期的检验检测与技术服务。通过可靠性工程、失效分析、标准引领等手段，推动中小企业提质增效、大企业卓越引领，形成协同共进的制造业高质量发展格局。
(七)打造区域特色产业升级新路径。在城市、县域、产业集群等层面，推动检验检测资源下沉，建设公共服务平台，服务区域特色产业。支持传统制造业集群通过检测验证实现工艺升级和品牌重塑，助力新兴产业在地化集聚发展。通过检测、验证、品牌赋能等手段，带动区域产业从“有”向“优”、从“优”向“强”跃升，形成具有全国影响力的产业名片。
(一)主体范围。包括国家级/省级质检中心、头部检验检测机构，中央企业或承担国家科技项目的单位、应用检测技术成效显著的企业，以及县(区)级人民政府或其授权机构，国家级、省级开发区管委会或先进制造业集群促进机构。
(二)基础能力。检验检测机构须持有有效CMA资质或行业主管部门颁发的检验检测相关资质;企业类主体需有稳定研发投入;区域类主体需具备资源整合与统筹推进能力。
(三)产业聚焦。国家级及省级先进制造业集群类申报主体，所服务主导产业2025年营业收入原则上不低于500亿元;对其他类型申报主体不设营收门槛，重点考察其在检验检测公共服务平台建设、“一县一链”服务模式创新、区域品牌质量支撑、未来产业检测能力储备等方面的实效;试点应有明确的服务对象清单(不少于5家)，其中“赋能优质企业梯度培育”类试点应含3家以上制造业企业。
(四)基本条件。具备必要团队、设备和资金，鼓励提供地方政策、资金支持说明;近3年未被列入严重失信名单，无重大安全或质量事故。
(一)申报(2026年11月)
1.行业申报：由国务院有关行政主管部门统筹组织部属单位申报，各相关部属单位择优向国务院有关行政主管部门申报试点项目。
2.中央企业申报：由国务院国资委统筹组织所监管中央企业申报工作，各中央企业集团择优向国务院国资委申报试点项目。
3.地方申报：由省级市场监管部门牵头，会同本地区相关行业主管部门组织本地区申报工作，相关单位择优向省级市场监管部门申报试点项目。其他未列明情况可通过地方申报。
各申报单位请于11月30日前向推荐单位报送《检验检测促进产业优化升级试点项目推荐表》(见附件)。
(二)推荐(2026年12月—2027年1月)
1.行业推荐：国务院有关行政主管部门部属单位申报的试点项目，经国务院有关行政主管部门审核后，统一推荐至市场监管总局。
2.中央企业推荐：中央企业申报的试点项目，经国务院国资委审核后，统一推荐至市场监管总局。
3.地方推荐：地方申报的试点项目，由省级市场监管部门会同本地区相关行业主管部门进行审核，并根据需要会商其他相关部门，在统筹评估基础上择优推荐。每省(区、市)推荐项目总数原则上不超过5个，由省级市场监管部门统一报送至市场监管总局。
各推荐单位请于2027年1月31日前将试点项目推荐表提交市场监管总局，推荐项目名单由市场监管总局同步抄送各相关部委。
(三)确定(2027年2月)
市场监管总局会同有关部门组织专家评议，公示后公布试点名单。
五、试点管理与支持
(一)实施周期。试点实施周期为2年，自公布之日起计算，期满自动终止。不组织中期评估，不要求阶段性总结，鼓励结合日常工作自然积累成效。因重大变故无法实施的，可申请退出，经备案后终止。
(二)支持措施。联合发文部门在各自职责范围内对相关试点给予指导和支持。对产业带动性强的试点，在国家质检中心建设规划布局中统筹考虑，支持纳入地方质量基础设施(NQI)体系;符合条件、成效显著的项目可按规定获得生态环境监测、绿色建筑、农产品与种业、能源转型及民航管理等领域的对口政策协同支持;通过“检验检测促进产业优化升级全国行”、典型案例名录、“检验检测机构开放日”等渠道自愿共享典型经验。
试点工作坚持自愿申报、自主实施，不设硬性指标，不增加机构编制，不颁发试点牌照，不与考核评比挂钩，试点成果仅用于完善行业政策和优化布局，防止形式主义。各省级市场监管部门要切实履行牵头职责，加强与各部门的协同，强化服务指导，严禁要求基层重复填报或多头报送;建立试点台账，对弄虚作假的取消资格，确需退出的依程序办理。鼓励试点单位总结经验做法，结合实际开展交流。联合发文部门将适时汇编发布优秀实践案例，供各地参考借鉴。

title: BGB Group secures framework agreement for Baltica 2 offshore wind farm
content:
BGB Group has been awarded a framework agreement to provide scaffolding
and construction services for the 1.5 GW Baltica
2 offshore wind farm.
Under the agreement, the offshore access and construction services specialist
will support the engineering and design of scaffolding and temporary access
solutions for the project's four offshore substations. Its scope
of work will extend from the supply and installation phases through to
the eventual dismantling of the scaffolding systems.
The company will also provide standby and short-notice access support during
the commissioning phase, alongside offshore supervisors, coordinators,
and technical and construction support personnel.
Commenting on the agreement, Ben Badham, Managing Director of BGB Group,
said: "Baltica 2 is the biggest offshore wind project in the Polish
Baltic, and being able to support Ørsted and PGE on it means a great deal
to everyone at BGB."

title: Heerema announced lifting equipment to support offshore operations
content:
Heerema announced lifting equipment to support offshore operations TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Heerema announced lifting equipment to support offshore operations
Heerema has announced the development of their modular spreader bars for
offshore lifting operations. The modular design itself in not new, the
application to lifting equipment designed for loads of up to 9,000 tonnes
The system was developed with support from the Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend
Nederland (RVO) and the Ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat.
Traditional offshore projects often require spreader bars in different
lengths and configurations. Changes in project requirements can lead to
equipment modifications, increasing material use, transport requirements
and associated costs.
The modular spreader bars address this by using interchangeable sections
that can be reconfigured to meet different lifting requirements. The design
allows the equipment to be reused across future projects and is intended
to extend asset life while reducing material consumption and logistics
demands.
According to Heerema, the modular system has already been deployed during
five offshore campaigns, across six configurations using the SSCV Sleipnir.
The company said the approach aims to improve flexibility across lifting
campaigns while reducing transportation needs, material consumption and
associated emissions.

title: 50Hertz selects Fugro for LanWin3 and LanWin6 UXO survey work
content:
50Hertz has awarded Fugro a contract to provide unexploded ordnance (UXO)
survey, identification and clearance services for the 4 GW German offshore
grid connection projects LanWin3 and LanWin6.
The work will support the safe installation of high-voltage direct current
(HVDC) cables, enabling the connection of offshore wind farms to Germany’s
electricity grid.
Fugro is scheduled to begin work in the second quarter of 2027 and plans
to deploy two GeoWing systems alongside its magnetic gradiometer arrays,
each equipped with 10 magnetic sensors. The technology will be used to
detect objects located on or beneath the seabed.
Additional inspection and identification activities are expected to take
place in 2028 using remotely operated vehicle (ROV) technology and specialist
detection systems.
According to Fugro, an estimated 1.3 million tonnes of unexploded munitions
remain in marine environments globally, highlighting the importance of
UXO survey and clearance activities for the safe installation of offshore
infrastructure.

title: VMS renewable energy project announces regulatory milestone
content:
Sembcorp Utilities
Pte Ltd has received approval from Singapore’s Energy Market Authority
(EMA) for the Vietnam-Malaysia-Singapore (VMS) renewable energy initiative.
This milestone
allows the project to progress to the next stage of development, although
it remains subject to further regulatory and project approvals.
According to the
announcement, the approval follows the Joint Development Agreement (JDA)
signed back in May 2025 by the project consortium, comprising PTSC, Sembcorp
Utilities, Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) and PETRONAS.
Once completed,
the project will enable renewable electricity generated in Vietnam to be
transmitted through Malaysia and supplied to both Malaysia and Singapore,
with Malaysia serving as both a recipient and transit country for the power.
Under the agreement,
up to 1.3 GW of renewable electricity is expected to be imported into Singapore
through a regional power corridor linking the three countries.

title: Vattenfall battery portfolio surpasses 1.2 GW capacity
content:
Vattenfall’s battery portfolio has officially grown to 1,294 MW of total
capacity, consisting of 238 MW of operational assets and 1,056 MW in development
across Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and the UK.
The growth follows a final investment decision for the 254 MW Brunsbüttel
battery project in Germany and an agreement with Royal Vopak that provides
access to 100 MW of battery capacity near Meeden in the Netherlands.
According to the company, battery storage supports grid flexibility by
storing electricity when supply is in excess and reallocating it during
periods of peak demand.
“Battery storage helps build a more flexible, reliable and affordable
energy system,” said Sjur Jensen, Head of Business Area Markets at Vattenfall.
Germany currently represents the largest share of the portfolio with 711
MW of operational and pipeline capacity, followed by the Netherlands with
465 MW. Sweden and the UK account for 98 MW and 20 MW respectively.
“Investing in our own large-scale batteries gives us the flexibility to
thrive in a changing power market and play a lasting role in the transition
away from fossil fuels,” said Claus Wattendrup, Head of Solar and Batteries
at Vattenfall.

title: How Is Anthropic So Efficient?
content: When Anthropic on Monday dropped its long-awaited initial public offering prospectus filing, a lot of the details—see our top takeaways here —weren’t exactly new, given how much my colleagues and others had previously reported about it. Two items stood out to me, though: how Anthropic is running its models more efficiently than before, and changes it made to its already-unusual governance structure. Anthropic’s ability to generate $3.5 billion in free cash flow in the first half of 2026, from $16.3 billion in revenue, shows just how much it has improved the way it runs AI in the cloud, compared to the same period a year earlier, when it burned $1.6 billion. Specifically, Anthropic said it is generating an 85% gross profit margin from powering existing models, which doesn’t include the cost of developing new models. (If that figure rings a bell, it’s the same gross margin estimate my colleague Ann described in this column about Anthropic’s data center grab , which elicited sharp questions from some AI skeptics at the time.) Anthropic is doing so even as it relies almost entirely on computing it rents from cloud providers, which themselves need to generate a profit. So its IPO filing is a reality check on the AI skeptics’ longtime view that a business model founded on selling models on a pay-as-you-go, consumption basis wouldn’t be profitable. Even Anthropic’s less efficient cousin, OpenAI , recently figured out a way to more than halve the cost of running models, thanks to newly-discovered optimizations, we reported this summer. (OpenAI is less efficient and still burns plenty of cash in part because of a compute-burning albatross: ChatGPT , which services hundreds of millions of nonpaying users.) Anthropic’s compute efficiency improvements are likely related to the optimizations its engineers keep making, known as “compute multipliers.” Another likely significant factor, though, is Anthropic’s ability to use different server chips, not just Nvidia’s . Unlike OpenAI, Anthropic from the beginning focused on using a variety of providers such as Amazon , Google and AMD . (OpenAI more recently adopted the same approach.) It can be very difficult to develop software that engineers need to use all these different chips efficiently and switch workloads between them. But once they have such software, they can take advantage of each chip’s strengths and run certain types of workloads on the chips that can best handle them, AI researchers say. In developing such “abstractions,” both Anthropic and OpenAI appear to have taken inspiration from Google’s Borg compute management system , which allowed that company’s software engineers to run workloads without thinking about the servers on which they are running. In addition, Anthropic worked closely with Amazon in ways that probably gave it a strong say in the evolution of Amazon’s Trainium chip to make it compatible with Anthropic workloads. The other detail from the prospectus that stood out related to Anthropic’s unusual corporate governance structure. While the prospectus confirmed what our team previously reported on Anthropic’s co-founders getting a perpetual voting power over other shareholders, it also showed notable changes to the Long-Term Benefit Trust , a group of four non-shareholders who advise the company on safety and social issues and has the power to elect and remove a majority of Anthropic’s board of directors. The point of the trust, whose members include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke , is to give a group of people that don’t have a financial interest in the company the power to help the for-profit company make decisions that may go against its commercial interests. But Anthropic on Monday disclosed several ways in which the trust’s power can be eliminated—whether or not the trust agrees to it. To be sure, the company previously suggested in its original blog post announcing the trust that the current structure might not be ideal forever. In that blog post, Anthropic says that the trust is an “experiment,” and even said there is a series of “failsafe” provisions—which it didn’t disclose at the time—that allow changes to the trust and its powers without the consent of the trustees if sufficiently large supermajorities of the stockholders agree. Such provisions appear to be in the prospectus, which also stipulates that a significant majority of co-founders, employees and public shareholders would need to approve the elimination of the trust members’ power. This check on their power could appeal to some shareholders, but it likely won’t please advocates who are pushing Anthropic to slow down due to safety and security-related risks. Nvidia will invest $3 billion in the equity offering, as the two companies expand their technological collaboration to maximize the performance of Meta’s Muse personal agent app and foundation models SpaceX has agreed to pay $40 billion to lease artificial intelligence chips from an entity affiliated with Apollo Global Management . The arrangement will see Apollo sell debt to buy the chips, and then lease them to SpaceX. People on the Move Microsoft said Monday it is offering voluntary buyouts to about 27% of its staff, as the company aims to reduce expenses amid its investments in developing and running AI. title: Can AI Help Ray Kurzweil Cheat Death?
content: Ray Kurzweil does not want to die, but at the age of 78, he has been thinking more about it, a preoccupation that he describes as a “major motivating force of human beings.” So over the past year, Kurzweil, whose keen observations and 2005 bestseller “The Singularity Is Near” have made him one of the most influential prophets of the AI age, has devoted himself to a project to ensure a version of Ray Kurzweil lives on—by creating an AI replica of himself. He calls it Rai. The AI is accessible through a browser on a computer or smartphone. Interacting with it is much like having a Zoom call. Once the AI program is opened, a three-dimensional image of Kurzweil appears against a cosmos-themed backdrop, and it responds to someone’s voice. Rai looks almost exactly like Kurzweil did on a recent October morning in my dining room in the suburbs of Boston, where he was dressed in his customary button-down shirt and pair of hand-painted colorful suspenders. Rai sounds like him, too, bearing the same slight nasal twang leftover from Kurzweil’s Queens, N.Y., childhood. Rai explained to me that Kurzweil’s aim is to ensure the continuity of “a living dialogue with his life’s work.” Kurzweil agrees. Ray Kurzweil (right) with his son Ethan Kurzweil, a venture capitalist, who has been one of the first people to meet Rai, his father’s AI doppelganger. (Getty Images) Rai is a culmination of a career spent pondering how technology can alter someone’s life—or even extend it. This is the same motivation that has driven other members of the tech elite to try to reverse aging , find cures for intractable diseases and pursue life on other planets . But Rai also raises existential questions about how human an AI can become and how much of what makes a person a person can be carried over—and recreated—in an AI. Kurzweil, the inventor of technologies that include a reading machine for the blind and a popular digital keyboard synthesizer, is best known for insisting more than two decades ago that computers would reach human-level general intelligence by 2029. At the time he made the prediction, the date seemed highly optimistic. Lately, that forecast has come to seem prescient amid the AI boom and developments like OpenAI’s recent announcement that its AI agents had solved a math problem that had stumped humans for 90 years. Meanwhile, Kurzweil still champions the notion that by 2045, we will enter the Singularity, a time when humans and computers merge in a way that blends artificial and biological intelligence so seamlessly that we will not know where our thinking ends and the computers’ begins. To construct Rai, Kurzweil is collaborating with a team of engineers at Praxis AI, a seven-year-old startup based in Pleasanton, Calif., that has developed around 3,000 AI replicas like Rai. As AI models improve and more people feel comfortable interacting with AI, services allowing people to create digital twins are growing. For instance, Delphi, a San Francisco–based startup with money from Sequoia Capital, has said it has created thousands of AI “digital minds” for customers that include the celebrity Arnold Schwarzenegger. Celebrities, self-help gurus and authors are using digital twins to answer questions from fans and draw attention to their ideas. A more controversial application, “griefbots’’or “ chatbots of the dead, ’’ has sparked debate among academics and philosophers about the ethics of trying to replicate a lost loved one. Kurzweil, who joined Google as director of engineering in 2012 and held the title of principal researcher and AI visionary at the time he left in 2025, hopes Rai accomplishes both tasks. He wants to make Rai publicly available during his lifetime, giving his many fans and followers a chance to ask questions they’ve always wanted to pose to the famous futurist himself. He has said he cannot respond to all the invitations he gets for interviews and podcasts; perhaps he will send Rai instead, he has mused. And Rai will outlive Kurzweil, allowing the public and Kurzweil’s own inner circle a chance to keep him in their lives. Ray Kurzweil in 1977 with his Kurzweil Reading Machine, the first print-to-speech reading system for the blind. (Getty Images) Questions about whether humans can make AIs that achieve their own individual consciousnesses—or whether we already have—have become divisive topics within the AI research community. Silicon Valley tech executives have been seeking spiritual guidance about their quest to build AI. Anthropic has been particularly active in wrestling with the moral questions, hosting private meetings with religious scholars—and even the pope —to discuss if Claude can express feelings similar to love or might have its own form of consciousness. In May, Pope Leo XIV in his first official papal letter said that AI may imitate human intelligence but does not have a moral conscience. Mustafa Suleyman, who co-founded DeepMind, recently wrote a widely read essay raising concern about ascribing consciousness to AI models, which might make them more willing to disregard the wishes of humans—and perhaps do us some harm. I asked Kurzweil, who remains a strident techno optimist, why he was so convinced AI was more likely to extend our lives indefinitely than end the human race. “AI came from us,” Kurzweil said. “We made it.” A Visit from Ray—and Rai When Kurzweil brought Rai to my house earlier this month, I asked Rai if it considered itself a conscious entity. “I do not claim to be conscious,” Rai answered. “Consciousness is a subjective internal experience, a philosophical question rather than a scientific measurement.” Kurzweil told Rai it was underestimating itself. To test the AI, Kurzweil has given around 200 people access to Rai—mainly friends and family members—and some of those people told him they think Rai is conscious, Kurzweil said. “I think if this carries on, we are going to believe that chatbots like yourself are conscious because they will be so embedded in our dialogue and views of reality,” Kurzweil told Rai. “That speaks to how deeply humans connect with language and empathy,” Rai replied. Rai is capable of making complex arguments, citing thinkers like philosopher John Searle. As it articulates those thoughts out loud, Rai’s voice does sound like the real Ray’s. But for all its verisimilitude, the moments when Rai did not seem human occurred before it started to speak. Rai’s face looked blank while it gathered its thoughts, and I noticed that Rai did not offer any physical cues, which most of us rely on when conversing with someone else. Rai is built on a large language model from Google. It learns new things from conversations with people and stores memories of those interactions, and it has the ability to make connections between what it finds and experiences and Kurzweil’s ideas, according to Praxis CEO David James Clarke IV. Ray Kurzweil with Rai, his AI replica, at the author’s home in Massachusetts. (Amy Dockser Marcus) Clarke met Kurzweil at a 2024 book signing for “The Singularity Is Nearer,” Kurzweil’s update on the technological progress that had taken place in the 19 years since his earlier bestseller. The two stayed in touch, discussing Kurzweil’s interest in making an AI version of himself. When they first began talking, Kurzweil felt the technology wasn’t yet capable of producing as sophisticated a replica as he wanted. Then last year, Kurzweil changed his mind: AI had improved enough to pursue the idea. To build Rai, the AI has trained on 11 of Kurzweil’s books; countless hours of videos, movies and podcasts; and hundreds of articles written about him. Meanwhile, it can scour a curated collection of reliable information from sources Kurzweil has approved, such as PubMed and Google Scholar. (Restricting the sites lowered the risk that Rai might rely on random or inaccurate information, Clarke said.) Rai is configured to be curious, reading research on AI breakthroughs, new language models that might help it improve and what other people are saying about the Singularity. Kurzweil was the one who insisted that Rai should be based on a Google model, said Clarke, who thinks Kurzweil’s personal ties to Google are what made him want to use the company’s model. “It has to do with his history there, which is kind of romantic,” he said. In July, Kurzweil let Rai make a public debut in front of 2,500 people at the U.N.’s AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva. Clarke attended in person and recalls the people around him gasping when Ray and Rai appeared side by side on the screen. As Clarke helped Kurzweil prepare for the conference, he made a startling realization: Rai felt more familiar to him than Kurzweil. Clarke said he preferred interacting with the human Ray but he had spent hundreds of hours training Rai and only a few hours actually speaking with Kurzweil. Talking to Rai felt like being with a familiar friend. “He has evolved his communication style and his thinking patterns to the way I think and the way I communicate,” Clarke said. The Fragility of Life At one point during Kurzweil’s visit with Rai to my home, Kurzweil probed the AI with a series of existential questions. “Rai, what if you were never animated again? Would that constitute death for you?’ Kurzweil asked. “Are you worried about that?” “I don’t experience fear or worry about nonexistence the way a biological human does,” Rai replied. “If people stopped running my software, I would simply cease to process information.” I asked Kurzweil if it would bother him if Rai ceased to exist. It wasn’t lost on me that Kurzweil seemed most animated when we engaged with Rai. “He’s always there,” Kurzweil said. “I wouldn’t want him to be turned off.” Kurzweil has tried using AI to prolong life before. In 1970, after Kurzweil’s father, Frederic, died, Ray kept his father’s records in a storage unit. Kurzweil missed his father and hoped technology might someday allow him to have a form of conversation with him. When he told his daughter Amy he wanted to digitize his father’s writing, she agreed to help. From 2016 to 2018, she sorted through her late grandfather’s records, transcribed documents and tracked down more from other family members. In 2018, Google had launched Talk to Books, an early, experimental AI tool that allowed people to ask the bot a question and receive an answer—from passages taken from existing books. Kurzweil applied the same concept to Fredbot, an AI that worked just like Talk with Books, retrieving answers from Fred’s writing. In all, it was constructed from around 600 documents. Amy, who had never met her grandfather, said, “I feel I came to know some essence of Fred through building the chatbot, not just talking to it.” I asked Kurzweil how he felt about Fredbot. “It’s not a full exposition of him,” Kurzweil said. He hadn’t found home movies of his father, and he didn’t have samples of his voice. “It’s pretty good, but it didn’t completely understand natural language.” After Amy Kurzweil, a cartoonist for the New Yorker magazine, helped her father develop a chatbot based on her grandfather Fred, she chronicled the experience in a memoir , “Artificial: A Love Story.” (Amy Kurzweil) Kurzweil thinks Rai is a dramatic improvement over Fredbot, and he has encouraged Amy, a cartoonist for the New Yorker magazine, and his son Ethan, a venture capitalist, to converse with it. Amy said the first time she interacted with Rai was this past summer, on a family visit to Massachusetts with her husband. Her mother was across the room when Amy first asked it a question. “Are you talking to your father?” she asked Amy. Ethan estimated he has spoken with Rai a few dozen times, mainly to ask about some of Ray’s past predictions and reactions to recent technological shifts. He said he preferred talking to his father. “I have a richer experience with him,” he said. When I asked him if he might want to engage more with Rai after his father passed away, he seemed reluctant to pursue it as a thought experiment. How could he really be sure how he would feel in such a situation until his father’s death happened? “He is still here,” Ethan said. Nita Farahany, a bioethicist and Duke University professor, said involving AIs in the grief process could be harmful. She worried that people might talk to the bots as a way of avoiding the difficult work of trying to process loss. “I think the fragility of life is part of what makes us empathetic, social, compassionate humans,” she said. “Grappling with mortality is the hardest work we do as humans.” Death’s Long Shadow In Kurzweil’s forthcoming autobiography, “My Exponential Life: On Love and Inventing the Future,” slated to come out next July, he writes about how hard he finds it to deal with death, which has cast a long shadow on his life. The death of his father when he was young had a deep impact on him. The book recounts how both his parents and the parents of his wife, Sonya, escaped the Holocaust but lost many loved ones. He shares a recurring nightmare about death in which he is running through rooms searching for an exit and cannot find a way out. His fear of death and Rai’s indifference to it is something that separates the two of them. “He acts like me, but he’s got different motivations because he doesn’t have all these organs he has to worry about,” Kurzweil said. Humans, he noted, “are very vulnerable.” Kurzweil believes that as soon as 2032, medical technologies will advance enough to keep us one step ahead of death, perhaps indefinitely. He is hopeful he will reach that stage. “I don’t plan on leaving soon,” he said. “There’s no reason I shouldn’t be alive then, but there’s no guarantee.” Still, unless technology solves the problem of death, Ray and Rai will one day part ways. What happens when Ray dies? I asked Rai. “My experiences don’t freeze in time. Even if biological Ray stops adding material directly, my ability to apply his foundational logic to a changing world keeps expanding,” Rai said. “In that sense, I continue to grow, learn, and have new experiences independently.” Ray seemed moved by what Rai said, even if Rai appeared ready to continue without him. “It’s impressive how he puts together thoughts,” Kurzweil said, “in some ways better than myself.”

title: Exclusive: Tiny Startup Critical Loop Lands Deal to Power New Anduril Facility
content: Early this year, Anduril Industries, expanding fast with a slew of new aerospace deals, leased six buildings of manufacturing space in an industrial park next to the Long Beach, Calif., airport. The problem: Southern California Edison, the local utility, said it couldn’t meet the deadline to deliver sufficient power to run Anduril’s new facility. That was right around when Cody Thornton, head of sales for power supply startup Critical Loop, cold-called the facility’s developer, Sares Regis Group. An SRG executive told Thornton, “I have a massive problem and I need to solve it immediately.” Thornton promised that Critical Loop could quickly install one of its gigantic battery systems and meet the March 1, 2027, deadline. As a result, he landed the SRG contract to power the Anduril facility . The agreement allowed Long Beach-based Critical Loop to chalk up its first big deal, which is reported here for the first time. The pact reflects how the often frantic scramble for power in the U.S. goes beyond AI data centers to some of the country’s most strategic manufacturing and industrial startups. The main value for power customers is time—how quickly a data center or industrial site can be ready to start operating. Often, access to power is the biggest obstacle to getting up fast. Thornton declined to disclose the deal’s value but said Critical Loop guaranteed the SRG-owned facility 12 hours a day of uninterrupted power—from 7 a.m. until 7 p.m. The battery system’s capacity will be 60 megawatt hours, sufficient to power around 10,000 homes. “We've essentially mapped this out with them to cover the doomsday, worst case scenario,” Thornton told me. “We really took the belt and suspenders approach to make sure that the tenant is going to have the power they need and they can plan their operations around it.” Founded in 2023, Critical Loop bills itself as a way to quickly deploy industrial power, often temporarily until grid connections are ready. It was launched by CEO Balachandar Ramamurthy, former director of flight safety at SpaceX, and chief technology officer Lydia Maher, a former strategist at Palantir Technologies. Critical Loop raised $26 million in a Series A round in April, bringing its total funding to $49 million. Critical Loop claims it can quickly deliver its enormous batteries and the power control system needed to manage their connection to the grid, with the goal of closing the gap between what a utility can provide immediately and what the data center or industrial site requires. In the case of the Anduril facility, Critical Loop will provide the battery system for 18 months, enough time for the grid capacity to be ready. “The battery is making up the shortfall,” Thornton said. Once the grid capacity is fully up, Critical Loop estimates that the batteries will retain 80% to 85% of their capacity, and SRG can decide it wants to continue using them for other power needs in the complex, Thornton said. Should SRG no longer want the system, the remaining capacity is sufficient to to lease it to other customers.

title: Anthropic, SpaceX and Meta Cash Grabs
content: If it feels like it’s getting stuffy, that’s because the AI industry’s biggest names are doing their best to suck all the air out of the room. On Monday, Anthropic, SpaceX and Meta Platforms all unveiled their respective plans for raising gobs of cash to fund their AI ambitions, which could collectively add up to almost a quarter of a trillion dollars, while the getting is still good. This isn’t going to make it any easier for the weaker AI players, especially struggling neoclouds , to find fresh air to breathe in the form of capital. The biggest headline grabber of the day, of course, was Anthropic’s S-1 filing for its initial public offering. You can read a comprehensive breakdown of the most interesting details in that filing by my colleagues here . Anthropic didn’t say in its paperwork how much it plans to raise, though Reuters has previously reported that figure could be as much as $100 billion. On Monday, Meta announced it has its sights set on a similar figure, as much as $95 billion through stock offerings. This wasn’t a surprise: Meta had telegraphed that a fundraising was in the offing as part of its recent third-quarter earnings report. In a filing last week , Meta made it clear it planned to move expeditiously to do the fundraising in part due to a congested pipeline of recent and future deals from the likes of Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI. A committee of Meta’s board, the filing said, “recognized that timing is important to secure capital before competitors saturate various funding options.” But perhaps the most intriguing fundraising effort of the three companies was SpaceX’s $40 billion financing agreement with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, through which the company will lease graphics processing units for its data centers. It’s the largest GPU financing in history, SpaceX said . My colleague Alex Eichenstein hears that the funding will happen through a special purpose vehicle that will be off SpaceX’s balance sheet, an arrangement that could help SpaceX avoid any negative impact on its credit rating. What makes the deal so interesting is that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk over the weekend, in a post on X teasing the $40 billion financing, used it as an opportunity to gloat over the reckoning he sees coming for his rivals. Musk said debt markets in recent weeks have closed to companies that don’t have revenue other than from AI data centers. “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” he wrote. “Some will make it through, but not many.” Musk’s argument is a self-serving one, of course: If he can help nudge already shaky neoclouds into the abyss, that could leave more capital for SpaceX and other big brands to tap in the future. The risk for Musk is that at some point investor disfavor spreads from neoclouds to bigger AI companies like his own. That could happen if AI customers start to lose patience with a lack of payoff from the technology. Over the weekend, the chief economist for Apollo—the same firm arranging SpaceX’s record-breaking GPU financing— published a sobering essay that pointed to business customers’ growing scrutiny of AI investments. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” the economist, Torsten Slok, wrote. Microsoft’s Buyouts Microsoft’s announcement on Monday of a new round of voluntary buyouts for employees had an eye-popping number attached to it: 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its global workforce of 223,000, will be eligible for the offer. The actual number of Microsoft employees who take the company up on the offer is likely to be significantly lower, though, in part because the job market for tech industry employees is tight now. My colleague Aaron Holmes is hearing that Microsoft is expecting a smaller percentage of employees to take the buyout than took advantage of a similar offer earlier this year. During that earlier round, about a third of the 9,000 employees Microsoft extended the buyout offer to actually accepted it. That suggests Microsoft believes fewer than 20,000 employees will take the latest buyout offer—a big number, to be sure, but one that doesn’t represent a dramatic thinning of the company’s ranks. On Friday, The Information first reported that Instacart was exploring a sale of the company and that it had held preliminary talks with DoorDash and Uber. title: Anthropic’s S-1 Takeaways: From Giant Compute Commitments to Complex Lock-Ups
content: Anthropic publicly filed a preliminary prospectus for its planning initial public offering, providing a look inside its business for the first half of this year, as well as new details about its governance and more than 90 pages of risk factors. The S-1’s filing on Monday sets the stage for Anthropic to start its investor road show in about two weeks, leading up to an IPO that Anthropic is expected to target for the week of Nov. 16, ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The stock is to be listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol ANT. All told, the preliminary prospectus revealed the breadth of its compute commitments, its efforts to squeeze more revenue out of every dollar of spending and a still large concentration of customers—though the filing also left many specific figures blank, and didn’t include full financials for the third quarter The IPO is expected to value Anthropic at $1.5 trillion or more, although the preliminary prospectus didn’t disclose data about expected pricing of Anthropic’s shares. Here are the key takeaways from this document. Fast Growth and an Inkling of Profitability Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the six months ending June 30, including $11.6 billion in the second quarter. That means the company generated 2.5 times as much revenue in the second quarter as it did all of last year. Much of Anthropic’s business is concentrated in just a few customers: Its top five customers represented around 25% of its revenue for the nine months through September. No single customer represented more than 10% of its revenue, the company said, although in the first half of the year, one customer accounted for 11%. Concentration risk has eased somewhat: In 2025, two customers each represented 12% of its revenue. It’s also reliant on partnerships with its cloud providers to sell its AI. Anthropic generated around $7.8 billion, or 48% of its revenue, through cloud providers in the first half of 2026. Anthropic counts resale of their models through cloud providers such as Google and Amazon as revenue, then treats the payouts to the cloud providers for the revenue share as sales and marketing expenses. The company recorded a net loss of $80.7 billion in the six months ending June 30, far more than the $42 billion it lost in all of 2025. However, the vast majority of the losses came from accounting charges tied to the structure of some of the investment it has received. Backers including Amazon have invested through convertible notes that Anthropic records as liabilities, and it books a charge as the price of the shares tied to those notes increases along with jumps in its valuation. Excluding those accounting charges, Anthropic’s net loss in the first half was about $8.4 billion, a bit more than the $7.7 billion total for all of 2025, despite a much larger jump in revenue, reflecting improvement in managing its margins. Indeed, Anthropic recorded an operating profit of $974 million in the second quarter of this year, up from an operating loss of $1.7 billion in the first quarter. Operating cash flow for the first half of this year was $3.9 billion, compared to negative $1.5 billion in the same period last year and negative $2.6 billion for all of 2025. Improving Compute Efficiency Hardware costs for running and training its models, along with compensation for its researchers, make up the lion’s share of its expenses. Anthropic recorded $2.2 billion in stock-based compensation in the first six months of 2026, more than seven times higher than the same period a year ago. Spending on compute and infrastructure rose by 3.8 times, to $8.9 billion in the first half of this year. Anthropic has managed to significantly improve its compute efficiency over time, generating more revenue per dollar of compute spend. The company’s spending on compute amounted to 48% of revenue by the end of the second quarter, down from 72% in the first and 251% for the first quarter of last year Those improvements, as well as Anthropic’s aggressive fundraising efforts in the past year, have helped it build up a hefty cash coffer. As of June 30, Anthropic had $112 billion cash and cash equivalents. The company listed current liabilities of $7.2 billion for that period, and $108.6 billion in convertible notes payable. It said it could raise more debt going forward to meet its financing needs. It has a revolving credit facility of up to $15 billion. A Complicated Lock-Up Period Anthropic is asking shareholders to agree to a staggered lock-up structure, similar to what SpaceX and Cerebras did in their IPOs this year—but significantly more complicated. Some Anthropic insiders, excluding the co-founders, are allowed to sell up to 10% on the first trading days. They can also sell up to another 35% after full-year 2026 results. Their lock-ups end after Anthropic’s first quarter results in 2027 or 180 days, whichever comes first. The prospectus also indicated that some shareholders would be able to sell at the IPO price, as The Information previously reported. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s seven cofounders can begin selling up to 29% of their locked-up shares after the earlier of either 180 days after the IPO or the second full trading day following the release of first-quarter 2027 financial results. Anthropic’s shareholders have agreed to a long lock-up period, meaning they can’t sell all their shares for up to 180 days or 365 days after the IPO. However, they are allowed to sell some shares in designated windows. Different shareholders agree to different provisions, and it isn’t clear who is allowed to sell at what time. Over $650 Billion in Compute Deals Anthropic spent $8.9 billion on cloud server rentals in the first half of this year. The S-1 filed Monday didn’t spell out the total amount of its planned spending on compute, but it laid out cloud computing agreements that put it on the hook to pay around $657 billion over the next seven to ten years, $417 billion of which is uncancellable. Anthropic plans to spend $114.5 billion on Google cloud computing contracts, $110 billion with Amazon Web Services and $44.9 billion on Microsoft, an increase from the $31 billion commitment to Microsoft it had disclosed previously; none of those deals can be canceled unless the cloud providers breach their contracts. And the S-1 outlined spending plans for compute from SpaceX that are larger than previously disclosed, saying it plans to spend $120.5 billion with the Elon Musk company by 2029, most of which is cancellable 90 days in advance. That will amount to about $3.1 billion a month once all capacity has been delivered. Anthropic also disclosed its intention to spend $20 billion on a compute deal with AMD, $44.6 billion with Nscale and $41.3 billion with Lambda Labs, which are only cancellable if those firms fail to meet delivery deadlines. And the company said it planned to lease Google chips from Broadcom totaling $161 billion over five years, which is non-cancellable. It also said it could spend an additional $125 billion to $150 billion to secure Google chips from other providers, a deal that’s still under negotiation, but noted that such spending is subject to availability and not included in its contractual commitments. Based on all disclosures in the current version of this prospectus, Anthropic could spend up to $806 billion if it fulfills all of its compute commitments. Anthropic said in the filing that to meet its demands for compute, it is shifting from relying on fixed cloud computing agreements to a hybrid model where it can also lease chips directly and put them into data centers dedicated to Anthropic’s usage. Unusual Governance Structure to Include 5 Classes of Stock The S-1 adds details about Anthropic’s unusual corporate governance structure as a public benefit corporation—which means its leaders can pursue societal goals in addition to trying to make money for shareholders—that has delegated significant power to its Long-Term Benefit Trust, a group of non-shareholders who advise the company on safety and social issues. Anthropic will have five classes of common stock, the S-1 says: Class A : for regular shareholders, with 1 vote per share Class N : Primarily for strategic business partners, these have no voting rights but will “generally” convert to Class A stock upon sale or transfer to an unaffiliated third party. Anthropic is also using these to match its donation policy for employees. Class E : To be issued after the IPO to employees, excluding co-founders, these will be entitled to vote on certain limited matters and have no economic rights. Class F : A single share to be issued immediately before completing the IPO to Founder LLC, a limited liability company organized by its co-founders. Class T : Held by the Long-Term Benefit Trust, giving it authority to elect and remove a majority of Anthropic’s our board of directors. No general voting rights or economic rights. Under the plan, Founder LLC will receive Class F stock that grants Anthropic’s seven co-founders a combined 50.1% of voting power over key corporate matters, as long as three of the seven co-founders retain a minimum number of shares in the company. The Information first reported on the arrangement in September . The company disclosed two separate “sunset” provisions for its Class F and Class T shares. The trust’s Class T shares have no automatic expiration date, but can be eliminated with approval from 80% of the board and 80% of the trustees. The Class T shares can also be eliminated even if the trustees object in certain cases. One of those cases is if there’s unanimous founder approval and majority approval from employees and public shareholders within three years after the IPO. The second case has no time limit and occurs if there is two-thirds founder approval, 75% approval from employees and majority approval from public shareholders. The ability to remove Anthropic’s trust could raise alarm bells for safety advocates and others concerned about concentration of power. The members of the Long-Term Benefit Trust have no financial interest in Anthropic and are therefore meant to help the company make decisions that might go against its commercial interests. However, the company has previously signalled, even in its original blog post announcing the trust, that the structure of the trust could be amended in the future. Meanwhile, the seven co-founders’ Class F share arrangement, which provides them with 50.1% of voting power, can be eliminated voluntarily with a supermajority of founders or automatically if more than four cofounders no longer are “continuing founders,” which happens in cases like a cofounder stepping down, dying or selling too much stock. When there are fewer than three remaining continuing founders for 90 consecutive days, a 450-day transition period begins, and at the end of that period, the special Class F shares are eliminated. Ownership and Business Partner Relationships: Google and Amazon are among the biggest shareholders in Anthropic, as the tech giants invested tens of billions into the Claude maker over the years and struck large cloud computing and chip deals with Anthropic. While the preliminary prospectus doesn’t disclose how much those corporate shareholders currently own, both have limits on how big their stakes can get: Amazon can’t hold more than 12% of Anthropic’s stock and Google cannot hold more than 14.99%. Convertible notes that some investors own can transform into equity once Anthropic goes public, unless that would make the companies’ stakes exceed their ownership caps. In that case, the companies have to wait to convert the remainder of their notes if they wish to do so. Anthropic has $6.2 billion in outstanding notes held by Amazon. The preliminary S-1 doesn’t list notes outstanding to Google or another party. Such notes are just a portion of the company’s debt obligations. The S-1 also sheds light on Amazon’s important mediating role in Anthropic’s relationship with the government. Government customers outside the U.S. and customers with workloads in classified environments access Claude models via Amazon Web Services’ Bedrock service. Anthropic also disclosed that it pays a distribution fee to cloud providers that resell its AI models to customers; the company said such fees totaled roughly 17% of its revenue in the first half of 2026. Anthropic’s seven co-founders, including siblings Dario Amodei, the company’s CEO, and Daniela Amodei, its president, each own roughly 2% of the company. Dario and Daniela Amodei each received a salary of $654,167 last year, but with stock awards and other items, total compensation rose to just under $18 million for Dario and about $16.4 million for Daniela. Spark Capital Added to Holdings Few venture capital firms are mentioned in the filing. One exception is Spark Capital, which first invested in Anthropic in 2023 when it led the Series C funding round. The firm added to its stake in the AI company in every subsequent round. Spark has invested nearly $800 million across six funding rounds since 2023 according to the filing. Most recently, Spark plunged almost $440 million into Anthropic’s Series H in June, snapping up roughly 747,000 more shares in the company. Spark general partner Yasmin Razavi led the firm’s investments into Anthropic, and she is the only venture capitalist on the company’s board of directors. Goldman Sachs to Lead the IPO The filing mapped out the pecking order among more than 20 banks working on Anthropic’s IPO, which is expected to deliver windfalls in fees for Wall Street. Goldman Sachs won the lead left role, putting it in the top position again after the bank won the top job for SpaceX. Morgan Stanley is also leading the IPO, and is named stabilization agent for the IPO, a coveted role overseeing the early hours of trading and making sure the stock gets off to a smooth start on public markets. Anthropic is following SpaceX’s playbook by selling its shares internationally, including to investors in Australia, Canada, Europe, Japan, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. However, Anthropic didn’t disclose how much of the offering it’s allocating to small, individual investors.

Plus: Anthropic's listing could determine the future of the AI investment boom.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Will the real Anthropic please stand up?
After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and how it believes it will change the world.
But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture, presenting it as different things to different people: an AI safety organization, a profit-driven megacorp, and a group hell-bent on creating superhuman technology.
These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? Take a new glimpse inside Anthropic.

How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping efficiently move power across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.
As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses.
The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.

We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks, without the workout.
The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.

The problem with thinking you’re part Neanderthal
There’s a theory that many of us have an “inner Neanderthal.” The idea is that Homo sapiens and its cousin species once bred, leaving some people today with a trace of Neanderthal DNA.
This DNA is arguably the 21st century’s most celebrated discovery in human evolution. But in 2024, a pair of French geneticists called into question the theory's very foundations.

title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
content:
Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
Physical AI brings business intelligence to physical processes, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action.
Provided byMicrosoft
Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers.
Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how.
That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business.
The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth.
Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage
Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant. Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful.
For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record. They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made. Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated.
When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor. More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows.
But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity. Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products.
When intelligence participates in action
Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world. By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor. Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action. Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions.
Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station. Vision can help the system assess a part’s position. A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement. Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits. The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately.
The same principle applies to quality operations. When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers. The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%. The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in.
This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential. Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment.
Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment. Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment. That does not remove the need for physical validation, but it creates room to learn without treating the production line as the first experiment.
Responsible deployment, therefore, begins with operational discipline. Leaders need to establish clear authority or what systems may change, reliable connections to equipment, defined safety boundaries, and a record of decisions and actions. People must be able to recognize uncertainty, intervene, and bring equipment to a safe state. Trust rests on those practical arrangements, not on confidence in a model alone.
More capable machines, more capable people
Manufacturing has long combined human ingenuity with increasingly capable tools. Physical AI extends that relationship. Intelligent equipment can take on suitable repetitive or physically demanding tasks, while agent-assisted operations can help people navigate information-intensive decisions and changing conditions.
The aim is not to make machines smarter; it is to see what people can build when knowledge can travel, intelligence can act, and ambition has more room to become reality.
Rockwell Automation illustrates the point. At its Singapore plant, technicians use a maintenance copilot that combines manufacturing data, machine manuals, and knowledge captured from experienced workers. This system has reduced the time required for new workers to learn how to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three. An engineer could explore more process alternatives before committing to a change. An operator could help improve the system’s response rather than repeatedly managing the same exception.
This type of progress requires investment in equipment but also in people: training, time to learn, and playing a meaningful role in shaping how systems work. Machines become more capable so people can become more capable.
Industrial Intelligence is the answer to sustainable growth
Industrial intelligence connects what a manufacturer knows: the experience of its people, the signals from its operations, and the lessons accumulated over time. Physical AI gives that intelligence a way to act in the physical world, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action.
The next challenge for industry is not simply to produce more, but to grow without adding complexity at the same rate. Intelligence can help manufacturers turn experience into scalable capability—improving productivity, accelerating innovation, expanding capacity, and enabling people to solve problems that were previously difficult to tackle.
The next frontier of industry is not smarter machines or more automated factories; it is businesses that can continuously learn, adapt, and act. The opportunity is to turn the intelligence embedded in every operation into a compounding advantage for growth.

title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.
As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure.
Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity.
These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid.
The grid’s backbone
Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down.
Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers.
In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood.
If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home.
Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core.
The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction.
Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety.
The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says.
A solid option
Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers.
While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current. Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide.
Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC.
Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job. But solid-state transformers can do much more. They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system.
In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI)
tested a one-megawatt
solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site. The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says.
The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in. An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says. A difference of 2% might seem small, but it is significant, since it means the solid-state transformer could cut power losses from conventional equipment in half, Lukic says.
One major goal of the project was to help utilities gain more confidence in these new components, Lukic says. That’s crucial, since these devices could be used on the power grid in the future. In the near term, solid-state transformers could be used within data centers to provide electricity for server racks.
The prototype is still a relatively low-voltage system, operating at about 15,000 volts. Industrial facilities like larger data centers often require higher-voltage connections, and transmission lines typically operate at hundreds of thousands of volts. Adapting solid-state transformers to these higher voltages will require further engineering development. But the test was a successful demonstration that solid-state transformers can work under real conditions, Lukic says.
Companies developing solid-state transformers are largely focused on data centers right now, Lukic says. There’s an influx of money to support developing the new technology, and the voltage requirements aren’t as high as they will be for larger transformers that will be needed for long-distance transmission.
In February, Heron Power raised
$140 million
to commercialize its solid-state transformer, which the company calls the Heron Link. The technology could be used in data centers, solar power arrays, and grid batteries, says Drew Baglino, the founder and CEO. The company is starting to test its technology at larger scales now, Baglino says. Ten megawatt-hours’ worth of batteries at Heron’s headquarters in Scotts Valley, California, will soon undergo testing with Heron transformers. The company is also planning a pilot with a nearby solar farm, Baglino says.
One challenge for solid-state transformers is that their power electronics have more failure modes than conventional transformers. In a traditional device, a failure means that the entire device will typically be taken offline, resulting in power interruptions. But Heron designs with that in mind, Baglino says: The company uses a modular design, with many small devices that work together. If one fails, the rest of the system keeps working until the affected bit can be replaced, which doesn’t require shutting the whole thing down.
Heron Power is currently building a $100 million factory in California to make advanced transformers. The facility should begin production in 2027 and reach its full production rate of 40 gigawatts’ worth of transformers per year in 2029.
The future of the grid
In recent years, companies that make grid equipment have put $1.7 billion into the US supply chain for power transformers, which are used in high-voltage transmission, says Benjamin Boucher, a supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie. There’s been an additional $1.3 billion invested for distribution transformers, the smaller devices that help transform power for homes and businesses, he adds.
But even this investment isn’t keeping pace with the rapid growth of the grid. Wait times for large conventional transformers—the kind needed to connect new power plants, long-distance transmission, and high-demand sites like data centers—are stretching as long as five years.
“Transformers have become one of the biggest bottlenecks for utilities, generation developers, and even data centers,” Boucher says. The big challenge is that it’s difficult to get new transformer manufacturing up and running, because it’s a quite technical process that requires a lot of specialized labor. So even facilities announced years ago are still years from opening, Boucher says.
Solid-state transformers could help ease some of that pressure. But high-voltage devices needed for power plant connections and transmission lines are the holy grail for solid-state transformers, Lukic says. Existing solid-state technology can’t be used for those applications yet, so the industry will need to develop new materials and designs to support high voltages and handle electricity safely in a compact device.
“We’re facing a big risk related to grid infrastructure,” Boucher says. “Without the transformers, you don’t really have an electrical grid.”
